# THE EMPEROR’S ASTRONOMY

<margin>
Center of Saturn: 5 signs, 9 degrees, 30 minutes, 29 seconds.
</margin>

¶ The Center of Saturn <note>original: "Centrum Saturni"; in this context, it refers to the center of the planet's epicycle relative to the Earth</note> is found in this way: Let a thread be drawn from Center A through the center of the Epicycle. In the circle G H I, this thread cuts at 5 signs, 30 degrees, and 29 minutes, which shows the true and equated Center of Saturn, a value necessary for inquiring into the latitude later on.

<margin>
Equated Argument: 9 signs, 17 minutes, 52 seconds.
</margin>

¶ To obtain the true and equated argument <note>The "argument" is the position of the planet on its epicycle</note>, let the thread be drawn from center A through the center of the epicycle as before. Note where it intersects the lower epicycle; that intersection is called the "true apogee" <note>original: "aux vera"</note> of the epicycle. Wherever this is located on the epicycle, count from it—following the order of the signs of the epicycle—the signs, degrees, and minutes up to the indicator Y. You will then have the true and equated Argument, which in this case is 9 signs, 17 degrees, and 52 minutes.

¶ Considering the "passions" <note>Conditions or astrological states</note> of Saturn, one sees the Epicycle is ascending southward in the deferent <note>The "deferent" is the large circular path carrying the epicycle</note>, for the epicycle is found between the "southern belly" <note>the point of maximum southern latitude</note> and the "head of the dragon" <note>the ascending node, where the planet crosses the ecliptic</note>. Furthermore, Saturn has recently passed its second station and is now direct in its motion. It is also "Occidental" <note>setting in the west after the sun</note>, because the Sun is moving toward it; for this reason, its light is diminished. It is also "diminished in number" because the line of mean motion precedes the line of true motion.

<margin>
The Example of King FERDINAND.
</margin>

¶ I wish to make this even clearer with another illustration. The birth of King FERDINAND occurred in the third year after 1500 <note>1503</note>, on Tuesday, March 10, at 8 hours and 47 minutes before noon. This is celebrated on the 9th day at 20 hours and 47 minutes <note>using the astronomical day starting at noon</note>. If this time is adjusted for the "equation of days" <note>the difference between solar and mean time</note>, it becomes the 9th day, 20 hours, and 39 minutes. If compared with the difference in meridians, it results in the 9th day, 23 hours, and 51 minutes—and with this final adjustment, we may begin calculating the motions of the stars.

<margin>
Root of the mean motion for the year 1500: 5 signs, 6 degrees, 6 minutes.
</margin>

Before all else, I seek the "root" <note>the starting position for a specific epoch</note> of the mean motion of Saturn for the year 1500, which is 6 degrees and 6 minutes of Gemini. I place the indicator M over this value. I stretch the thread to the 2nd year on the rim of the wheel (since two years have elapsed since 1500), and move indicator M there. After this, I direct it through the 9th day, 23rd hour, and 56th minute <note>rounding for precision</note> in the month of March, and reset the indicator M. I now have the wheel ready for the intended calculation. I place the indicator P of the second circle on the apogee of Saturn—which the fourth proposition showed to be 13 degrees and 10 minutes of Leo—and thus I have prepared the second wheel for use. Once this is finished, I see which degree indicator M holds in circle G H I, from which I pass along the line to the circumference K L M. Drawing a thread from the center E of the "equant" <note>a mathematical point used to account for the observed speed of planetary orbits</note> through that found point, I place the epicycle with its center—along with the cross ☩ of the lower epicycle—beneath the thread. Thus, I have correctly positioned the lower epicycle.

<margin>
Root of the mean argument for the year 1500: 8 degrees, 23 minutes, 53 seconds.
</margin>

Once these are placed, I take the root of the Argument for the year 1500 from the table, which is 8 signs, 23 degrees, and 53 minutes. I seek that on the lower Epicycle and add the indicator Y of the smaller epicycle. Furthermore, I stretch the thread through the second year of the highest epicycle as if it were already completed, and again substitute indicator Y. Finally, I apply the thread to the 9th day, 23rd hour, and 56th minute, and join indicator Y to it. Now I behold the "equatorium" <note>the paper instrument</note> perfectly set for the time of King FERDINAND'S birth. Now one may observe whether Saturn is opposite the deferent and epicycle, whether it is in station, moving direct, or retrograde.

<margin>
The true location of Saturn is 28 degrees 36 minutes of Gemini.
</margin>

¶ Extending the thread through the planet shows its true place in the zodiac to be 28 degrees and 36 minutes of Gemini. If the thread is extended through the center of the epicycle, it shows the planet's true and equated Center to be 5 signs, 21 degrees, and 56 minutes in circle G H I. In the larger epicycle, it shows the true apogee; counting from that apogee to indicator Y, one finds 8 signs, 23 degrees, and 39 minutes, which is the true and equated Argument. These last two values—the equated Center and Argument—will later provide the latitude.

<margin>
Operation for times before Christ.
</margin>

¶ If you desire to know the motion of any of these three planets for a time before Christ, observe how many hundreds of years are included in the date. If the years added beyond the hundreds are fewer than one hundred, they must be added to until they make a hundred, for all "roots" correspond only to whole centuries. Look up the final sum in the table of roots; across from it, under the heading "Before Christ," the Root of the mean motion and argument is given in signs, degrees, and minutes. Then subtract the opposite time from those hundred years and keep the remainder.

<margin>
Observation of the motion of Saturn at the time of the Flood.
</margin>

¶ Now let indicator M be placed over the root, and thread A over the remaining years, etc. Act in a similar way to find the argument. Let this be a brief demonstration: suppose you wish to find the true motion of Saturn at the time of the Great Flood. The date of the Flood must first be taken from the temporal table, which is given as 3103 years and 219 days <note>before Christ</note>. This number testifies that the Flood preceded the birth of Christ by that span of time. To find the motion of Saturn for this time, one should choose the Root of the mean motion before Christ for the year 3200, which shows 9 degrees and 51 minutes of Scorpio. Now subtract 3103 years and 219 days from 3200; there remain 98 years and 14 days, which brings us to the 27th day of May.

¶ Let indicator M hold the root of 3 signs, 51 minutes. Move the thread to the 98th year, moving the pointer beneath it, then place the thread over the 27th

<column-break/>

day of May, and place indicator M beneath it again. In this way, the wheel is adjusted to the time of the Flood, with indicator M reporting the mean motion of Saturn in the Zodiac—namely, 13 degrees and 39 minutes of Gemini. Do the same with the argument, and the true motion of Saturn will be obtained. We advise that one should work in the same way for other years preceding Christ.

<margin>
Saturn in Gemini 13° 39' at the time of the Flood.
</margin>

---

### THE SEVENTH PROPOSITION

¶ The easiest and most prompt way to recognize the latitude of Saturn—that is, its distance from the ecliptic.

BEFORE YOU ATTEMPT TO FIND the latitude of Saturn using the following instrument, I urge you to learn its parts, members, and divisions thoroughly. First, you will encounter two terms on the outer rim: CENTER OF SATURN. These indicate that the Center of Saturn is to be counted on this outer circle. The thread must be fitted over it; the signs and degrees are to be sought on the outer circle from the 10th degree of the 4th sign to the 20th degree of the 10th sign. However, when the center is less than 4 signs and 10 degrees, or greater than 10 signs and 10 degrees, it must be taken from the inner rim. Next follows the line from B to C. It is cut toward the Center into 6 signs counting upward, and 6 signs counting downward; you see this inscribed as the EQUATED ARGUMENT. To understand Saturn's latitude, one should direct the thread fixed at Center A over line B C. Place the "pearl" <note>original: "margarita"; a sliding bead on the thread of the instrument</note> <margin>Observation of latitude.</margin> on the equated argument, and move the thread along the rim until it marks the sign, degree, and minute of the planet's true and equated Center. The bead will then show the true latitude of Saturn in the area of the instrument. On the right half it shows southern latitude, and on the left, northern. One latitude is marked with S <note>Septentrionalis/North</note> and the other with M <note>Meridionalis/South</note> near the Ecliptic. If the pearl touches line G, the southern latitude is one degree. If line I, it is two. If line L, it is three. Conversely, if it touches line F, the northern latitude is 1 degree; if H, two; if K, three. All other lines represent minutes.

<margin>
The Example of Emperor CHARLES.
</margin>

¶ In the previous Imperial example <note>Referencing Emperor Charles V</note>, the true Center of Saturn was 5 signs, 30 minutes, and 27 seconds. The equated Argument was 9 signs, 17 degrees, and 52 minutes. Now, if you investigate the latitude of Saturn according to what has been taught, the bead falls on line I, which demonstrates that Saturn at that time was distant from the ecliptic by two degrees toward the south, as indicated by the letter M.

¶ It is also called "southern ascending," because on the following days the bead lies upon the Ecliptic (that is, line D E). This appears on the outer rim (where the center is currently counted) when the order of signs and degrees of the equated Center is counted toward the Ecliptic, rather than away from it. As soon as the equated Center reaches 7 signs, 12 degrees, and 11 minutes, it will be called "northern ascending."

### THE EXAMPLE OF KING FERDINAND

<margin>
The Example of FERDINAND.
</margin>

¶ Beyond the Imperial lesson, receive also the Royal one. At the birth of FERDINAND, as previously stated, the Center of Saturn was 6 signs, 21 degrees, and 56 minutes. The Argument was 8 signs, 21 degrees, and 39 minutes. To one seeking the latitude of Saturn according to the rules, it appears as 0 degrees and 47 minutes southern. This is 9 lines from line D E toward G. However, since the thread moves more and more toward the ecliptic (line D E), it becomes clear that the latitude is subsequently decreasing, and therefore Saturn is said to be "southern descending." Yet, when considering the location in the deferent of the epicycle more carefully, it is found between the "southern belly" and the "head of the dragon"; for this reason, Saturn is also called "southern ascending." Thus, at the same moment, the same planet is called different things—one by the name of its latitude, the other by the name of its deferent position.

# THE LATITUDE OF SATURN

->CENTER<-
->OF SATURN<-

->♄<-
<note>The astrological and astronomical symbol for the planet Saturn</note>

->OF SATURN<-
<note>original: "LATITVDO SATVRNI"; refers to the angular distance of the planet north or south of the ecliptic</note>

->NORTHERN.<-
<note>original: "SEPTENTRIONALIS"</note>
->SOUTHERN.<-
<note>original: "MERIDIONALIS"</note>

->ECLIPTIC<-
<note>original: "ECLIPTICA"; the central line representing the Sun’s apparent path. A planet has zero latitude when it is exactly on this line</note>
->S M<-
<note>original: "S M"; likely abbreviations for Septentrionalis (Northern) and Meridionalis (Southern) markers on the scale</note>

<term>Latitude</term> (from the Latin *latitudo*, meaning "breadth"): In astronomy, this is the measurement of how far a celestial body is from the ecliptic. While we often think of orbits as flat, the planets' paths are tilted, meaning they spend half their time "above" (North) and half "below" (South) the path of the Sun.

<term>Ecliptic</term>: The "great circle" on the celestial sphere that the Sun appears to follow. It serves as the fundamental reference plane for the coordinate system used in this manuscript.

<term>Septentrionalis and Meridionalis</term>: Traditional Latin terms for North and South. *Septentrionalis* refers to the "seven oxen" (the stars of the Big Dipper pointing to the North Star), while *Meridionalis* refers to the midday sun in the South.

<term>Zeus</term> <note>original Greek: ΖΕΥΣ</note>, known in Latin as <term>Jupiter</term>, is of a hot and moist nature, matching the best of the humors—specifically, Blood. We stated that the courses of <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, and <term>Mars</term> do not differ in their mechanics; however, because the "belly," head, and tail of the "dragon" <note>The "dragon" refers to the path of the planet as it crosses the ecliptic. remain perpetually in the North. From this, it is clear that while the <term>Epicycle</term> is carried from the northern belly (which is not far from the northern apogee) according to the succession of signs until the other belly, it is called "Northern descending" from the upper belly to the tail, and then "Southern descending" from the tail to the lower belly. Likewise, in the other half, it is called "ascending": "Southern ascending" while in southern latitude, and "Northern ascending" from there to the opposite belly. # CAESAR'S ASTRONOMY
<note>original: ASTRONOMICVM CAESAREVM</note>

It is almost at the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the observer; here, the highest point of the epicycle</term> of the epicycle. It is, however, a short distance from the opposite point of the deferent <term>deferent: the large circular path upon which the smaller epicycle travels</term>, which its center indicates. For when the center holds 5 degrees of Cancer 6 minutes, the epicycle holds exactly the opposite position of the deferent. Nor should it be overlooked that the ☉ Sun may be joined with the planet shortly thereafter, because it approaches the apogee of the epicycle, just as we have said before.

-> I believe the preceding demonstration of the matter is not sufficient. <-
-> Therefore, I also add the evidence of a royal birth. <-

<margin>Royal Example: FERDINAND.</margin>
¶ It is well known that King Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), Holy Roman Emperor and brother of Charles V</note> was born at Medina in Spain. Now, because the reference roots <term>radices: the base astronomical values for a specific epoch</term> correspond to the meridian of Ingolstadt <note>The city where the author, Petrus Apianus, taught and printed this book</note>, the hour of birth must first be equalized in this way. In the table of regions, I found 1 hour and 12 minutes assigned to the city of Medina, which must be added to the motions of the planets. Therefore, to the birth time—that is, the 9th day of March at 20 hours and 47 minutes from noon—I added 1 hour and 12 minutes, resulting in 21 hours and 51 minutes. However, since the birth falls on the 10th day of March, I investigated the equation of days <term>equation of days: the correction between solar time and uniform clock time</term> for that date using the fifth enunciation found previously, where I found 7 minutes and 30 seconds should be subtracted. After subtracting these, 9 days, 21 hours, and 51 minutes remained; this is the true and equated time for which the motion of Jupiter may now be sought. First, therefore, I collect 1500 years in the attached table, and under the title ROOT OF THE MEAN MOTION OF JUPITER AFTER CHRIST, having found 5 degrees of Cancer 3 minutes 47 seconds, I place the M index over it. Directing the thread through the remaining two years, I withdraw the index again. Thirdly, I stretch the thread through the 9th day and 21st hour of March, and bring the index back under the thread, which reveals the mean motion of Jupiter as 5 degrees of Cancer 10 minutes 12 seconds. Consequently, looking at the root of the Argument of Jupiter under the title AFTER CHRIST for the year 1500 as if already completed, I learned it was 5 degrees of Aries 15 minutes 31 seconds. With the remaining two years, 9 days, and 21 hours, as has often been done above, the calculation is made. Having performed these tasks, I rendered the wheel <note>referring to the volvelle or paper instrument</note> entirely conforming to the proposed birth. I found the true motion by this path afterward: I stretched thread A through the star of the epicycle, which cut the Zodiac at 5 degrees of Cancer 46 minutes—namely, the sought motion. The equated center was revealed as 5 degrees of Cancer 27 minutes 25 seconds by directing the thread through the center of the epicycle on the arc GHI. I also observed the location of the lower epicycle cut by the thread (which was the true apogee), from which I counted up to the index at 5 degrees of Cancer 10 minutes for the True Argument to enter the latitude calculation. Still observing the epicycle in the equant <term>equant: a mathematical point used to account for the observed speed changes in planetary orbits</term> or deferent, between the southern belly and the Dragon's Head <term>Dragon's Head: the ascending node of a planet's orbit</term>, I named it the Southern Ascending. I leave aside the remaining accidents of stations, directions, and retrogradations, because anyone can most readily grasp them for themselves.

<margin>The position of Jupiter at the time of the city's founding.</margin>
¶ The CITY OF ROME was founded 753 years before the arrival of Christ. For that time, desiring the true position of Jupiter, I subtract 753 from 800, since that is the nearest century. This leaves 46 years remaining. From the region of 800 years, under the title MEAN MOTION OF JUPITER BEFORE CHRIST, I take the root: namely, the sign 0, Cancer 10 degrees 47 minutes. Next to this is also held the root of the Argument of Jupiter: 5 degrees of Taurus 21 minutes 36 seconds. I also take the apogee sought earlier for this time in the fourth enunciation, namely 22 degrees 28 minutes of Leo. I then set the M index to the root of the mean motion, and drawing the thread through the 46 years, I set it again with the index. Then, with the thread stretched through the 21st day of April, the mean motion of Jupiter—namely 11 degrees 6 minutes 38 seconds—is cut by the thread, to which the M index is again applied. In this way I also examine the argument, and by placing the P pointer at its apogee, I have all the wheels truly arranged. There I now see the Equated Center at 6 signs 15 degrees of Leo. The True Argument at 1 sign 13 degrees. And I observe the epicycle, by reason of the deferent, to be Southern Descending. I contemplate the true position of Jupiter in the Zodiac by the thread drawn through the star of the epicycle at 14 degrees 30 minutes of Cancer, just as was once produced by the mathematician Lucius Tarutius, as Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler</note> records.

# TENTH PROPOSITION.

->### To quickly and easily determine the course of Mars according to ###<-
->### the longitude of the Zodiac at any time. ###<-

---

MARS, THE THIRD PLANET from Saturn, is of a hot and dry temperament, and is therefore considered the lord of wars because it produces something not unlike yellow bile in human bodies. This is the reason why the Greeks call it *Pyroeis* <note>original: ΠΥΡΟΙΔΑ; meaning "the fiery one"</note>, that is, ignited. I urge whoever wishes to know its motion to examine the wheels one by one. You will see that these do not differ much from the previous ones, except that in Mars, the "belly of the dragon" <note>A term referring to the point of maximum northern latitude in the planet's orbit.</note> is held exactly at the apogee <term>auge; the point in an orbit farthest from the center</term> of the deferent, and it always faces toward the north from the ecliptic. The southern belly, however, is situated opposite the apogee and remains steadily in the southern latitude. 

To find the course of MARS, one must take the nearest preceding minor century from the table, provided the time is after the birth of Christ. Furthermore, the roots <note>Base values used for astronomical calculations.</note> of the mean motion and the argument should be sought in the same Zodiac, with index M placed over them. Next, look at the years exceeding the century on the rim of that wheel; when thread A is stretched through them, index M should be set underneath again. Once thread A is joined to the days and hours of the chosen time, the index is substituted once more. This done, the wheel will be set according to the operator's will. The mean motion of Mars is then seen in the Zodiac. By applying pointer P to the apogee of Mars (which the 4th proposition taught how to find), you will have properly placed the wheel. 

Coming to the epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one (the deferent); used to explain retrograde motion.</note>, note the contact of the line of index M and the circle G H I; observe the same place in circle K L M, following the second line, through which thread E is drawn. Let the center of the epicycle be placed under it with the cross (+) of the apogee. With the epicycle thus arranged, seek the root of the argument previously taken from the table on the lower rim, and fit index Y of the upper circle over it. In the upper circle, also count the remaining years, and with the thread of the epicycle, note them with index Y moved to the same spot. Furthermore, by acting similarly with the days, the epicycle will be perfectly placed.

### How the true place of Mars, the Argument, and the center are found. ###

¶ You will see the true place of Mars in the Zodiac by drawing thread A through the star of the epicycle. The same thread stretched through the center of the epicycle gives the true center in the G H I circle. By counting from the section of the outer epicycle to the index Y of the upper one, you will have the true Argument. Having kept the center and Argument, perform the work for the latitude below.

After the cross (+), the root of the argument taken from the table, where it was numbered, should be marked with index Y. Let the thread of the epicycle again be extended through the 99 years (and this on the rim of the upper epicycle) with pointer Y moved to it. Finally, let the thread be drawn through the 23 days, 16 hours, and 20 minutes of February. If you substitute the index for this thread again, the mean argument of Mars appears on the rim of the lower epicycle as 8 Signs, 20 Degrees, and 31 Minutes. ## The second [example] will exhibit a summary according to the birth times of King FERDINAND.

<margin>
Example of King FERDINAND.
</margin>
¶ We know the King was born in the year 1503. At that equated time, the 9th day, 23 hours, and 53 minutes of March arise. Here, because 1500 years have elapsed—which constitute perfect centuries—both roots <note>the astronomical values at a fixed starting point in time</note> should be looked for under the years since Christ: one root is for the mean motion, which makes 8 Signs, 5 degrees, and 5 minutes; the other is for the argument, which is 3 Signs, 14 degrees, and 32 minutes. Having the root of the mean motion in the Zodiac, I place index M, and extend the thread through 2 years of the same wheel (for two years have been fully completed after 1500), and I again place index M under the thread. Through the 9th day, 23 hours, and 53 minutes of March, I send the thread, with the index positioned beneath it, where I finally behold the mean motion of Mars corresponding to the present hour of birth: 10 Signs, 3 degrees, and 46 minutes in the Zodiac. I note further the contact of index M with circle GHI. Moving from that contact along the line into circle K L M, I direct thread E through the point offered there, with the center of the epicycle <margin>After the word "behold," add these: Then the apogee, which is established through the 4th theorem—namely 14 degrees, 59 minutes of Gemini with index P where it is required in the Zodiac—I express. I note further the index, etc.</margin> and the cross precisely located beneath it. Afterwards, I mark the root found in the table for 1500 on the rim of the lower epicycle with the index of the upper one. Likewise, for the remaining 2 years, I stretch the thread with the index positioned in the upper epicycle. For the 9 days, then 23 hours and 53 minutes of March, I lead the same thread of the same epicycle with the index fixed, and I have all the discs of the instrument conforming to the appointed time. The true course of Mars, which is the 24th degree and 6th minute of Leo ♌, will be demonstrated by thread A in the Zodiac, drawn straight through the star of the epicycle. If you raise the deferent, you will find the epicycle a little before the opposite of the apogee; this opposite is also called the "belly of the southern dragon" <note>this refers to the point of maximum southern latitude</note>. Mars, however, being found in that place, is called "southern descending," which is made manifest by the letters M D <note>original: "meridionalis descendens"</note>.

¶ The True Center, which is 5 Signs, 16 degrees, and 15 minutes, is indicated by thread A drawn through the center of the epicycle in circle G H I. The same thread refers to the true apogee in the lower epicycle, from which if you count to index Y, the True Argument—which is 1 Sign, 19 degrees, and 58 minutes—will come forth. The use of the Center and Argument will be required hereafter for the latitude.

### A third exemplification follows, prescribing the method of operating with years before Christ under Trojan history.

<margin>
The location of Mars at the times of the destruction of Troy.
</margin>
¶ Histories testify that Troy was overturned in the year 1149 before the Savior was given to the world. Proposing the following century of this number, that is 1200, I enter the table. Taking out the root of the mean motion, which has 0 Signs, 22 degrees, and 25 minutes, and the root of the argument, which is 8 Signs, 6 degrees, and 53 minutes. Similarly, the apogee is established in the 9th degree and 5th minute of Capricorn ♑...

<column-break/>

...found from the 4th theorem, I take it and place index M over the root. From here, subtracting 1149 from 1200 and finding the remaining 51, I seek them on the rim of the lower wheel. I hold the thread drawn through these, with index M placed beneath. Thus, with that disc completed, the mean motion of Mars corresponding to the century of the Trojan slaughter appears. Then, with the epicycle fixed by a similar method after the root, the true motion is also shown, which was in the 17th degree and 30th minute of Taurus ♉. They demonstrate the True Center to be 11 Signs, 3 degrees, and 40 minutes, and the Equated Argument to be 3 Signs, 36 degrees, and 51 minutes. If the deferent is afterwards raised, the epicycle is also found in the Northern Ascending position, very near the apogee of the equant and threatening the "head of the dragon" <note>the ascending node, where the planet crosses the ecliptic moving North</note>.

# ELEVENTH ENUNCIATION

## To manifest the elongation of Mars from the ecliptic on both sides, by proposing three examples.

### ON THE LATITUDE OF MARS

I have nothing else to bring forward than what was stated above concerning Saturn and Jupiter. Therefore, without ambiguity, I will insist on declaring the previous examples.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'D' containing a detailed woodcut of a celestial globe or armillary sphere, showing the earth at the center with orbital rings and stars.</image-desc>

**D**

### Example of Charles

<margin>
Example of Emperor CHARLES.
</margin>
¶ At the time of the Emperor's birth, the Equated Center of Mars held 5 Signs, 10 degrees, 16 minutes, and 50 seconds. The True Argument was 5 Signs, 8 degrees, 10 minutes, and 31 seconds. With the thread now placed on line B C, and the bead <note>original: "margaritā"; a sliding pearl or bead on the instrument's thread used to mark specific values</note> holding 8 Signs, 10 degrees, and 31 minutes, let the thread again be moved on the rim over the Center, which is 5 Signs, 10 degrees, and 50 seconds, and the bead will show the latitude of Mars: specifically 59 minutes, Northern descending.

<margin>
Example of FERDINAND.
</margin>
¶ Example of King Ferdinand. In the birth of FERDINAND, let the Center and Argument shown in the preceding theorem be repeated. With the thread placed on line B C, join the bead to the argument, namely 3 Signs, 19 degrees, and 58 minutes. When the thread has been placed over the True Center, that is 5 Signs, 16 degrees, and 15 minutes, the bead intersects at 0 degrees and 17 minutes inclining South from the ecliptic. Therefore, the latitude is increasing, demonstrating the planet is ascending.

### Example of the destruction of Troy.

<margin>
What latitude Mars obtained at the time of the Trojan slaughter.
</margin>
¶ At the destruction of TROY, it had a Center of 11 Signs, 5 degrees, and 40 minutes, and an Argument of 0 Signs, 56 degrees, and 51 minutes. From these, the Northern latitude of Mars from the ecliptic is gathered as 3 degrees and 10 minutes. It is understood to be Ascending, because it glides more and more toward the Equator.

# TWELFTH ASTRONOMICAL PROPOSITION

## To find the true location of the Sun at any moment of time without calculations and labor.

<image-desc>A small circular astronomical diagram embedded in the text, containing letters G, H, I, K, L, M, N, P, used to represent parts of an instrument or "wheel". This is a volvelle, a paper instrument with moving parts.</image-desc>

THE image OF THE PRESENT FIGURE is different from the preceding ones. For in this one, you will see that both the epicycle <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; it was used to explain variations in planetary speed.</note> and the years on the wheel **m** are missing, unlike what was held in the previous figures. Furthermore, the use of only a single thread sent out from the center **A** is required. Therefore, for those who wish to know the course of the Sun in a few steps, let any time whatever be defined. If the date is after the coming of the Savior <note>original: "Salvatoris adventu," meaning AD (Anno Domini).</note>, its lesser century should be learned immediately from the table, the base value <term>radix|The "root" or starting coordinate for a calculation.</term> of its mean motion <note>The "mean motion" is the average position of the Sun if it moved in a perfect circle at a constant speed.</note> having been extracted, and the sum of the remaining years, not neglecting those completed. If, however, the time was before Christ, a century larger than the proposed number must be chosen, and the proposed number subtracted from it; the numbers remaining from the subtraction (which are called the "remaining years") are kept, and the base value of the mean motion is obtained from the table inscribed BEFORE CHRIST.

When you have the base value, whether inscribed before or after Christ, enter the second table titled REMAINING YEARS beyond the century, etc. In this table, for the one seeking the remainder, minutes and seconds (or one of the two) occur on the right, with the letter **M** or **A** joined thereafter. Of these, **M** means to be subtracted <note>original: "minuenda"</note> and **A** means to be added <note>original: "addenda"</note>; it teaches how many minutes and seconds should be applied to the base value. With the additions added or subtractions taken away, the result is called the "adjusted base value." This is sought on the Zodiac and marked with the pointer **M**. Afterwards, on the rim of the lower circle, find the month, day, and even the hour if you can, and express it with the thread; then join the index **M** back to the thread. With the wheel thus fixed, move the pointer **P** to the Sun's apogee <note>The point where the Sun is furthest from Earth, previously calculated in the 4th proposition.</note>, and observe the point where the index contacts the circle **G H I**, and the corresponding point situated across from it in the circle **K L M**. Indeed, that point is the "argument" of the Sun, which is numbered from the apogee to that point on the upper small wheel, and it reveals the Sun's place on the eccentric path. The thread placed from center **A** upon this point designates the true location of the Sun in the Zodiac. As we have done consistently, we will follow these instructions with an even clearer explanation in three parts.

<margin>
Example of Emperor CHARLES.
</margin>

¶ When the adjusted time for CHARLES the Fifth <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor (1500–1558).</note> is the year 1500, the 23rd day of February, at 16 hours and 20 minutes: the base value of the mean motion for the century 1400 (under the title "After Christ") is seen to be 9 signs, 18 degrees, and 34 minutes. After subtracting 1400 from the proposed completed years (that is, 1499), 99 years remain, along with the 23rd day of February, etc. Then, the 99 years are sought in the table inscribed REMAINING YEARS, etc. Once found, you see that 44 minutes are attached with the note **M**, which warns that this amount must be subtracted from the base value of the mean motion. From this, 9 signs, 18 degrees, and 33 minutes result, which is the verified base value for the year 1499. Having found that base value on the Zodiac, you will mark it with the index **M**, taking the day of the month, hour, and minute (if possible). Next, let the thread **A** be extended through it, and the pointer be moved under the same again; and immediately you will see the mean motion of the Sun in the Zodiac—namely 11 signs, 12 degrees, and 27 minutes—expressed by the thread. Then, you place the pointer **P** at the Apogee of the Sun (found in the fourth proposition as 3 degrees, 11 minutes), and you will observe the contact of the circle **G H I** and the index **M**. From there, moving along the line into the circle **K L M**, you find the location of the Sun on the eccentric circle. Now, counting from the apogee to the present location, 8 signs, 1 degree, and 16 minutes are presented, which can be called both the Center and the Argument of the Sun. Finally, the thread **A** passing through that point of the argument represents the true location of the Sun in the Zodiac, which is 14 degrees and 23 minutes of Pisces (♓).

<margin>
Example of King FERDINAND.
</margin>

¶ The adjusted time for King FERDINAND <note>Likely Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V.</note> is the year 1502, the 9th day of March, at 21 hours and 51 minutes. The century base value for 1500 makes 9 signs, 19 degrees, and 18 minutes. In the table of remaining years, next to "two years," 28 minutes and 43 seconds are found with the letter **M**. Subtracting these from the mean base value, 9 signs, 18 degrees, and 49 minutes remain. Apply the index **M** to this base value found on the Zodiac. Extend the thread through the 9th day of March, 21 hours, 51 minutes; this demonstrates the mean motion of the Sun, 11 signs, 26 degrees, 45 minutes on the Zodiac, with the pointer **M** substituted for the same thread. Finally, by moving the index **P** to the apogee of the Sun (which is 3 degrees, 12 minutes), look for the point of the argument on the circumference **K L M** (as has been shown more than once), which reaches 8 signs, 25 degrees, and 32 minutes. Having drawn the thread through these, you will have the true location of the Sun: namely 28 degrees and 55 minutes of Pisces (♓), which is what you intended.

<margin>
The location at the death of Alexander, King of the Macedonians.
</margin>

¶ The death of Alexander the Great is recorded as before Christ. The table of times teaches that it was 311 years and 93 days before the time of Christ. The larger century number for this is 400. The base value of the Sun's mean motion for that century is 9 signs, 5 degrees, and 21 minutes. The remaining years are 88, to which 38 minutes and 47 seconds must be added; from this, 9 signs, 5 degrees, and 59 minutes result. Having found these on the Zodiac, they should be marked with the index **M**, and with the thread drawn through the 29th day of September, the index **M** should again be substituted. Finally, let the apogee of the Sun be directed over 6 degrees and 20 minutes of Gemini (♊), and following the aforementioned rule, it will be found that the Sun was at 2 degrees and 8 minutes of Aries (♈) at the time of Alexander's death.

# TWELFTH ASTRONOMICAL PROPOSITION

## To find the true location of the Sun at any moment of time without calculations and labor.

<image-desc>A small circular astronomical diagram embedded in the text, containing letters G, H, I, K, L, M, N, P, used to represent parts of an instrument or "wheel". This is a volvelle, a paper instrument with moving parts.</image-desc>

# THE CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY
## THE THIRTEENTH PRONOUNCEMENT.
-> To find the position of Venus in the Zodiac very quickly without any calculation of numbers, and with almost no effort. <-

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut containing a large ornamental initial 'F' and a scientific diagram. The diagram shows a large circle with points G, H, I on the circumference and a smaller inner circle with points L, K, M. A line connects these points. Inside the woodcut, the Greek words ΦΩΣΦΟΡΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΣΠΕΡΟΣ (Phosphoros and Hesperos) are printed in the upper right corner.</image-desc>

F<gloss>the Light-bringer and the Evening Star</gloss> <note>original: ΦΩΣΦΟΡΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΣΠΕΡΟΣ; these are the Greek names for Venus when it appears in the morning and evening</note>, which in Latin is called Lucifer, Vesper, and Venus, consists of as many circles as the other planets, though the lowest of these with the index M is used slightly differently than the previous ones. For it does not carry years from 1 to 100 on its outer rim like the superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>; rather, it carries months and days, and is regulated in the same manner as the circle of the Sun, in this way: The "root" <note>term: radix; the base astronomical value for a specific starting date</note> of the mean motion of Venus, which was the same as the mean motion of the Sun, is to be taken from the following table, choosing the century closest to but less than the date set after the birth of Christ. For if the date is before Christ, the root is taken for the century closest to but greater than the date. Once chosen, it is set aside. The remaining years elapsed beyond the century are to be found in the first order of the tables; you must then add or subtract the minutes and seconds found there, as the letter M <note>original: M; for "Minue," meaning subtract</note> or A <note>original: A; for "Adde," meaning add</note> requires. The root will then fully correspond to the chosen years. This same root, once identified in the Zodiac, shall be fixed with indicator M. Then, the days, hours, and minutes—as precisely as possible—are expressed on the rim of the M wheel with the thread, and the indicator M is firmly stabilized. The apogee <note>term: Aux; the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> of Venus, which is perpetually the same as the Sun's, is held by the P index. The intersection of circle G H I and indicator M will be noted; opposite this place in circle K L M is a point through which, when the thread is drawn, both the center of the epicycle and the cross (+) will be aligned, and thus you will have secured the lower epicycle. You will then hunt for the ROOT of the Argument of Venus <note>term: Argumentum; an angle used to find a planet's position within its epicycle</note> in the third column of numbers, just as you did for the mean motion before. Place indicator Y over this Argument. Also look for the remaining years on the rim of the upper epicycle; stretch the thread to the values found, and move indicator Y to the thread. Then, find the days, hours, and minutes in the calendar of that same small circle using the thread, and let the overlaying indicator receive them. Once this is done, you will have set the entire mechanism of the instrument. If you now extend thread A through the star on the epicycle, you will declare the true position of Venus in the Zodiac.

<margin>The apogee of Venus is nearly the same as the Sun's forever.</margin>

...you will learn from the Zodiac. If you extend the same <note>The thread or line used for alignment.</note> through the center of the epicycle, you will see the **True Center** in circle G H I. From the intersection touching the lower epicycle, if you count to the index, you will discover the **True Argument** <note>The "argument" is the position of a planet on its epicycle, used to calculate its deviation from the mean motion.</note>. Finally, by adding 1 Sign <note>A "Sign" refers to a 30-degree segment of the Zodiac.</note> and 6 degrees to the True Center, you may proceed to the latitude. To understand the previous instructions more clearly, I will propose the matter through a practical example:

☚ You already hold the frequently repeated adjusted birth chart of **CHARLES, Emperor of the Romans**, <note>Emperor Charles V (1500–1558). Although he was born in 1500, the calculation here uses his "root" year of 1499.</note> for the year 1499, February 23rd, at 16 hours and 20 minutes. The root <note>term: radix; a base value for a specific epoch used in astronomical tables.</note> for the year 1400 is 8 Signs, 18 degrees, 34 minutes. For the 99 remaining years, the additions for M, Mercury ☿, and Jupiter ♃ are found to be 44, which, when subtracted from the mean root, produce the adjusted position: namely, 9 Signs, 18 degrees, 34 minutes. If viewed on the Zodiac, the pointer M will be applied, revealing 20 degrees 30 minutes of Pisces ♓︎. By moving the same, showing the mean motion of Venus on the Zodiac as 11 Signs, 12 degrees, 28 minutes, it should be aligned again with the index M. Placing the pointer P over the Apogee <note>original: Augem; the point in the orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> held above in the motion of the Sun ☉, which was 1 degree 11 minutes of the Sun (for the apogee and mean motion of the Sun and Venus always agree with each other), at the same time...

<column-break/>

...he will note the meeting of the index M and the circle G H I, and the corresponding degree of the circle K L M; for through it he will draw the thread of the equant <note>term: equant; a mathematical concept used to explain the observed speed changes of planets.</note>, and below it he will position the epicycle with the center and the cross ✛. Then, having sought the argument owed to the 1400 years (which is 0 Signs, 24 degrees, 40 minutes), the index Y should be brought over it. After this, let the index M be joined to the thread expressing the years, days, hours, and minutes, which shows the mean argument in the lower epicycle as 3 Signs, 0 degrees, 59 minutes. 

The extension of the thread through the star of the epicycle reveals the **True Place of Venus**, which is 26 degrees 39 minutes of Pisces ♓︎. The passage of the same through the center of the epicycle represents the **True Center**, which is 8 Signs, 12 degrees of circle G H I; if 1 Sign and 6 degrees are added to this, it becomes suitable for inquiring into the latitude. Furthermore, by calculating the distance of index Y in the lowest epicycle from the intersection of the thread and the epicycle, the **True Argument** of 3 Signs, 2 degrees, 58 minutes (also serving the latitude) will spring forth. Finally, with the deferent <note>term: deferent; the large circular path along which the center of the epicycle moves.</note> raised slightly, the epicycle standing in the apogee of the deferent and again hanging over the ecliptic, it emerges entering from the north (for which reason it is also called the descending northern node).

# THE CAESARIAN ASTRONOMY

<margin>The example of King Ferdinand.</margin>
The calculation for the King's birth in the year 1502, on the 9th day of March at 21 hours and 51 minutes, is as follows. First, from the second table, take the mean motion of Venus for the year 1500 (matching the nearest completed century): 9 Signs, 19 degrees, and 39 minutes. From the first table, for the 2 remaining years, you find 28 degrees and 43 minutes <note>original: "♈ 28 Z 43" refers to the movement across the signs</note>, which you subtract from the root of the mean motion. This leaves 9 Signs, 18 degrees, and 50 minutes. If the pointer **M** is moved over the Zodiac and correctly applied to the days, hours, and minutes, it will most truly show the mean motion of Venus to be 11 Signs, 26 degrees, and 45 minutes. Furthermore, the pointer **P** is set with the apogee <note>The furthest point in an orbit; here 1 degree 32 minutes of Taurus, as previously established for the Sun</note>. The epicycle is likewise arranged with its Cross. Once arranged, take the root of the Argument <note>term: Argument — the position of a planet within its smaller epicycle circle</note> from the third table for the century 1500. This root is 7 Signs, 12 degrees, and 14 minutes. Placing the pointer on the epicycle for this value, prepare the remaining years, days, hours, and minutes with the thread and pointer as you have been taught. Behold, the indicator now gives the mean Argument of Venus in the epicycle as 11 Signs, 26 degrees, and 3 minutes. The thread, drawn through the star of the epicycle, indicates the true location of Venus in the Zodiac: that is, 26 degrees and 3 minutes of Aries <note>original: "♈"</note> at the time of the King's birth. The true and equated center, which is 8 Signs and 28 degrees, is seen on the circle **G H I** by the thread **A** directed through the center of the epicycle. To find the latitude, add 1 Sign and 6 degrees; the same thread on the lower epicycle points to the apogee or the <unclear>am</unclear> of the epicycle. Computing from that place to indicator **Y**, the true Argument of Venus is offered as 11 Signs, 22 minutes, and 40 seconds. These two examples teach how to find the motions after the birth of Christ. The third following example works and instructs on times before Christ.

<margin>The location of Venus at the time the City was built.</margin>
The city of Rome began to be founded in the year 753 before Salvation was brought to the world, on the 11th day before the Kalends of May <note>April 21st</note>. If we believe the mathematician Lucius Tarutius, it was between the second and third hour of that day. However, the hours must be counted starting from sunrise; thus, by astrological reckoning, April 21st is considered an incomplete day. Counting the hours from noon, it is set at 19 hours and 30 minutes. Although some (including Plutarch) claim Rome began to be built on the 12th Kalends of May <note>April 20th</note>, this does not save Tarutius from being found intolerably straying in his calculations of the motions, as will be very clearly established to any reader here. For even if a difference of 30 or 40 years occurred (which is impossible), such an absurdity of motions as happened to Tarutius would never need to be feared by anyone using our instrument. To see the motions referring to the origin of the Roman city, first, as often advised, take 753 years and subtract them from the next largest century, which is 800. After subtracting, you will see 64 complete years remain. The root of the mean motion of Venus, which is 9 Signs, 2 degrees, and 25 minutes from the second table (seeking those before Christ), is then found alongside the remaining years <note>original: "♊ 9 Z 17"</note> with the letter **M** in the first table; this must be taken from the root, leaving 9 Signs, 2 degrees, and 15 minutes. Mark this number with pointer **M** in the Zodiac. On the limb of this lower wheel, look for April 20th, 19 hours, 30 minutes. When the thread is drawn and pointer **M** placed, the wheel is correctly ordered. Its pointer **M** in the Zodiac will show the mean motion of Venus as 0 Signs, 21 degrees, and 29 minutes. From the third table, the root of the Argument is taken for 800 years, which makes 11 Signs, 13 degrees, and 26 minutes. For the apogee, found by the 4th Enunciation, move indicator **P** to 0 degrees, 17 minutes of Gemini <note>original: "♊"</note>. Place the epicycle along with its center and cross under the thread **A**. With indicator **Y** fixed to the root and the elapsed years, days, and hours arranged as usual, thread **A** in the epicycle shows the true Argument as 10 Signs, 27 degrees, and 50 minutes. The equated center in circle **G H I** is 10 Signs, 22 degrees, and 50 minutes; if 1 Sign and 6 degrees are added, it results in 11 Signs, 28 minutes, and 50 seconds. The thread drawn through the star of the epicycle indicates the place Venus held at that time in the Zodiac: 9 degrees and 25 minutes of Aries. What, then, bewitched Lucius Tarutius to dare to place Venus in Scorpio at the time the city was founded, along with Mercury, Saturn, and Mars? This is found to be true only for Saturn, which is known to have held 2 degrees and 20 minutes <note>of Scorpio</note> then. In Mars it has no place at all, as it occupied 1 degree and 15 minutes of Cancer <note>original: "♋"</note>. Nor did he determine anything more certain for Mercury, which he placed in Scorpio, as this is diametrically opposed to the truth. For it was not in Scorpio, but in Taurus <note>original: "♉"</note> at 3 degrees and 15 minutes. It is established from theory that the line of Mean Motion for the Sun, Venus, and Mercury is perpetually the same. Since the motion of these three is the same, it is easy to guess that the centers of their epicycles are never far from the line drawn from the Sun toward the center of the world. While this is so, it is necessary that Venus never be elongated from the Sun by more than 48 degrees, whether preceding or following it. Mercury, because it revolves in such a small epicycle, is never further than 27 degrees from the Sun on either side. On what basis, then, did Tarutius dare to place the Sun in Taurus and Venus and Mercury in Scorpio? This would mean Scorpio and Taurus are diametrically opposed, a difference of half the circle, or 180 degrees. I wish any prudent judge to estimate how great an error this is in Solinus. It also comes to mind here to mention Julius Firmicus, who wrote in Book 6, Chapter 14 about the quadrature <note>A 90-degree aspect between planets</note> of Venus and Mercury; yet such a thing has never been seen by anyone in any age, nor can it be seen. Since Venus does not recede more than 48 degrees from the Sun, and Mercury no more than 27, even if both planets were placed on opposite sides of the Sun,

<margin>The line of Mean Motion for Venus, Mercury, and the Sun is perpetually the same.</margin>
<margin>The maximum distance of Venus and Mercury from the Sun.</margin>
<margin>The notable error of Tarutius.</margin>

<column-break/>

so that one took the right and the other the left, you will still see them separated by only 77 degrees. But a "fourth aspect" <note>The quadrature or square aspect</note> requires 90 degrees. Since Venus and Mercury cannot be that far apart in aspect, it follows that a quadrature of Venus and Mercury can never happen, contrary to Firmicus’s opinion. But you say, it might be possible by the rays of aspect that a "fourth" of Venus and Mercury could happen. But unless you concede that this happens at 83 degrees (as it actually does), I do not know what "fourth" you are talking about—unless 83 degrees creates a square just as 90 creates a sextile. Furthermore, Tarutius places the Sun in Taurus, which we reject as no less a mistake. Someone might say the cause is that he decided the city was founded on the 11th Kalends (rather than the 12th, as Plutarch and others wish); but truly, this difference of one day is far from absolving Tarutius (as it only accounts for a one-degree difference). Even if he had erred by 30 or 40 years regarding the certain day, he still should not be blameless for moving the Sun into Taurus, and much more foolishly, shifting Venus and Mercury into Scorpio. Ptolemy, in the 3rd book of his *Great Construction* <note>The Almagest</note>, hands down data from which it is most clearly gathered that in his time (specifically 132 years after the birth of the Savior), the vernal equinox occurred on March 22nd. If one goes back from there to the birth of Christ, the equality of day and night is found to have been on March 24th and 25th. Calculating further back to the time of the Roman city, it will be clear that the day and night were equal on March 29th or 30th. Even if the date of the city's founding were shifted by 40 years, we must admit the time of the equinox remains the same in that span of years. Since it is certain that the Sun moves no more than 1 degree a day in the Zodiac, it is plain that from March 29th (when the equinox was at the time of Rome's founding) to April 21st, the Sun traveled no more than 22 degrees into Aries. Thus, it shows itself clearer than day that the Sun was in Aries, and not in Taurus, while Rome was being built.

## THE FOURTEENTH ENUNCIATION

->To investigate the digression of Venus—that is, its latitude from the ecliptic—using the present instrument.<-

<margin>1. The first cause of latitude.</margin>
<margin>The second cause.</margin>
<margin>The third cause.</margin>
Regarding the LATITUDE OF VENERIS, although much could and should be said, we are forced to be brief because the paper (as is evident to your eyes) cannot support such length. Three things cause the latitude of this planet. First, the ratio of the deferent: for when its epicycle is at the "head" or "tail" of the dragon <note>The lunar nodes where the orbit crosses the ecliptic</note>, its deferent is carried in the surface of the ecliptic; but as soon as the epicycle stands outside these intersections, then the deferent together with the epicycle inclines toward the North, which is why it is called "northern" in the name of the deferent. The second cause is the apogee of the epicycle, whose diameter is then below the surface of the deferent. The third cause of latitude is the reflection of the diameter passing through the middle longitudes. However, there is no need for a longer explanation to teach you how to find the course of Venus, since the work or method of acting is the same for all planets. Therefore, I will treat the whole matter briefly through examples, as is my custom.

<margin>Example of the Emperor CHARLES.</margin>
The Imperial example <note>The birth of Charles V</note> had a True Center of 8 Signs and 13 degrees, to which was added 1 Sign and 6 degrees. From this addition came 9 Signs and 19 degrees. The True Argument was 1 Taurus 2 <note>original: "1 ♉ 2"</note> with 58 minutes, which will now be observed on line **B C** written with double zeros. Because 1 Taurus 2 etc. is the Argument, it must be taken in the black number of signs ascending from **C** toward **B**, to which the thread with the bead is joined. Therefore, the Signs of the Center (9 Capricorn 19) must be sought in the same color of numbers written on the outer limb. If the thread is placed under these, the pearl <note>term: Margarita — a bead moved along the thread of the volvelle</note> reaches ♋ 20 minutes, South, which is also called "Ascending" because it approaches the ecliptic. This is understood from the movement of the thread in the center through 1 or 2 of Cancer, where it immediately appears whether the bead approaches the ecliptic or leaves it.

<margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin>
King Ferdinand had a true Center of Venus's motion of 8 Signs and 28 degrees, to which 1 Sign and 6 degrees were added, establishing the latest equated Center at 1 Taurus 10 <note>original: "1 ♉ 10 ♌ 4"</note>. The Argument was 11 Capricorn 22 minutes and 40 seconds, which is to be seen on line **B C** in the white number of signs; you will apply the bead to this. Bring the thread to the Signs and degrees etc. of the Center found in the inner circumference; having done this, the pearl shows 42 minutes: that is, South-Ascending latitude, as it diligently hastens toward the ecliptic.

<margin>Latitude at the time the city was built.</margin>
Rome, when founded, had a Center of ♈ 10 degrees, 22 minutes, and 50 seconds, to which was added 1 Sign and 6 degrees, giving a true Center of 11 Signs, 28 minutes, and 50 seconds. The Argument was 10 Signs, 27 minutes, and 50 seconds, from which it is gathered that Venus at that time was inclined from the ecliptic by 38 minutes, and thus was called South-Ascending.
The instrument for the latitude of Venus follows.

### NOTE

The latitude <term>latitude: the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic, which is the Sun's apparent path across the sky</term> of Venus, no differently than that of the other planets, is to be sought using the equated Center and Argument <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the "Center" and "Argument" are specific angles used to track a planet's movement on its primary orbit and its smaller circular path (the epicycle)</note>, by the consensus of all astronomers.

However, as for my instruction here that Mercury [☿] and Venus [♀] be added to the Center, that was done on the authority of the astronomer **Rabbi Abraham Zacuto** <note>original: "Rabi Abrahæ Zacuti"; a famous 15th-century Sephardic Jewish astronomer and mathematician whose tables were essential for the voyages of Vasco da Gama and Christopher Columbus</note>. For through long and diligent observation, he discovered that it was necessary to proceed in this way.

Truly, let each person have free judgment in this matter. Nevertheless, the ancient astronomers are to be followed if you wish to know the latitude of Venus as it is written in the **Ephemerides** <term>Ephemerides: pre-calculated tables providing the daily positions of celestial bodies</term>.

# CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY
## FIFTEENTH PROPOSITION
->To investigate the motion of Mercury with the greatest ease, and to determine<-
->its numbers most exactly.<-

<margin>Another proper [motion] of Mercury</margin>
MERCURY, which is called *Stilbon* <note>original: "ΣΤΙΛΒΩΝ"; meaning "the gleaming one"</note> (the radiant) by the Greeks, is of a varied nature. For to whichever of the planets he approaches, he becomes similar to it both in power and action. He is not unlike that fabled Proteus <note>a Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will</note>, who expresses present things by imitation. For if he is joined to any more benign planet, either by conjunction, or by a sextile <note>an aspect of 60 degrees</note> or trine <note>an aspect of 120 degrees</note> aspect, he himself first puts on a benign nature. If he forms an opposition <note>180 degrees</note> or a square <note>90 degrees</note> with a more malevolent one, he immediately turns malignant himself. He who desires to know his truly admirable motion should immediately, from the beginning, contemplate the spheres or orbs, and how many and of what kind they are, in the following figure. Before all else, the wheel nearest the Zodiac is presented with a certain pointer *M*, such as was held in the [models for] the Sun and Venus, on whose rim nothing but the months and days of the year are placed; you shall arrange it in this manner: Taking the root <term>root: the starting value for an astronomical calculation at a specific epoch</term> of the Mean Motion of the Sun from the second table for the years after Christ (corresponding to the lesser century) or before Christ (corresponding to the greater century), you will seek the remaining years beyond the centuries from the first table. There you will find minutes and seconds, as the letters *M* or *A* <note>original: "M vel A"; standing for *Minus* (subtract) and *Adde* (add)</note> urge, and you shall add to or take away from the root. Whatever remains from the subtraction or addition, seek it on the Zodiac and fix it with the index *M*. Then, similarly, mark the given position in the Calendar with the thread *A*, and subtract the index *M*; once this is done, you shall consider the first wheel finished. Succeeding this is a wheel narrower than the previous one, carrying the index *P* with three circles. The first is *G H I*, to which the black numbers from the sign of Aries <note>♈</note> up to 12 are referred. The second is called *K L M*, both of which we have used in the instruments of other planets until now. The third and smallest is called *N O P*, in which the ciphers are white in color and proceed against the order of the outer ones, so that if the circle *G H I* is read from left to right, then the circle *N O P* is read from right to

<margin>Another proper motion of Mercury</margin>
MERCURY, which is called *Stilbon* <note>original: "ΣΤΙΛΒΩΝ"; meaning "the gleaming one"</note> (the radiant) by the Greeks, is of a varied nature. For to whichever of the planets he approaches, he becomes similar to it both in power and action. He is not unlike that fabled Proteus <note>a Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will</note>, who expresses present things by imitation. For if he is joined to any more benign planet <note>such as Venus or Jupiter</note>, either by conjunction, or by a sextile <note>an astrological aspect of 60 degrees</note> or trine <note>an aspect of 120 degrees</note> aspect, he himself first puts on a benign nature. If he forms an opposition <note>180 degrees</note> or a square <note>90 degrees</note> with a more malevolent one <note>such as Mars or Saturn</note>, he immediately turns malignant himself. 

He who desires to know his truly admirable motion should immediately, from the beginning, contemplate the spheres or orbs, and how many and of what kind they are, in the following figure. Before all else, the wheel nearest the Zodiac is presented with a certain pointer *M*, such as was held in the models for the Sun and Venus, on whose rim nothing but the months and days of the year are placed; you shall arrange it in this manner: Taking the root <term>root: the starting value for an astronomical calculation at a specific epoch</term> of the Mean Motion of the Sun from the second table for the years after Christ (corresponding to the lesser century) or before Christ (corresponding to the greater century)...

# THE EMPEROR'S ASTRONOMY

N O P is understood from the right side downwards. The index <term>pointer</term> P must be placed over the <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> of Mercury found above from the pronouncement. The third circle enjoys the pointer Q, which is to be applied to the middle center of Mercury in the circle N O P. Finally, the <term>deferent</term> <note>the large circular path</note> and <term>epicycle</term> <note>the smaller circle upon which the planet moves</note> are present, as is clear in the others. Having thus understood the parts of the instrument, I shall reveal its use in the usual manner with three examples.

<margin>Example of the Emperor CHARLES.</margin>
¶ When you have heard that the Emperor was born at the time of the year 1500, on the 23rd day, at the 16th hour and 20th minute. The root of the century 1400 is 9 signs, 18 degrees, 34 minutes. With 99 years remaining thereafter by subtraction, entering the first table, you will find 0 minutes and 44 seconds with the letter M; therefore, subtracting these from the root, you perceive the mean motion of Mercury for the 1499 elapsed years to be six signs, 9 degrees, 18 minutes, 34 seconds; which signs, degrees, etc., being taken in the Zodiac, the index M ought to express. For Thread A, now extended through the 23rd day of February, the 16th hour, and 20th minute, will manifest the mean motion of Mercury in the Zodiac as 11 signs, 12 degrees, and 27 minutes. If you place index M over this location, you will have perfectly ordered the wheel. After this, having investigated the apogee, known before, as 6 signs, 7 degrees, 0 minutes, 25 seconds in the Zodiac, you will fix it with pointer P, and likewise return the second small wheel to its place. To fix the third, see where index M touches the circle G H I, which happens at 4 signs, 12 degrees, 2 minutes. Seek that many signs, degrees, and minutes in the circumference N O P, and adding pointer Q to them, you have gained your wish. Afterward, at the intersection of circle G H I and index M, imagine a line produced as far as circle K L M, and establish a point there, through which Thread E of the <term>equant</term> <note>a mathematical concept used to account for the observed speed changes in planetary orbits</note> is drawn, with the center of the epicycle and the cross ✙ adorned, so that the cross turns toward the Zodiac. The lower epicycle remains unchanged until the end of the operation. Next, in the third table, look at the root of the mean <term>Argument</term> <note>the position of the planet on its epicycle</note> of Mercury near the elapsed 1400th century, where 11 signs, 7 degrees, 27 minutes are held; seek these in the lower epicycle, with index Y of the upper signs. In the rim of the same epicycle, seek 99 years, through which draw Thread F, with index Y substituted. Furthermore, extend the thread to the line due for January (for January is whole and complete) and again join pointer Y. Finally, lead the thread also through the 23rd day, 16 hours, 20 minutes, as much as can be done, and place index Y beneath it. When this is done, the labor of the entire instrument will be finished. Now it can be seen from the arc whether the star's place on the epicycle is near the Earth, or how much it is distant from it, and many such accidents. To see the true place on that night, you will look at Thread A led through the star in the Zodiac, which is 20 degrees of Pisces ♓. With the wheels unmoved, you will recognize the center of the equant and the true Argument, both of which Thread A, drawn through the center of the epicycle, returns. The center of the equant is 4 signs, 9 degrees in circle G H I. From the thread expressing the apogee of the lower epicycle, if one counts as far as the root Y, following the order of the signs, 5 signs, 15 degrees, 34 minutes will come forth, which are the true Argument. ¶ But if you still doubt, here is another way of working.

<margin>Example of FERDINAND.</margin>
The equated time of King FERDINAND <note>Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V</note> is almost said to be: the year 1502, the 9th day of March, 21 hours and 51 minutes past midday, all elapsed. In the current year 1503, March 10, at 8 hours and 47 minutes before noon, the nearest century is 1500; take the root of the mean motion of Mercury from the second table, which makes 9 signs, 19 minutes, 18 seconds. Further, two years still remain elapsed, with which, entering the first column of numbers, you will find 28 minutes and 41 seconds, to be subtracted by reason of the letter M. These being taken from the root, there remain 9 signs, 19 degrees, 47 minutes, which, sought in the Zodiac, shall be marked with pointer M. Then draw Thread A through the 9th day of March, 21st hour, 51st minute, which will report the mean motion of Mercury in the Zodiac as 11 signs, 27 degrees, 42 minutes; if index M is joined to these, the fixed wheel will be useful. Through the 4th pronouncement, you shall know the apogee of Mercury, which, held at 0 degrees and 26 minutes, may be announced in the Zodiac and expressed with index P. After this, investigate the section of pointer M of circle G H I, which is in 4 signs, 27 degrees, 15 minutes, counting from the apogee or index P; it is called the mean center. Take these signs, degrees, and minutes in circle N O P, and add index Q, which being finished, you will have established the three small wheels according to your wish. To fix the deferent with the epicycle, you shall act thus. You shall lead an imaginary line from the incision of index M and circle G H I between the middle degrees into circle K L M, where you will also place a point, through which, with Thread A extended, the epicycle with the center and the cross ✙ shall be placed beneath. Afterward, take the root of the mean Argument from the third table for the year 1500, which root is 1 sign, 13 minutes, 46 seconds; counting those signs, degrees, and minutes etc. in the lower epicycle, fix them with pointer Y. Draw Thread F through 2 years in the circumference of the upper epicycle, with index Y again pushed under. Then place the thread on the line of February (since February is also full and exact), with pointer Y brought under the same. Finally, cut off the 9th day, 21 hours, 51 minutes with the thread, with index Y again placed beneath. With all the small wheels thus ordered, Thread A will give the true place of Mercury in the Zodiac, directed through the star of the epicycle, at 29 degrees of Pisces ♓. Through the center of the epicycle, the extended thread determines the true center in circle G H I, which is 4 signs, 25 minutes, 30 seconds, just as it also shows the apogee in the lowest epicycle. From which apogee, if you count as far as pointer Y, you will understand 0 signs, 12 degrees, 45 minutes, which is the true Argument. ¶ Now, what form there is for finding the motion before the times of Christ

<column-break/>

must be brought forward. <margin>The foundation of the city of Rome.</margin> Let the foundation of the city of Rome, therefore, be brought as an example, made 753 years before the dawn of salvation <note>original: "ante salutem exortam," a common way to say B.C. or before the birth of Christ</note>. Then the greater century will be taken, which is 800, from which the same 753 will leave 46 years with 20 days of March, 19 hours, 30 minutes remaining. <margin>Example of motion before Christ.</margin> The root of the mean motion corresponding to the 800th century has 9 signs, 2 minutes, 25 seconds. For the 46 years in the first table, you see 0 minutes and 17 seconds with the note M, wherefore they are subtracted from the root. And the true root exceeds 9 signs, 2 minutes, 15 seconds. Let this, therefore, be sought in the Zodiac, and being located, let it be marked with pointer M. Furthermore, you will verify the day, hour, and minutes in the way you know, with the thread and index, when the index reports the mean motion of Mercury in the Zodiac as 5 signs, 0 degrees, 23 minutes, 29 seconds. Likewise, let the apogee, which was 29 degrees and 31 minutes of Scorpio ♏, be noted with pointer P. You shall order the remaining circles according to the precepts of the preceding example. The root of the argument near 800 years is 6 signs, 6 minutes, 46 seconds. <margin>The error of the mathematician Tarutius.</margin> Afterward, establish the years, days, and hours of the epicycle in the due manner; with all these things rightly performed, at the proposed time, it will appear that Mercury possessed 3 signs, 15 minutes, 8 seconds (which nevertheless Julius Tarutius, as was said before, falsely transferred into Scorpio). Indeed, in Tarutius's opinion, Mercury was 180 degrees away from the Sun, when it varied by no more than 10 degrees and 27 minutes; <margin>Why it appears [so].</margin> indeed, in reality, it can never be distant from the Sun ☉ by more than 27 degrees. It is not hidden from those moderately skilled in Astronomy that the Sun, Venus, and Mercury are perpetually connected by mean conjunctions, wherefore it happens that Mercury can never be further from the Sun, especially because of the smallness of its epicycle, which is also the reason why it is so rarely seen. The true center of Mercury is 5 signs, 22 minutes, 35 seconds. The true Argument is 5 signs, 15 minutes, 43 seconds, which two must be observed to consequently know the Latitude.

### SIXTEENTH PRONOUNCEMENT

#### To investigate the latitude of Mercury immediately and without the burden of calculating.

**M**ERCURY ALSO PRESENTS A TRIple cause of its latitude, which if I were to review in several ways, I would do so, but because it hinders, as is evident by the narrowness of the paper, I prudently omit it. The deferent of the epicycle has this in common with the surface of the ecliptic: that when the epicycle consists in the node of the tail or the head <note>the ascending and descending nodes, often called the Dragon's Head and Tail</note>, then the surface of the deferent is the same as the surface of the ecliptic. But with the epicycle departing from the intersection, the half of the deferent immediately declines toward the south as far as the belly of the dragon, in which place the maximum declination is 45 minutes. From here, it again approaches the ecliptic, proceeding toward the other belly. For as soon as the epicycle reaches the node, the surface of the deferent becomes one with the surface of the ecliptic; but when the epicycle with the deferent again departs from the node, then it begins again to move from the ecliptic into the south. Thus, Mercury's epicycle (namely, when it is outside the nodes) continually perseveres in southern latitude, just as Venus remains in the northern. How the planet moves according to latitude in its epicycle will be declared more fully elsewhere, since these few things completed here deny it for the present. This instrument of Mercury's latitude contains the twelve signs of the Center twice, once on the left, where the numbers of the signs are such as I, II, III, IIII, V, etc., to which number belongs the Sign of the Argument from 0 as far as VI completed signs, written with the same alphabetic ciphers. <margin>Example of CHARLES</margin> That which you will more clearly perceive from the birth of the Emperor CHARLES. Where the true Argument is 6 signs, 15 degrees, 34 minutes, and is found on line B C, to which after the union is led. The true Center will be sought in the left rim, which is similarly expressed by the numbers I, II, III, etc. Having these, you will know the latitude of Mercury on the day of the Emperor's birth to be 3 degrees northern ascending. <margin>Example of FERDINAND</margin> In the same way, since the Argument of King FERDINAND is less than 6 signs, namely 5 signs, 12 minutes, 45 seconds. The Center is sought on the left side, which is of 4 signs, 25 degrees, 30 minutes, from which you collect the latitude to be 1 degree, 5 minutes southern, namely ascending. Similar things clearly happen in the third example (which is about the founding of ROME). <margin>Latitude of Mercury for the city.</margin> For here likewise the true Argument does not reach 6 signs, for it has 5 signs, 15 minutes, 42 seconds for the Center. Wherefore the thread with the bead ought to express the signs of the Center in the left half of the rim: six signs, 6 degrees, 23 minutes, 15 seconds. From which the latitude of Mercury is found to be 1 degree, 15 minutes southern descending. But when it happens by use that the true Argument is greater than 6 signs, then in the right half of the rim, the true and equated Center must be investigated with the thread placed over it. But if it happens that the true Argument comprises almost 8 signs, and the true Center 5 signs, 19 minutes, 20 seconds, then the Center must be sought in the right half of the rim. For the thread led to it in the area of the instrument also expresses exactly 3 degrees, indicating a southern descending latitude.
