### SEVENTEENTH PROPOSITION

->*To find the course of the Moon before and after the time of Christ, without the labor of calculation.*<-

---

It was shown before that the Sun has no small shared connection with the remaining planets. The three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> were seen to accommodate their epicycles <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets</term> to the motion of the Sun; Venus and Mercury have the mean speeds of their courses equal to the Sun; and the Moon likewise is seen to possess something peculiar in common with the Sun. For unless you first know the mean position of the Sun, you will in no way be able to obtain the true motion of the Moon. Accordingly, the outermost part of the spheres marked with the letter **M** is inscribed with the name of the Sun. But, lest the order of the planets be neglected, we ask that the matter be covered briefly (for if it were done at greater length, it could not be contained within the present column). Therefore, putting aside general precepts and rules, we shall come to the illustrative method of teaching which we have been accustomed to use until now.

<margin>Example of the Emperor CHARLES.</margin>
¶ The equated time <note>original: "tempus æquatum"</note> for the Divine CHARLES—namely, the year 1500, the 23rd day of February, at 16 hours and 20 minutes—will be worked out from the aforementioned steps. The "root" <term>radix: the base or starting value used for astronomical calculations at a specific epoch</term> of the mean motion of the Sun for the century mark 1500, as a full and perfect number, will be taken from the first table: namely 9 Signs, 18 degrees, and 34 minutes. Seeking these same values on the edge of the Zodiac, the marker letter **M** shall be attached. Afterwards, the remaining 99 years will be sought in the circle **RS**, and the point **e** that is found shall be aligned with thread **A**; then, with the wheel moved back a little, the point **f** is again substituted under the thread. With that orb thus fixed, you further take the 23rd day of the month of February in the Calendar; the passage of thread **A** through that place will reveal the mean motion of the Sun on the edge of the Zodiac: 9 Signs, 7 degrees, and 18 minutes. You then move the index **M** under this thread **D**, and the wheel of the Sun will be perfectly situated. Next, search the following table for the root of the mean motion of the Moon for the century 1500; having found it to be 3 Signs, 10 degrees, and 12 minutes, and having counted it out on the Zodiac, express it with the pointer **P** of the second wheel. On the edge of the same, mark the remaining 99 years with thread **A**, and bring index **P** back under it. Thirdly, mark the day, hour, and minutes with the thread (any degree expressed within represents an hour), and substitute the index **P** again. Once these are completed, look at the degree on the Sun's wheel, namely **VXY**, shown by the index. 90 degrees and 28 minutes will occur, proceeding from **X** through **Y** (just as the letter **g** teaches); count just as many degrees by passing from **X** through **V**, mark the end of the number with point **h**, and place the pointer **Q** over that point. With these established, one may observe with one's own eyes how the Sun, with its mean motion, always holds the middle ground between the Moon's mean motion and the "deferent" <term>deferent: the large circular path along which the center of a planet's smaller epicycle moves</term> line of the apogee. Now, to fix the deferent together with the epicycle, you lead thread **A** over index **P**, and the deferent with the epicycle under the same. That being done, you send thread **E** through the center of the epicycle, with the cross or apogee of that same cycle subordinated. Finally, from the table of the "argument" <term>argument: the position of a planet within its epicycle, used to calculate its distance from the mean position</term> next to Table 8, seek the mean argument of the Moon fitting for the year 1400: 3 Signs, 10 degrees, and 12 minutes, and having taken it on the lower epicycle, bind it with the pointer **Y**. In the edge of the upper epicycle, seek the remaining 99 years. Having found them, move index **F** there, and place index **Y** beneath it. After this, place thread **A** over the line for the month of January (for January is completed) and join index **Y** to the same thread. Finally, look for the 23rd day, 16 hours, and 20 minutes in the circle representing the spiral (each day is divided into 6 parts, each of which constitutes four hours); stretch the thread through the found points, and stop the indicator **Y** beneath it (which produces 5 Signs, 6 degrees, 11 minutes, and 31 seconds, namely the mean argument of the Moon in the lower epicycle). Now, about to observe the true location of the Moon, you will extend thread **A** through the point of the interior circle expressing the true circulation, where in the Zodiac you see 7 degrees and 7 minutes of Cancer, which is what you seek.

<margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin>
¶ We have learned that the accession of King FERDINAND was in the year 1502, 9 days, 21 hours, and 51 minutes; from which I take the root of the mean motion of the Sun corresponding to the century 1500 from the first table: 9 Signs, 18 degrees, and 34 minutes, and to these I join the pointer of the Sun, **M**. I arrange the remaining years, days, hours, etc., in the usual manner. At the end, therefore, finding the mean motion of the Sun to be 11 Signs, 26 degrees, and 45 minutes, I mark it with the index **M**. Taking the root of the mean motion of the Moon, 3 Signs, 20 degrees, and 22 minutes, I mark it with the letter **P** in the Zodiac. Proceeding with the years, days, hours, and minutes according to the instructions, I see that I find the pointer **P** for the mean motion of the Moon suitable to the natal hour, namely 4 Signs, 26 degrees, and 7 minutes. You now see the circle **VXY** being cut by the index **P** at point **i**, near 207 degrees and 21 minutes; you will count that many degrees from **X** through **Y**, and there you will write point **R**, and apply the pointer **Q** to that point. Now indeed, with thread **A** placed over the letter **P**, subordinate the epicycle with the center. This being mixed, lead thread **E** through the center of the epicycle, and connect the cross of the lower cycle to it (yet let the cross + face the Zodiac). From the third table of the following proposition, you will seek the root of the Lunar Argument, which is 9 Signs, 28 degrees, and 54 minutes; you bring this over pointer **Y**. Furthermore, you will fix the upper epicycle according to the aforesaid method; with it fixed as is proper, index **Y** will show the mean argument: namely 9 Signs, 26 degrees, and 39 minutes on the lower edge of the epicycle. Now thread **A**, stretched through the point of the moon existing in the true circulation of the epicycle, will give the true place of the moon in the Zodiac: namely 1 degree and 21 minutes of Pisces. A third example from before the time of Christ I intentionally omit in this place, intending to resume it below in its proper place where eclipses will be treated.

### SEVENTEENTH PROPOSITION

->*To find the course of the Moon before and after the time of Christ, without the labor of calculation.*<-

ASTRONOMICUM CAESAREUM, EIGHTEENTH ENUNCIATION.

### To very quickly find the position of the Head and Tail of the Dragon, as well as the true argument of the Moon’s latitude and the latitude itself.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' containing a woodcut illustration of an astronomer or scholar at a desk with astronomical instruments.</image-desc>

Therefore, from the attached table, find the hundreds for the given year; use the smaller number if the year follows the birth of Christ, and the larger if it preceded it. Beside these, you will find the position of the <term>Head of the Dragon<note>The 'Head' (Caput Draconis) and 'Tail' (Cauda Draconis) are the lunar nodes: the two points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic. The Head is the ascending node.</note></term> distinguished by Signs, degrees, and minutes. After you have counted this position in the Zodiac, mark it with the index of the Head. Then, with the thread drawn through the remaining completed years, place the pointer of the Head accordingly, working likewise with the month, day, and hour (the narrowness of the instrument does not allow for minutes). The index then reveals the true position of the Head, to which the Tail is diametrically opposed. Soon after, let the thread be drawn through the position of the Moon obtained from the preceding enunciation; the intersection of the thread with the inner circle will give the latitude of the Moon, expressed in degrees and minutes. Each of the degrees refers to 5 minutes (up to the point where 4 degrees 50 minutes are completed, beyond which any degree contains only one minute). That same thread will also show the true <term>Argument of Latitude<note>original: "Argumentum latitudinis." This is the angular distance of the Moon from its node, used to determine how far north or south of the ecliptic the Moon is.</note></term> on the outer circle near the rim; this will be entirely useful for one who is about to investigate eclipses.

->Example of Emperor CHARLES<-

¶ In the Imperial <note>horoscope</note>, the position of the Head was found at Sign 6, degree 9, minute 54 for the century 1400; you shall place the index of the Head upon this. With the thread extended through the 99 <insert>additional</insert> years, the index of the Head is again substituted. Thirdly, let it be drawn through the day of February 23, with the same pointer placed beneath it; this shows degree 12, minute 15 of Pisces ♓︎ in the Zodiac, which is the true position of the Head. The preceding enunciation taught that the Moon was at degree 7, minute 7 of Aries ♈︎; by applying the thread to these in the oval cycle (so to speak, because it resembles an egg), you will recognize the latitude of the Moon, namely 2 degrees 6 minutes Southern. Moreover, on the circle near the rim, the thread shows the Argument of the Moon's latitude, namely Sign 6, degree 24, minute 53. Between the rim and the circle representing the Moon’s latitude, two letters are seen: **M D**, signifying the Moon is Southern Descending <note>original: "meridionalem descendentem"</note>, because it is seen to be moving further and further away from the ecliptic.

->Example of King FERDINAND<-

¶ King Ferdinand has the Head of the Dragon at degree 25, minute 45 of Taurus ♉︎, corresponding to the century 1500. If you add the pointer of the Head to this, and again draw the thread through the remaining years (namely two), and through the 9th day and 21st hour of March, with the index of the Head moved simultaneously under the thread, the index finally shows the true position of the Head in the Zodiac: namely degree 13, minute 27 of Taurus ♉︎. From the previous enunciation, the Moon was said to have held 1 degree 21 minutes of Gemini ♊︎; the thread now passed through these will indicate in the oval circle the Moon’s latitude of 3 degrees 24 minutes Northern Descending <note>original: "Septentrionalem defendentem" [likely a typo for descendentem]</note>, as the letters **S D** teach. The same thread on the circle closest to the rim itself indicates Sign 4, degree 15, minute 53, which is the Argument of latitude.

<margin>Finding the true and equated argument.</margin>

¶ Since nothing else seems to be lacking for all <note>calculations</note>, and especially for eclipses, except the True Argument of the Moon (for that was omitted in the previous sections due to the narrowness of the paper), it is now appropriate to mention it. Therefore, when you seek the True Argument of the Moon, you must first properly form all the spheres of the Lunar theory as previously described. Once these are done, if you direct the thread from center A through the middle of the epicycle, it shows the true apogee <note>original: "augem"</note> of the epicycle in the lower epicycle. Then, if you count from the true apogee to the index V, you will see the true and equated Argument of the Moon. The Emperor's birth Argument of the Moon is: the mean is as seen above, Sign 6, degree 11, minute 31; the true is 5 Signs, 29 degrees, 3 minutes. ¶ In the Royal birth <note>of Ferdinand</note>, the mean Argument of the Moon held Sign 9, degree 26, minute 39; the true and equated was Sign 9, degree 17, minute 53.

<meta>This page continues the technical instruction on using the instruments in the "Astronomicum Caesareum," focusing on astrological aspects—the significant angular distances between planets—and how the orientation of the observer (astronomer vs. geographer) changes their perspective of the heavens.</meta>

# THE NINETEENTH PROPOSITION

-> To discern at any moment, by means of the following instrument, the possibilities of the aspects (as they are called) or possible events, insofar as they occur within the Zodiac. <-

<margin>What an aspect is and what is to be understood by it.</margin>
<margin>The number of aspects.</margin>
An aspect is a specific distance between the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets.</note> in the Zodiac, according to which we judge their existence to be sometimes healthy and sometimes unhealthy. For good aspects threaten things with ruin, while good ones promise safety. There are four aspects in number: the Sextile, the Trine, the Square, and the Opposition. Although there are some for whom the conjunction also deserves to be called an aspect, in truth it is not, because it contradicts the definition; for no distance can be said to exist in a conjunction.

---

<margin>What a conjunction is.</margin>
-> Conjunction, the symbol for which is ☌ . <-

Although we have advised that it is not permitted to call a conjunction an aspect, since its necessity is so pressing that it must be observed no less than any aspect—indeed, even more carefully—it was necessary to treat it as much as the present matter requires. ¶ A conjunction, therefore, is the joining of two or more stars in the same Sign, degree, and minute. This is understood according to their longitude in the Zodiac. For if they should meet equally in latitude as well, so that one is placed directly under or over the other in diameter, then such a conjunction is, by a certain emphasis, more worthy of observation than others. For without controversy, such a conjunction is of more powerful efficacy. Both kinds of conjunctions are called "truest" by all, and should be studiously observed by astrologers <note>original: "gemethliacis," those who cast birth charts</note> in nativities, judgments, and all directions. Some, and especially those who scrutinize the state of the air and the accidents of the world, are accustomed to use much weaker conjunctions, such as when one of the planets is near another to the point that their rays touch each other. This happens when a faster planet overtakes a slower one, as for example, if you place the Sun in the 14th degree of Pisces (the place where it was at the time of the birth of Charles <note>Emperor Charles V</note>), Mercury at either 25° Pisces or the Sun at 28° Aries (as King Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V</note> had at his birth), and Venus at 25° Aries.
<margin>Charles. Ferdinand.</margin>
These kinds of "radial" conjunctions generally cause variations in the air and more mature effects of change. In my judgment, these modest conjunctions are believed to produce entirely minor anticipations of effects, except for the meetings of the Sun and Moon, which are occasionally notable.
<margin>How far the planets cast their rays: ♄ 9 deg. ♃ 9 deg. ♂ 8 deg. ☉ 15 deg. ♀ 7 deg. ☿ 7 deg. ☽ 12 deg.</margin>
The rays of the planets, which are also called "orbs," are as follows: Saturn emits rays all around to 9 degrees, Jupiter likewise to 9, Mars to 8, the Sun to 15, Venus and Mercury to 7, and the Moon to 12. These rays are displayed on the rim of the present instrument, next to the individual aspects of each, with their own markings.

-> The Sextile has a symbol like this: ⚹ <-

<margin>What the sextile is, and what is to be understood by it.</margin>
This aspect is good, yet it indicates a friendship that must be worked for; it consists of six points in the manner of a star because it occupies 60 degrees, that is, the sixth part of a circle. For whenever two planets are distant by two signs, they are said to be joined in a sextile aspect. One and the same planet can have all the aspects at the same moment of time (except for conjunction and opposition). You will know this as soon as you move the index of the following revolving wheel to the beginning of Cancer; for then the "left" sextile expresses the first degree of Taurus, and the "right" sextile expresses the first degree of Pisces.
<margin>How one about to apply themselves to Astronomy should sit in their study.</margin>
It occurs to me here in passing, and I would not want it to be hidden from you, that whoever intends to devote effort (at least, not in vain) to the study of astronomy should perpetually face the South <note>original: "meridiem"</note>. In this way, you will both learn the study of astronomy more correctly and retain it more readily. For to astronomers, the East is called "left" and the West "right." While they primarily investigate the swifter motions of the stars, they can have neither their rising nor their completion except by being turned toward the South. This will be made clear by the next instrument if you fix its index to the beginning of Cancer.
<margin>How one about to work on Cosmography should sit.</margin>
Nor let it be hidden from you that as you apply yourself to Cosmography <note>The study of the earth and its features in relation to the heavens.</note>, you should always wish to be intent toward the North <note>original: "septentrioni"</note>. For if you look toward the South, it will never be sufficient for you (unless you have mastered the matter thoroughly and hold it in memory). In Cosmographic instruments, the altitude of the pole is diligently observed, for which reason the North must be firmly looked upon; otherwise, something absurd will happen. For whatever faces East on Cosmographic maps or instruments will seem to point West to a reader turned toward the South, and conversely, what ought to be the West of the map will simulate the East. The same disorder of South and North will also arise.
<margin>The parts of the world or cardinal points are used differently by theologians and poets.</margin>
Just as Astronomers conflict with Cosmographers in this matter, so too do theologians and poets disagree. For that which is "right" to theologians is called "left" by poets. Since theologians, when performing divine rites, look up to the rising sun <note>the East</note>, while poets, on the contrary, in their distinctions of the heaven or the regions of the world, are accustomed to look toward the setting sun <note>the West</note>. Thus, the North Wind must be to their right and the South to their left, which is made clear from Book 3 of Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, where he addresses the Arabs moved to Rome, who no longer marvel at "left-hand shadows"—that is, southern shadows—in these verses: "Arabs, you have come into a world unknown to you, wondering that the shadows of the groves do not go to the left." <note>original: "Ignotum vobis Arabes venistis in orbem, Vmbras mirati nemorum non ire sinistras."</note> The following figure represents all these things graphically.

<meta>The catchword "Trinus" indicates the next section deals with the Trine aspect.</meta>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A circular diagram (volvelle component) centered on a figure labeled THE COSMOGRAPHER. Around the central circle are directional labels: SOUTH (at the top), EAST (on the left), WEST (on the right), and NORTH (at the bottom). The labels RIGHT and LEFT are positioned at the sides. In the four corners outside the circle are figures representing different disciplines: THE THEOLOGIAN (bottom left), THE ASTRONOMER (bottom right), and THE POET (top right). The diagram illustrates how different observers orient themselves: Astronomers face South, Geographers face North, and Poets face West.</image-desc>

<margin>The Trine aspect.</margin>
-> The Trine aspect has a symbol like this: △ <-

The Trine occurs when there is a difference of four signs, that is, 120 degrees, between the planets. It is called an aspect of perfect friendship, beneficial, helpful, and harmonious; the latter because planets looking at each other in such an aspect, with combined forces, mutually assist one another. It can be both "right" and "left" like the others, which appears when the index is placed at the start of Cancer: the trine on the left touches Scorpio, and on the right, it touches Pisces. One aspect—that of the left side—follows the order of the signs; the other—of the right side—strives against the order.

<margin>What the Square aspect is and what it is called.</margin>
-> The Square aspect is written thus: □ <-

The Fourth or Square aspect (or in Greek, *tetragonos*) happens when planets vary by three signs, that is, 90 degrees. It is called a malevolent aspect of imperfect enmity, as its rays, fighting each other, stir up a certain discord and grudge. It is capable of occupying both sides at the same moment of time, just like the others.

-> Opposition is marked in this way: ☍ <-

The opposite aspect or "diametrical radiation" is said to occur when planets are opposed from across the diameter in some part of the Zodiac. This admits neither right nor left, being one in itself, and it also denotes perfect enmity. This kind of radiation happens if planets are distant by 6 signs, that is, 180 degrees, which is half of a circle; for then they strike each other with adverse rays like opposing winds. It is better to use an example so that the benefits of the instrument may be more truly understood.
<margin>Example of Emperor CHARLES</margin>
¶ You will learn what the aspects were at the time of Emperor Charles in this way: Mark the degree of the Sun with the index, which is 14° Pisces. Seek the location of the Moon in the Zodiac, namely 7° Cancer and 7° Virgo; there you will immediately find a sextile aspect to the Moon. For if you pull a thread from the center through 7° Cancer or 7° Virgo, it will manifest that it falls in the dark-brown area between the letters *b* and *d*. However, that aspect is only "radial," because the Sun merely touches the rays of the Moon, joined to the Moon by its own rays. Consequently, find the place of Saturn, which is 17° 40' Virgo. Insofar as Saturn falls within its own limit (that is, between *h* and the symbol ♄), it is rightly said to make a Sextile with the Sun.
<margin>Example of FERDINAND</margin>
¶ At the time of the Imperial birth <note>of Ferdinand</note>, Jupiter held 7° 21' Pisces; if you repeat this in the Zodiac, it will appear not joined with the Sun, but "combust" <note>When a planet is so close to the Sun—usually within 8.5 degrees—that its influence is said to be burned up or hidden.</note>, because it is elongated from the Sun by only 7°. Mars, positioned in 24° 38' Virgo, has no aspect with the Sun, because the Sun's sextile aspect does not reach the limit of Mars's rays. Venus, since she possesses 26° 39' Virgo and is further away than to touch the Solar body with her rays, is nevertheless covered by the Solar rays. Mercury comes very close to the Sun; therefore, if you say he is joined in conjunction ☌, you would not be in error. In this way, you have sufficiently contemplated the aspects of the Sun with the remaining planets. Now direct the index over the degree of Saturn, namely 17° 40' Virgo, considering at the same time which of the other planets it shares an aspect with (except the Sun, which has already been examined); for the other planets, the method of acting is the same.
¶ In the Royal birth <note>Ferdinand's</note>, similarly join the index to the 28° 55' of Aries of the Sun. Second, place each of the planets in its own location which it inhabited at the time of birth: the Moon in the 1st degree 20' of Virgo, Saturn in 28° 30' Gemini, Jupiter in 5° 46' Gemini, Mars 24° 6' Pisces, Venus in 26° 3' Aries, Mercury 28° 56' Pisces. With these so arranged, the Moon has no aspect with the Sun, Saturn has a Square, Jupiter a Sextile ⚹ (though only radial), Mars likewise none, and for Venus and Mercury, legitimate conjunctions are seen. Thus, when you have seen the Sun, know that you must act in the same way with Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and the rest. This repetition of the demonstration has surely taught you the use of this instrument abundantly; therefore, omitting further examples, let us proceed to another consideration of the aspects.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for using the paper instruments (volvelles) included in the *Astronomicum Caesareum*. The previous pages likely established the planetary positions; this section focuses on the precise timing of "aspects" (astrological angles) between the Moon and other planets.</meta>

ASTRONOMICAL CELESTIAL-BOOK

### TWENTIETH PROPOSITION

To predict the aspect of the Moon alone with other planets—whether they are moving in retrograde or direct motion—at a specific hour and minute using the following instrument (provided their daily motion and distance are already known).

<margin>Finding the daily motion of the planets.</margin> Through the preceding figure, it has been shown how to know whether on any given day a planet was going to meet with the Moon by some aspect. For when you placed the indicator at the Moon's location and arranged the remaining planets according to their places in the **Zodiac**, you saw which planets approached the lines of the aspects. If any planet approaches a line so closely that it is thought it could reach it within 24 hours, then seek the true position of that planet for both the present and following days, as well as the position of the Moon. Once both motions are found, subtract the smaller from the larger, unless the planet is <term>retrograde<note>Retrograde motion is when a planet appears to move backward in the sky from east to west, contrary to its usual direction.</note></term>; for then the motion of the following day must be taken from the motion of the preceding day. This is because in retrograde motion, the movement of the following day is consistently smaller, as it decreases over time, which is different for the Moon. The Moon's subsequent motion is always greater than the previous one. Whatever the case may be, always (to put it simply) subtract the smaller from the larger, and the result is the daily motion of the planet. I warn you not to overlook the transition of any planet into another sign. For if a planet moves into a new sign, the position must be subtracted from the whole sign, and the distance remaining until the end of the sign must be added to the motion the planet completes on the following day. Afterward, the distance between the Moon and the planet is taken, which is found by subtracting the Moon's position from the planet's position. This distance is searched for on the <term>limb<note>The 'limb' is the graduated outer edge of the circular instrument.</note></term> of the following instrument and marked with a hidden point. If the planet is moving in <term>direct motion<note>Direct motion is the standard west-to-east movement of a planet across the sky.</note></term> (for the Moon always remains direct due to its speed), its daily motion is subtracted from the Moon's daily motion, and the remainder is sought on line F G according to the degrees and minutes. The line going from the center to the limb is divided into 9 parts—that is, from 9 degrees to 18—and each degree is subdivided again into 20 parts, each containing 3 minutes. The resulting remainder is expressed using the <term>bead<note>original: "margarita". A sliding bead on a thread (filum) used as a cursor on 16th-century astronomical instruments.</note></term> placed over it. After this, let the **thread** be stretched to the point of distance previously marked with the hidden point, and the bead will immediately show, in the area of the instrument, the hour and minute of the aspect. Both of these can be stated by anyone using a just ratio of proportion.

<margin>Example of Emperor CHARLES regarding a planet in direct motion.</margin> But the matter will become clearer through an example. On the birthday of Emperor Charles, we learned that Jupiter was not far from a left **sextile** aspect <note>A sextile aspect occurs when two celestial bodies are 60 degrees apart.</note> with the Moon, when we set the index X over the position of the Moon. Therefore, for the following day (February 24), we took the Moon's position via the instrument. The Moon's position was found at 11 degrees 48 minutes of **Pisces** ♓︎; Jupiter's at 7 degrees 26 minutes of **Pisces** ♓︎. Since on the proposed day of birth, the Moon held 27 degrees 9 minutes of **Aquarius** ♒︎ and Jupiter held 7 degrees 12 minutes of **Pisces** ♓︎, the Moon's daily motion was 14 degrees 39 minutes, and Jupiter's was 0 degrees 14 minutes. Now, subtract Jupiter's motion from the Moon's motion (the smaller from the larger); 14 degrees 25 minutes remain. Take this remainder and express it on line F G with the thread and bead. After this, look at the distance—that is, the space the Moon must travel until it reaches Jupiter's position—which is found by subtraction. When this is done, 10 degrees and as many minutes remain. Taking these on the limb, cast the thread over them; when this is done, the bead will simultaneously reveal 16 hours and 36 minutes in the area of the instrument. Count this many hours and minutes after noon on the established birthday. At that time, the Moon will enter into a sextile aspect with Jupiter.

<margin>Example of CHARLES regarding a retrograde planet.</margin> Thus far we have dealt only with direct motion; now concerning a retrograde planet. While observing the Moon and Mercury for the Emperor's birthday, it appears the Moon is already departing from a <term>quartile<note>original: "quarto"; a square aspect of 90 degrees.</note></term> with Mercury. Since on that same day (understanding the day as from the noon of the preceding February 22 until the noon of the birth) the aspect occurred on the twenty-second hour of the day, the Moon's motion was found to be 13 degrees 4 minutes, and Mercury's 21 degrees 9 minutes of **Pisces** ♓︎. However, the motion corresponding to the birthday for the Moon is 27 degrees 9 minutes, and for Mercury 20 degrees 30 minutes of **Pisces** ♓︎. Now, because Mercury is seen to be retrograde, its motion is usually subtracted. The Moon's daily motion is 15 degrees 5 minutes; Mercury's daily motion is 0 degrees 39 minutes. Whereas before the motion of a direct planet was subtracted from the Moon, now, because of the retrograde motion, you add them. Examine the resulting number, 15 degrees 44 minutes, on line F G with the thread and bead. Afterward, express the distance of 8 degrees 12 minutes between the Moon and Mercury on the limb with the thread. Once extended, the bead shows the hour and minute of the past aspect: namely 12 hours and 30 minutes.

->A distinguished document, and extremely useful for every astronomical business.<-

It has been found more than once to be very troublesome for many that the authors of **Ephemerides** <note>Daily tables of planetary positions.</note> nowhere note the hours and minutes together for aspects, except in the conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and Moon. They do so very little for squares, sextiles, or trines, just as they assign no minutes with hours for the aspects of other planets in general. Indeed, those who are about to construct these celestial figures (at least for changes in the weather),

<sig>first</sig>

<column-break/>

hesitate at the very first threshold. They desire moments of time defined to a hair's breadth, yet they do not have enough natural skill to distinguish such things by themselves. Therefore, I judged it not a vain labor to provide some common dogma or rule, understood in a general sense, regarding all these matters, and to make this same rule clearer through the examples sent before. Thus, whoever wishes to know the hour and minute of any aspect, let him first propose the day on which he knows it will happen. Soon, let him investigate the positions of that day and the following (namely of the two planets whose aspect is required). Once both motions are obtained, let him subtract the smaller from the larger; when this is done, the daily motion will result. Afterward, by subtracting the motion of the faster planet from the slower one, the distance will remain. If both planets are direct, let the smaller be taken from the larger. But if one is direct and the other retrograde, the motions are joined together. Whatever the subtraction or addition yields, resolve all of it into seconds through multiplication, starting from the degrees, which are first cut into minutes by 60, and then from minutes into seconds by another 60. Divide all those seconds by 24; keep the quotient, which shall be called the "divisor." Afterward, the distance is similarly resolved into seconds, and once resolved, it is cut by the divisor already obtained. When this is finished, the quotient will give the hours. The remainder is multiplied by 60 again, and once multiplied, examined by the said divisor, and the minutes of time will come forth in the quotient. In this way, you may see both the hours and minutes of any occurring aspect most exactly.

<margin>Example of Emperor CHARLES.</margin> I will give this rule more clearly through an Imperial induction, and first through the sextile of the Moon and Jupiter, in which you saw the daily motion of the Moon was 14 degrees 39 minutes. Resolve 14 degrees into minutes by 60, and add 39 minutes; they will be 879 minutes. Resolve these again into seconds by 60; 52,740 seconds will result. These being saved, go to the daily motion of Jupiter, which is 14 minutes. 14 minutes multiplied by 60 produce 840 seconds. Since both are direct, take the smaller from the larger—that is, 840 from 52,740—and 51,900 will remain, which, divided by 24, gives 2,162, which will be the divisor. Now approaching the distance, which is 10 degrees 10 minutes, resolve this also into seconds, and there will be 36,600 seconds. Dividing those by the divisor 2,162, you will have 16 in the quotient for the hours. After they have stuck in the remainder, resolve 2,018 again into minutes, whereby 121,080 result; repeat these by the divisor, and the quotient yields 56 minutes. Thus, 16 hours 56 minutes, counted after noon, define the sextile aspect of the Moon ☽ and Jupiter ♃. Now I will repeat this for the Moon ☽ and Mercury ☿, which we do more gladly because Mercury is retrograde. The Moon's daily motion is 15 degrees 5 minutes; resolved, they make 54,300 seconds. We know Mercury's daily motion is 39 minutes, which resolved similarly are 2,340 seconds. Because Mercury is retrograde, the seconds of both planets must be added according to the rule; from these combined, 56,640 result. After division, these produce 2,360, which will be the divisor thereafter. The distance is then resolved in the same way; namely 8 degrees 12 minutes resolved make 29,520. These being divided give 12 hours, and the remainder 1,200, which if reduced again to seconds by 60 and divided, will cause 30 minutes of an hour. Therefore, the hours of this aspect appear to be 12 hours 30 minutes in the afternoon.

<margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin> But lest I depart entirely from the proposal I have solved so far, I will also bring the King's birthday into the demonstration, through which the aspect may similarly be learned. King Ferdinand is known to have been born on March 10 before noon. It is known that on that day the Moon looks upon the other planets. We first consider the motion of the Moon; it is clear it was 20 degrees 10 minutes of **Cancer** ♋︎. Now if you apply the index X of the earlier instrument to this degree and minute, and distribute any of the others in their places, you will see that Mars is almost opposite the Moon, being carried in 23 degrees 37 minutes of **Capricorn** ♑︎. Because you see no occurrence of an aspect so near as this, take the Moon's position of the following day for examination, which is 2 degrees 26 minutes of **Leo** ♌︎, and the position of Mars on the same following day, namely February 10 <note>The text says "10 Februarii" here, though the context started with March; this is likely a printer's error in the original Latin for March 11.</note>, 24 degrees 24 minutes of **Capricorn** ♑︎. Seek the daily motions of both; the Moon's daily motion will be 12 degrees 16 minutes. The daily motion of Mars has 0 degrees 47 minutes. With the motion of Mars taken from the motion of the Moon, the distance remains, namely 3 degrees 27 minutes. Because Mars is direct, let it be subtracted from the Moon, and let 11 degrees 29 minutes remain, which are marked on line F G with the thread and bead. With the thread stretched again to the distance, which makes 3 degrees 27 minutes, the bead reports 7 hours 12 minutes after noon of the 9th day of February <note>Again, the month names in the Latin text are inconsistent with the starting date of March 10; the mechanics of the calculation remain the focus.</note>, when the exact opposition of the Moon and Mars took place. Before I finish, I wish the student of astronomy to be advised: whenever he is to deliver any judgment on astronomical matters, let him perpetually collect the course of each planet, the <term>Head and Tail of the Dragon<note>The lunar nodes: the points where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note></term>, as seen in the Ephemerides, for the noons of both the present and following day. In this way, everything will be ready and at hand, as they say.

# THE TWENTY-FIRST PROPOSITION

### How to determine the alignments of all planets with one another, except for the Moon, using the present instrument.

One should not demand anything more curious regarding the use of the diagram, as it has been sufficiently and abundantly established before; nevertheless, so that you do not have to wander too far back to previous sections, I will explain the practice of this instrument in a single word. To understand the hour and minute of any <term>aspect<note>An 'aspect' is an angle or alignment between planets that astrologers believe influences earthly events.</note></term>, first consider the possibility of it by the help of the 19th proposition—that is, whether an aspect can occur on your appointed day. This is done in the following way: The index X is moved to the positions of the planets; if any of the planets touches the lines of the aspects or falls near their boundaries, it is said to be "aspected" by another; if not, then no. By this act, you will abundantly know what you intended to find. Therefore, the "two-day courses" of the planets, as we said before—that is, the motion of two days—must be prepared, from which a truer knowledge of the aspects arises. When you are certain of some aspect occurring on whatever future day, observe the locations of those planets in the Zodiac. Align them to the beginning and end of that day—that is, to the preceding noon and the following noon—from which you will hunt for the daily motions of the planets without difficulty. If both are <term>direct or retrograde<note>'Direct' motion is the standard west-to-east path; 'retrograde' is the apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky.</note></term>, you will subtract the smaller from the larger; if one goes backward and the other forward, you combine both. You will seek the remainder of the subtraction or addition on the line FG, and you will add the found union upon it. Soon you will require the distance of the planets and express it on the counted rim with a string held tight; while holding this, you will observe the position of the <term>margarita<note>Original: "margarita." In these paper instruments, a 'margarita' (literally 'pearl') was a small bead slid along a string to mark a specific point on the scales.</note></term> among the hour lines, for there you will see both the hours and minutes of the aspect, whether past or future.

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram or volvelle base featuring a central point with radiating lines and multiple concentric scales. The outer scales are marked with degrees (10, 20, 30...) and segments. Within the circle, there are horizontal and vertical coordinate lines labeled with letters like F and G at the axes.</image-desc>

<margin>
The example of Emperor CHARLES.
</margin>
You may learn this even more clearly from the example of the Emperor. The Divine Charles, forever Augustus, took up the Roman Empire at Frankfurt am Main in the year of our Lord 1519, on the 28th day of June. On that day, I labor to know the planetary aspects. I therefore seek all the locations of the planets for the noons of the 27th and 28th days (I specifically say the 27th preceding and not the following, for I seek the morning aspects of the 28th day; whereas if I wanted the afternoon ones, I would examine the motion of the 29th day with the 28th). Having found these, I approach the instrument according to the rule of Proposition 19, and I see that there are no radiations between the planets except for Jupiter and Venus. Now, desiring to know the hour and minute of that aspect, I mark the motion of Jupiter for the 27th day, which is 11 degrees and 35 minutes of Cancer <note>Original: ♋</note>. And for the 28th day, at which it was 11 degrees and 40 minutes of Cancer. I also find and record the position of Venus on the 27th day at 10 degrees and 34 minutes of Cancer, and on the 28th day at 11 degrees and 46 minutes of Cancer. When I have the daily motion of each by subtraction—Jupiter being 5 minutes and Venus being 1 degree and 12 minutes—I subtract the smaller (5 minutes) from the larger (1 degree and 12 minutes), because both are moving direct. Finding the remainder to be 1 degree and 7 minutes, I mark it on the line FG with the union. After this, I subtract the position of Venus (10 degrees 34 minutes) from the position of Jupiter (11 degrees 35 minutes); there remains the distance called 1 degree and 1 minute. When this is counted on the rim and expressed with the string, the bead demonstrates 21 hours and 39 minutes after the noon of the 27th day. If I reduce this to our hours, I find this aspect of Jupiter and Venus was at 9:39 in the morning on the 28th day of June.

<margin>
The <term>Sextile<note>An aspect of 60 degrees, considered harmonious and beneficial.</note></term> of Jupiter and Venus at the time of the election of Emperor Charles V.
</margin>
No one will fail to admit that the stars showed themselves so kindly to the Emperor for this reason. For the astrologers of old certainly knew and proved that the Sextile and <term>Trine<note>An aspect of 120 degrees, also considered very fortunate.</note></term> portended dignities, powers, and majesty. That this was true in the election of Charles V can be understood more certainly than certainty itself. Add to this that not only did a sextile of Jupiter and Venus occur between themselves—both being most happy planets—but also a sextile of the Moon and Jupiter, and a conjunction of the Moon and Venus concurred on that same day of his creation. Thus, one might not wrongly affirm that heaven itself desired Charles as Emperor. We will also teach how to perform this same task through numbers, if perhaps anyone prefers it that way. The daily motion of Jupiter (5 minutes) resolved into seconds makes 300; the motion of Venus (1 degree 12 minutes) dissolved makes 4,320 seconds. With the smaller number now subtracted from the larger due to both being in direct motion, 4,020 seconds remain; these, divided by 24, yield a divisor of 167. The distance, namely 1 degree and 1 minute, is regulated by a similar process. Multiplied, it gives 36,600 seconds, which, when shared with the divisor, leaves 21 hours. The remaining 53, likewise dissolved and divided, returns 19 minutes. This being done, it is clear whether or not you have worked well with the instrument. If, however, a different result occurs in either part—whether by the work of the instrument or the work of calculation—be certain that you have erred, for when both agree, neither is wrong. No one studious of this art should fail to embrace this rule vehemently, since it brings admirable use to the Ephemerides <note>Tables showing the predicted positions of celestial bodies.</note>.

<margin>
New investigation of aspects through numbers.
</margin>

<margin>
The example of King FERDINAND.
</margin>
Another example. On the birthday of King Ferdinand, specifically March 9th, an aspect of Saturn and the Sun was found from Proposition 19. The motion of Saturn on the 9th day is 28 degrees and 35 minutes of Pisces <note>Original: ♓</note>. On the 10th day, it is 28 degrees and 37 minutes of Pisces. The motion of the Sun on the 9th day is 28 degrees and 5 minutes of Pisces. On the 10th day, 29 degrees and 0 minutes of Pisces. You find the daily motion of Saturn to be 2 minutes, and the Sun's to be 55 minutes; therefore, subtracting the smaller, as both are direct, 53 minutes remain. Once sought, let the union express this on the line FG. After that, the distance, which is 0 degrees and 34 minutes, is taken on the rim and marked with the string extended; let the bead be observed noting 14 hours and 22 minutes; for so much

<column-break/>

time after noon do Saturn and the Sun claim for themselves, which is the 2nd hour of the 10th day, 22 minutes before midnight. I will prove this same thing further through calculation. The distance of the Sun and Saturn was 34 minutes. The daily motions of both were: Sun 59 minutes, Saturn 2 minutes. I advise that you know these three things as especially necessary. Now therefore, since they are direct, I subtract 2 from 59, and 57 are left, which, reduced again into seconds, make 3,420; divide the same by 24, and the divisor will arise. Similarly, multiply the distance of 34 by 60, and 2,040 will result. Distribute these with the already known divisor, and 14 hours are redundant. Divide the remainder of 52, multiplied again, and 22 clock minutes will come forth. Thus you cannot be deceived, and you may dare to assert certainly that this conjunction occurs at 14 hours and 22 minutes. I did not add this rule so that you must use it in movements that are quite sluggish and close to each other, but for the sake of faster planets and those very far apart, so that nothing at all might seem to be missing in this part for the perfect investigation of motions.

¶ In the previous proposition, we enumerated the more general distinctions of aspects, and those which are called principal. Now, however, we will review the more specific and, if you prefer, less principal differences. These are of this kind: Combustion, Oppression, Vacancy, Besiegment, Application, Separation, Prohibition, Translation of light, and its relation or, so to speak, Restoration, Pulsation, Reception, etc.

->**Combustion**<-

¶ A planet is said to be in **Combustion** when it is positioned less than 15 degrees away from the Sun on either side; for the solar orb contains that many degrees, and within that interval, it most powerfully pours out its rays everywhere.

->**Oppression**<-

¶ A planet is called **Oppressed** when it is less than 12 degrees away from the Sun; this, however, does not need explanation, as it is obvious to everyone.

->**Vacancy**<-

¶ we call a planet **Vacant** by reason of its course; for it is vacant when it exits from one aspect and does not slide directly into another, but proceeds deprived of all radiation. <note>Often referred to today as 'Void of Course.'</note>

->**Besiegment**<-

¶ **Besiegment** is a name, as if an occupation and irritation, when it runs from the aspect of one more malignant planet into the aspect of another planet, also malignant (Saturn and Mars are called the "bad" planets); for thus it is carried from one evil to another, as if against its will. For example, if the Moon is joined with Mars, and departing from Mars it falls upon Saturn, which would happen if the Moon and Mars held the beginning of Cancer, and Saturn held the third or fourth degree of Libra; for in this way the Moon would seem to add evil to evil, and therefore would be called "besieged," a term accepted among those skilled in the stars.

->**Application**<-

¶ **Application** happens between two planets whenever they are distant from each other by so much that the swifter in its course can reach the orbs of the slower with its center—that is, reach the slower one with its own center's orb. Then the faster is said to "apply" itself to the slower. For instance, Jupiter projects its rays for 9 degrees; if Mars, which is swifter in motion (provided it was not retrograde), is distant by that much space, it now touches the rays of Jupiter and is said to be "applying" to the same, because it seeks to be joined to Jupiter. Ptolemy, however, does not allow it to be called application except through a distance of 3 degrees. It should be known, moreover, that application usually occurs not only in conjunctions but also in other aspects.

->**Separation**<-

¶ **Separation** is plainly the opposite of the former. Separation occurs when the planets depart from conjunctions, and the faster moves entirely away from the slower (so that it no longer touches the other with its rays)—that is, it is separated or flows away. Some examine this even more precisely and want the faster to be "separated" after it is removed from the slow one by only a single minute. More differences of aspects or "passions" can still be reviewed, such as Pulsation, Translation of light, etc.; but because they do nothing for the present matters, I omit them. If it pleases you to read them, they are available in chapter 7 of the book of <term>Avenezre<note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar whose works on astrology were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note></term>.

# CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY

## THE TWENTY-SECOND PROPOSITION.

*To perceive easily, throughout the entire course of time—both before and after the birth of Christ—the Conjunctions, Oppositions, and middle Quarters of the Sun and Moon, from which one may recognize an eclipse of the Sun at the New Moon, or a defect of the Moon at the Full Moon.*

<margin>Method of operation</margin>
Since it is established that the Sun and Moon exist as the primary sources of nature and the most powerful causes of all things—both those coming into being and those passing away—and since they best pour out their powers, virtues, and effects into nature when they are least obstructed, but conversely languish, are hindered, and even corrupt nature when something stands in their way, we have judged that those obstacles <note>meaning eclipses</note> ought to be considered with great care and not without utility. For this reason, we have chosen to treat the oppositions <note>Full Moons</note> and mean conjunctions <note>New Moons</note> of the Sun and Moon, as well as eclipses, by which the affairs of the world are altered beyond dispute, more diligently in this place. However, because it was not possible to include all these matters in a single instrument, I have been forced to distribute them among several; partly so that nothing at all would be left to be figured out with difficulty, and partly so that the examination of the matter would be more exact and complete. Accordingly, we have subordinated these four following instruments in a continuous series, as if they were linked together. Indeed, if the hour of the Conjunction or Opposition (the use of which is primary in making judgments, specifically regarding those things which happen in the world) is not held precisely, it is impossible to construct a true figure of the heavens <note>a horoscope or celestial map</note>, and much less to establish a certain judgment concerning affairs; therefore, I wished to be quite careful in this section.

Whoever wishes to know the Conjunction of the Sun and Moon, or the Moon and the Dragon’s Head <note>the North Node of the Moon, where eclipses occur</note>, should consider the present instrument, composed of four disks and a certain Calendar. The first disk, which is the lowest, carries an index for the Dragon’s Head (☊), where you see years inscribed from 1 to 100—though arranged in a jumbled order—the use of which is required for seeking conjunctions and oppositions. The second disk, with the Moon indicator, similarly shows years from 1 to 100 and is suited for investigating the conjunctions of the Moon and the Dragon’s Head. The third wheel is marked by the Aries (♈) index; on its circumference, little black circles like this 🌑 appear here and there together with the conjunction symbol ☌, marking the unions of the Sun and Moon. Just as in the images on the plate, these symbols 🌑 🌒 🌓 🌔 and the horned crescents 🌓 represent the quarters of the luminaries. The fourth disk embraces the Aries (♈) pointer and several Dragon’s Heads and Tails, the method for using which follows.

To know the conjunctions, oppositions, or quarters of the Sun and Moon, a "root" <note>a base astronomical value</note> must be taken from the attached table, choosing the century root closest to but less than the target year. In this way: on the left side, look for the century preceding the proposed year; immediately next to it, on the right, the days, hours, and minutes of the conjunction will present themselves. You will search for these same values in the January section of the instrument, with the Aries (♈) index first moved over it; this January setting will remain fixed until the end of the operation. Likewise, choose a root for the Moon and the Dragon’s Head from the second table, where the neighboring days, hours, and minutes are taken as before; seek these in the January section of the rim and fix them with the Dragon's Head (☊) indicator. Now secure both disks with wax, otherwise they will not stay properly in place. Indeed, these instruments can rarely last for a full hundred years if one requires a time other than that century. Now, look for the proposed and current year on the surface of the Aries (♈) wheel, and stretch a thread through it, with the Aries (♈) pointer located at the 14th, 15th, or 16th day of January. From there, the operator must see which New Moon (🌑) or Conjunction (☌) of the third wheel is closest to the thread, and it should be brought under the thread; once brought under, the wheels will finally be arranged according to your wish.

If it should happen that two conjunctions are equidistant from the thread on either side, then you may act at your discretion and place whichever one you like under the thread without distinction. Only remember that the Aries (♈) index must always be moved to January, not to February or December. After this, move the thread to whichever conjunction, opposition, or quadrature you prefer, and it will immediately report that day of the future or past aspect on the rim of the Calendar.

There are, however, three things worthy of notice here. First, that in a leap year <note>original: "anno bissextili"</note>, it may not accurately show the Conjunction, Opposition, or New Moon from February 24th until the end of the year; for that reason, one day must always be subtracted—that is, from the day of the conjunction or opposition—and once subtracted, the sought result emerges. Second, if a Conjunction ☌ with a clover ♣ mark indicates December, it is considered as nothing; but if it falls in January, the day must be kept according to the aforesaid rules, for that is called the first opposition of the passing year. Third, a conjunction ☌ with a cross ✝ symbol that falls in December is the very last of the current or proposed year; but that which touches January will be entirely useless. This matter will be made easier by this method:

In the observation of judgments, astronomers studiously prepare figures of conjunctions or "preventions"—that is, those which immediately precede births. Therefore, we will teach, by way of example, a certain way to complete the conjunction of the luminaries immediately prior to the birth of the Emperor Charles. From the table of numbers (that is, the one containing the Roots), first seek the root for the conjunction for the current year 1500, in which CHARLES is said to have been born. You find Day 0, Hour 22, Minute 54. <note>In 1500, the future Holy Roman Emperor Charles V was born.</note>

<margin>Caution to be observed in a Leap Year.</margin>

->ASTRONOMIA CAESAREA<-

# THE TWENTY-SECOND PROPOSITION

To clearly perceive, without labor, the conjunctions, oppositions, and middle quadratures <note>The four main phases of the moon: New Moon, Full Moon, and the two Half-Moons.</note> of the Sun and Moon throughout the entire course of time, both before and after Christ, from which a defect <note>original: "defectus"; an eclipse.</note> of the Sun at the New Moon or of the Moon at the Full Moon is recognized.

Since it is well-established that the Sun and Moon exist as the primary sources of nature and the most powerful causes of all things—both those coming into being and those passing away—their powers, virtues, and effects are best poured into nature when they are least hindered. Conversely, when something stands in their way, nature is impeded, becomes languid, and is even corrupted. Therefore, we have judged it not unprofitable to carefully consider those obstacles. For this reason, we have chosen to treat more diligently in this place the conjunctions (☌), middle oppositions, and eclipses, by which the affairs of the world are altered beyond dispute. However, because it was not possible to encompass all these matters in a single instrument, I was forced to distribute them among several; partly so that no troublesome thought would be left behind, and partly so that a more exact and perfect re-examination could be made. Accordingly, we have arranged these four following instruments in order, as if they were linked together. Indeed, without having the hour of the conjunction or opposition exactly "to the fingernail" <note>An idiom meaning "perfectly" or "precisely."</note> (the use of which is primary in making judgments, specifically regarding those things that happen in the world), it is impossible to construct a true figure of the heavens, much less to establish a certain judgment about affairs. Therefore, I did not wish to be carelessly curious in this section.

He who wishes to know the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, or of the Moon and the Dragon’s Head <note>The Dragon's Head (Ascending Node) and Tail (Descending Node) are the points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path, essential for predicting eclipses.</note>, should consult the present instrument, composed of four disks and a certain calendar. The first disk, which is the lowest, carries the index **X**, where you see the "inferior years" from 1 to 100 marked, though somewhat disordered and without a strict sequence between them; this is used for seeking conjunctions and oppositions. The second disk is visible with the indicator **Z**, likewise prescribed with years from 1 to 100, suited for investigating conjunctions (☌) and oppositions (☍). The third wheel is marked by index **Y**, on the circumference of which appear little blackened circles <note>original: "rotulæ nigrisculæ"</note> here and there along with the character ☌, signifying the union of the Sun and Moon, just as these small images ☽ ◑ and the horned little moons ☽ represent the quarters of the lights. The fourth disk embraces the indicator **Y** and contains several Dragon’s Heads and Tails, the method for using which follows.

<margin>Method of operation</margin>
For one attempting to know the conjunctions, oppositions, or quarters of the Sun and Moon, the root <term>Radix: The base value or starting point for an astronomical calculation.</term> must be taken from the attached table—the root corresponding to the nearest preceding century—in this manner. On the left side, find the century prior to the proposed year; immediately next to it, on the right, the days, hours, and minutes of the conjunction will present themselves. You will track these same values in the January section of the instrument, first moving index **X** over them, which will remain unchanged until the end of the operation. Similarly, choose the root for the conjunction of the Moon (☽) and the Node (☊) from the second table, where the closest days, hours, and minutes are taken, as before, and sought in the January of the rim; fix these with indicator **Z**. Now secure both disks with wax, as they will otherwise not stay properly in place. The center of the wheel **I** can give the perpetual years if someone requires no other time than that century. Now, on the surface of wheel **X**, look for the proposed and current year, and through this, pull the thread as desired. As for January, locate it at 14, 15, or 16, from which the operator must see which conjunction is closest under the thread of the third wheel, and lead that under the thread. Once moved, the wheels are finally arranged as desired. If it happens that two conjunctions are equally distant from the thread, you may act as you please and substitute whichever of the two you prefer without distinction. Only remember that index **Y** must always be moved to January, not to February or December; after this, move the thread to whichever conjunction, opposition, or quadrature you prefer, for it will immediately report the day of that future or past aspect on the rim of the Calendar.

<margin>Caution to be observed in a leap year</margin>
There are, however, three things worth noting here. First, that in a leap year <note>original: "anno bissextili"</note>, the conjunction (☌) or opposition (☍) may not be found accurately from the beginning of January until the 24th day of February; for this reason, another day must always be added, and after this addition, the sought result finally emerges. Second, if a conjunction marked with the ‡ symbol falls in December, it is null; but if it falls in January, the day must be kept according to the previous instructions, for it is called the first opposition of that passing year. Third, a conjunction of the Sun and Moon with the sign of the Node (☊) that falls in December is the very last of the current or proposed year; that which reaches into January will be entirely useless.

<margin>Example of Emperor CHARLES</margin>
This matter will become familiar through an exemplary method, thus: In the observation of judgments <note>meaning astrological or horoscopic predictions.</note>, astronomers are accustomed to carefully examine the figures of conjunctions or preventions—that is, those which closely precede births. Therefore, we will teach, by way of example, the conjunction of the lights immediately prior to the Imperial birth through a certain perfected path. From the numerical table—that is, the one containing the Roots—first look for the designated root of the conjunction for the current year 1500, in which CHARLES is said to have been born. You will find the day 29, hour 11, minute 38, by which

->ASTRONOMICVM CAESAREVM<-

<column-break/>

having observed these in January, you bring in index X <note>Index X is one of the movable pointers on the paper instrument.</note>, because the birth is considered a centenary one <note>Refers to the 'root' or base calculation starting from a hundred-year mark.</note>, and is not yet fully completed. After this, with the thread <note>A measuring string attached to the center of the instrument.</note>, mark February 24, which is Caesar’s <note>Emperor Charles V.</note> birthday. From there, move the same thread against the order of the days until it meets either the Sun (☉) or the Moon (☾) in conjunction (☌). The Moon is offered, which in this "preventional" birth—to use a somewhat clumsy term well known to astrologers, though you might prefer to call it the "preceding" birth—will be called an opposition or something else, since that opposition precedes the birth. When you have drawn the thread through this, you will see in the Diary or Calendar the day of February 14, on which this kind of opposition occurs. Although it is a Leap Year, there was no need to subtract a day, since the light of the preventional or preceding opposition does not exceed February 24; indeed, the 14 days found are to be accepted as they are.

<margin>Example of the Reign of FERDINAND</margin>
We know King FERDINAND'S birth year is 1503. Just as before, index X similarly lies over January, day 0, hour 22, minute 54. Now place pointer Y over January 15 or 16, and the third year (the royal one) expressed on the rim of wheel X must be marked with the thread. Beneath the thread, the next Moon (☾) marked with a conjunction (☌) on small wheel Y must be brought forward. After this, when the thread has been placed on March 10, the King’s birthday, and moved backward from there until it meets the Moon (☾) or Sun (☉), a conjunction will first occur. The thread will be seen to fall a few hours after February 25. The conjunctions (☌) standing by this indicate that it is the second of the present year. This royal birth will be called "conjunctional" by astronomers because a conjunction occurs first. The order to be followed for years before Christ will be handled a little further below.

### THE TWENTY-THIRD PROPOSITION

Given any year, day, and month, to find the middle conjunction of the Moon and the so-called Head or Tail of the Dragon <term>The lunar nodes: the points where the Moon's path crosses the Earth's orbital plane. Eclipses can only occur near these points.</term>, and to predict through this whether or not any darkening of the luminaries <note>An eclipse of the Sun or Moon.</note> will occur in that same space of time, without difficulty or doubt.

<margin>Example of Emperor CHARLES</margin>
<image-desc>A small rectangular woodcut depicting the relative celestial positions and indices for 'CAROLI' (Charles V) and 'FERDI' (Ferdinand I).</image-desc>
**I**N THE SAME WAY THAT THE DAYS on which the Sun and Moon are joined or opposed were just investigated, you shall also know when the Moon and the Head of the Dragon come together. Using only a different "root" <note>The base value for calculations.</note> taken from the present table, move index Z to its place. This will become clearer with an example. The year 1500, the birth year of Caesar CHARLES, has a root of 11 days, 23 hours, 14 minutes. This same root, observed in the January of the preceding figure, should be marked with index Z. But because the year is not yet full, index V should also be joined with Z; by doing so, the wheels will be arranged conveniently enough. Now, pass the thread in a circle over all of them, both conjunctions and 

<margin>By the "Dragon’s line," he understands the ecliptic limit. Whenever the Tail (☊) etc. ends the ecliptic, specifically whenever the thread falls there, it demonstrates that a solar eclipse is about to happen. However, it shows a lunar eclipse whenever the thread touches a specific figure [symbol]. In some copies, the lunar limit is placed like this [symbol].</margin>

oppositions; if any line of the Dragon’s Tail or Head falls under the thread, you can pronounce that a future eclipse will occur at that conjunction or opposition. However, it is possible to know the hour of the future node <note>The exact moment of the eclipse.</note> until you are certain whether that conjunction or opposition occurs by day or by night. For a lunar eclipse can happen to no one during the day, just as the Sun is never seen to fail at night. Let it suffice for now to have known whether the future eclipse will be by day or night. As on May 12, the Sun (☉) and Moon (☾) are seen near the tail; on that day one might predict an eclipse, unless it were clear from what follows that the opposition exists during the day. Likewise, although the Moon appears on the 27th of that same month, because it is nocturnal it is not to be noticed at all. So also the conjunction of the tail on June 11: because the Moon has already wandered further away, it will no longer be expected. But on November 6, according to the middle conjunction (☌), a lunar eclipse is entirely certain to occur, because the nocturnal and true opposition happens on the 5th day. Considering the remaining oppositions of the present year, another is seen near the tail on November 20, but since it is somewhat further distant, no eclipse should be expected there. A different logic holds for an eclipse of the Sun, where even if the lines of conjunctions and the heads or tails do not coincide exactly, it is nevertheless possible for an eclipse to occur, and that by reason of the "diversity of aspect" <note>Parallax; the difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note>, as the ecliptic limit (☊) demonstrates.

King FERDINAND obtains the same root as Caesar; 
<margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin>
therefore pointers X and Z remain the same. But with small wheel V placed for the 3rd year on the rim of Z, and wheel Y for the 3rd year also on the rim of X (since the king is said to have been born 3 years after the year 1500), and correctly located, you will have correctly arranged all four wheels. With the instrument thus ordered, bring the thread to each conjunction and opposition, 

<column-break/>

where if some Head or Tail comes under the thread, you can certainly predict a failure of some luminary, such as a solar eclipse on March 27 (unless it were at night), and a lunar eclipse on April 11 and October 5, if they did not happen during the day. For times before Christ, the method of operation is no different from the previous one, except that you subtract the proposed year from a larger century, and the remainder is called the "remaining years." Then you mark the sought root of the larger century with pointers X and Z. The remaining years you express with indices Y and V, just as was said above.

### A SUPPLEMENT OR COMPLETION OF THIS TWENTY-SECOND PROPOSITION.

**A**LTHOUGH THE PRECEDING PROPOSITION stands sufficiently on its own, it was nevertheless pleasing—indeed necessary—to add another besides. This is because the thread of the former does not denote every day of conjunctions, oppositions, and eclipse possibilities quite so exactly, owing to a fault in the paper <note>original: "papiri vitio." Apianus is noting that humidity can cause the paper to expand or contract, affecting the precision of the printed instrument.</note> which, I know not how, while absorbing moisture a little too freely during the printing process, is accustomed now to stretch, now to shrink. In the present instrument, everything can be known even more precisely. Although you might do the same with the spiral instrument as with the instrument full of dragons, no common difficulty lies in the operation or use of it. But because one requires the service of the other, and neither works perfectly alone, we have placed both opposite each other, so that no one is forced to turn the page—by which action instruments often lose their position and verification. It should further be known that the two small wheels of this instrument accomplish the same thing as the four of the previous instrument do; however, the use of the present one is of this kind: When you have correctly arranged the left wheels of the former instrument, arrange the two of the present instrument in the same way. Seek the same root of the conjunction or opposition that you used in arranging wheel X of the former one in the January of the calendar inserted there—that is, the spiral calendar. First, having the day of the root, look for the hours of the root on the outer rim; each degree designates one hour, from which the minutes of the root can also be gathered. The thread is drawn through those minutes, and index X Y of the lower wheel is substituted for it. Next, on the rim of the same orb, the current year is required for which the conjunction, opposition, or possibility of eclipses is desired. That year is marked with the thread, and pointer X Y is again joined to it (specifically of the lower wheel), so that 

<margin>Why each orb has double letters.</margin>

those times have reached their final place. That index is marked with the letters X and Y because it performs as much as those two on the previous orb, one marked with X and the other with Y. From here, arrange the upper wheel no differently than that one, bringing it to the root of the conjunction of the Moon and the Dragon’s Head, and this in the days and hours of January. This wheel likewise bears two letters, namely Z and V, for it does the same as the other two separately, one marked with Z and the other with V, above which are the Dragons (specifically of the former instrument). Thus those two wheels are arranged entirely for use. 

<margin>Use of the instrument.</margin>

With both instruments thus ordered, one must see on the first one which figure marks the conjunction or opposition you wish to know, then when it happens—whether it is the first, second, or third made from the beginning of the year. While you extend the thread through it, it marks in which month and day the conjunction 

<gloss>direction or opposition, namely the first with the thread, while or the opposition on the instrument where they stayed, the color expresses</gloss> 

or opposition falls. Look for the same number or figure on the later instrument in small wheel X Y, either of conjunctions (which the blackened faces represent) or opposition (the kind which the yellow color of the Moon expresses). Place the thread over the straight diameter of that face, which, when so extended, denotes the hour and minute on the outer rim of the conjunction or opposition. In addition, observe where the thread touches the month in which the conjunction or opposition was found by the first instrument; for the figure then shows the true day of the middle conjunction or opposition, both those past and those to come. You will know the day thus: from the extended thread, go backward against the order of the signs or the count of days until the names of the months occur; but do not go according to the order of days, for you could be deceived in that way, especially if the names of the months first encountered were those in which the number of days begins. Among these months, therefore, seek that month whose conjunction (☌) or opposition (☍) you found on the first instrument. In its spiral circle, move your finger up to the thread, next to which you will recognize the true day—and this if the current year is a Common or Civil year. The same happens in a Leap Year, but only from the beginning of the year to February 24. After which, if a conjunction or opposition occurs, one day must always be subtracted. 

<margin>How to proceed in a Leap Year.</margin>

For example, if the thread indicates the first of March, let February 29 be taken for it; or if the thread marks March 2, let the first be taken for the second. It is done in a similar way for the rest. This instrument was not made so that you might track hours and minutes through it, but only the day, and that most truly. However, once the day is known for certain, you must go to the nearest instrument to find the hours and minutes. For in that instrument, nothing is lacking for one seeking the feast days. Furthermore, if you desire to know whether in a year any eclipse, whether of the Sun or 

<margin>By what means a future eclipse of the Sun (☉) or Moon (☾) may be known.</margin>

the Moon, or whether one or more are to occur, then consider on the first instrument how many times a Tail or Head concurs with a conjunction or opposition, with the figure meanwhile diligently noted.

How the true possibility of conjunctions or oppositions should be recognized has been discussed elsewhere.
