Conversely, a failure of the Moon <note>A lunar eclipse.</note> occurs whenever the thread is drawn into such a figure <image-desc>a small rectangular box containing the ascending node symbol ☊</image-desc> or such a figure <image-desc>a small rectangular box containing the descending node symbol ☋</image-desc>, but that opposition must occur at night.

## THE EXAMPLE OF Emperor CHARLES

¶ If you direct the index X Y to the "root" of the Emperor's birth <note>In astronomy, a "root" is a starting value for calculations.</note> at day 0, hour 22, minute 54 of January, you will have set this wheel in its place, for the year has not yet elapsed. Likewise, move the pointer of the upper circle Z V to day 11, hour 23, minute 14, and it will be positioned for use throughout the whole year. Now, if you look into the first instrument, you will find a mean conjunction on the 12th day of May, the fifth in order. Therefore, if you lead the thread through the fifth conjunction of the instrument, it will show on the circle of the month of May roughly day 13, hour 20, minute 10. But by reason of the Leap Year, you subtract one day here, and 12 days will remain. Since the Tail of the Dragon is found near this node in the first instrument, it must be thought that an eclipse will occur. Consequently, the following instrument must also be inspected (with the thread remaining over the opposition) to see whether the thread encompasses the ecliptic limits of the Moon at the fifth Tail; and indeed, it seems to be encompassed. Therefore, you may assert without doubt that the Moon fails <note>The Moon is eclipsed.</note> at this opposition. However, because that opposition occurs during the day, it is necessary for the Moon to stand below the horizon, and for that same reason, it cannot be visible to us. Furthermore, a certain conjunction is found in May, on the 28th day of the same month; this is the sixth conjunction from the beginning of the year, happening near the sixth Head of the Dragon. Therefore, if the thread is drawn through the sixth conjunction of the following instrument, it shows the 28th day in the circle of May, and also the 14th hour. Because of the Leap Year, it is taken as the 27th day. Now, if the sixth Head of the Dragon is seen, it is also observed that the limit of the same solar eclipse is touched by the thread, so that a failure of the Sun must occur; this is understood according to the mean position of the Sun. But because the true eclipse happens around the middle of the night, as following sections will teach, it cannot be seen in our region. But on the 6th day of November, at the eleventh opposition, it is shown near the twelfth Head of the Dragon; if you examine this through the following instrument, the thread cuts the twelfth limit of the lunar eclipse at the Head of the Dragon. Therefore, that opposition, which happens for us at night, is undoubtedly visible.

## THE EXAMPLE OF KING FERDINAND

<margin>Example of King FERDINAND</margin>
¶ King FERDINAND has the same "roots" as the Emperor at his birth; therefore, the wheel X Y is set to day 0, hour 22, minute 54, and then the thread is drawn through the third year in the rim of the same wheel, and the pointer is moved again, and that circle is rectified. Likewise, arrange the upper circle in this way, bringing it first to the root, which is day 11, hour 23, minute 14, then to the third year. After this, looking at the first instrument, it first occurs that the second conjunction of the Sun happens on the 12th day of March, reaching the third Tail. Therefore, it must be seen whether a lunar eclipse can happen. Now, if you stretch the thread through the second Tail in the posterior instrument, you see that it does not fall within the lunar limits at all; because of this, no eclipse is to be expected. This is understood as far as the mean Sun is concerned; as for the true Sun, it could still happen that it falls within the limit and an eclipse occurs, which the following sections sufficiently clarify. Still in the same year, on the 27th day of March, the third conjunction touches the fourth Head of the Dragon; therefore, the thread of the second instrument, directed through the third Head, shows the 27th day in the circle of March, and the 4th hour on the outer rim. Furthermore, it reaches the limit of the solar failure at the fourth Head, wherefore an eclipse of the Sun is certainly asserted to be in the future; however, unless it happens around the middle of the night, as you will know consequently, you should expect none. The same reasoning applies to all the rest.

# THE INSTRUMENT FOR FINDING ECLIPSES

<note>This page consists of a complex, hand-colored astronomical volvelle—a paper instrument with rotating parts (though here represented as a flat diagram) used for calculating celestial events without complex long-form math.</note>

->**CIRCLE OF OPPOSITION**<-
<note>original: *CIR OPPOSITIO*. This refers to the "Full Moon" phase, when the Moon and Sun are on opposite sides of the Earth. A lunar eclipse can only occur during this phase if the alignment is precise.</note>

->**CIRCLE OF CONJUNCTION**<-
<note>original: *CIRCULVS CONIVNCTI*. This refers to the "New Moon" phase, when the Moon and Sun are aligned on the same side of the Earth. A solar eclipse can only occur during this phase.</note>

### THE OUTER SCALES AND TABLES
The octagonal frame contains scales divided into units of ten (10, 20, 30, 40, 50), while the inner rings contain data tables written in both black and red ink. These likely represent the "ecliptic limits" mentioned on the previous page—the narrow windows of time and degree where an eclipse is possible.

### THE CENTRAL FIELD
*   **The Lunar Phases:** One ring is marked with Roman numerals **I** through **XII** and features small icons showing the changing face of the Moon.
*   **The Eclipse Indicators:** Two yellow circles with dark shadows represent the Sun or Moon undergoing an eclipse.
*   **The Calculation Thread:** A blue string is attached to the central floral boss. As instructed on the previous page, the user would pull this thread across the scales to see if the date of a conjunction or opposition falls within the "limits" marked by the symbols for the Head <term>Ascending Node (☊)</term> or Tail <term>Descending Node (☋)</term> of the Dragon.

CAESAR’S ASTRONOMY

# THE TWENTY-SIXTH ENUNCIATION

### *With the mean Solar and Lunar arguments obtained for the time of mean conjunction and opposition, to also determine the limits of true conjunction or opposition—that is, the hours and minutes.*

**W**ith the mean times and arguments <term>Argument: the position of a celestial body within its orbit, used here to calculate its distance from the apogee</term> having been found through the previously mentioned enunciation, we shall now investigate those same true values. At the start, seek the mean Lunar argument on the line of this figure—namely E F—looking for the Sign of the argument on both the right and left sides. You will find it on the right side if the argument is less than 6 Signs <note>a "Sign" is a 30-degree segment of the zodiac</note>, among the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. On the left side, however, if the argument is greater than 6 Signs, you will find it with numbers such as VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII. Once the Lunar argument is taken on the right by ascending through the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, then the Solar argument must be sought, either in the small circle near the center, or in the signs described on the inner part of the rim which begin with the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, etc., next to the letter C. If the Lunar argument is taken on the left side by descending on line E F, then the Solar argument will be sought among the signs on the outer part of that rim, which begin next to the letter D and are marked with these numbers: I, II, III, IIII, V, VI, etc. Now, having gathered both the Solar and Lunar arguments, bring the thread across line F E, and let the bead <note>original: "margarita", literally "pearl"; a sliding bead on the instrument's string used as a pointer</note> be placed over the Lunar argument. Again, let the thread be joined to the Solar argument (which is done on either the outer or inner rim, whichever of them corresponds to the Lunar argument in digits or letters); immediately the bead will show the hours and minutes to be added or subtracted from the time of the mean conjunction <note>symbolized by ☊, the New Moon</note> or opposition <note>symbolized by ☋, the Full Moon</note>, from which the true conjunction or opposition will result.

I wish for you to understand it thus: whenever the Lunar argument does not exceed 6 Signs, observe that small circle where "SUBTRACT" is written on one half and "ADD" on the other. Now, if the bead (with the thread marking the Solar argument in circle C) falls near the small circle so that it strikes within the thick black perimeter where the word "ADD" appears three times, then the hours and minutes expressed by the junction must be subtracted from the time of the mean conjunction or opposition. But if the bead falls within the "SUBTRACT" arc and the outer rim, then you shall use "SUBTRACT" for the conjunction. For you follow the label of subtraction or addition that is closest to the bead in the circle of the Solar argument, which the small circle near the center now indicates—though its degrees, for the sake of clarity, are taken on the larger rim. And if the Lunar argument is sought on the left side (which happens when the argument exceeds 6 Signs), the bead is moved to this point, and the Solar argument must be observed on the outer rim, starting from the letter D. With the thread placed on the end of the argument, the bead shows the hours and minutes to be added or subtracted. Which of these you should do, you shall know thus: consider the label "SUBTRACT" or "ADD" from the outer rim toward the center nearest to the bead, for that is what must be followed.

<margin>The preceding syzygy of Emperor Charles.</margin>
## Example of / CHARLES / the Emperor.
¶ The following customary examples will illustrate these instructions. We said that the syzygy <note>the astronomical alignment of the Sun, Moon, and Earth</note> preceding the Emperor’s birth was on the 14th of February; the time of the mean opposition was 6:00 PM. The Solar argument was 8 signs, 1 degree, 44 minutes; the Lunar argument was 2 signs, 14 degrees, 47 minutes, as given by the preceding enunciation. Therefore, the Lunar argument, since it is less than 6 signs, must be looked for on the right side, and the degrees on line E F, and the thread together with the bead must be placed over it. The Solar argument must now be sought in the small cycle near the center; likewise, the degrees and minutes can be taken in circle C. If you again lay the thread over this argument, the bead simultaneously reveals in the area 13 hours and 23 minutes to be added—added because the small circle representing the Solar argument is the closest label to the center. After you have added these to the mean opposition, 19 hours and 23 minutes remain, and it is now called the true opposition. This time shall furthermore be ratified by two methods. First, through the 5th enunciation, from which you will borrow the equation of days, proceeding in this manner: in the rim, you will seek the 14th day of February, through which the passed thread cuts off one minute in the circle of equation; this, being added to the time found afterward, will constitute the time of the true opposition, called "with equated days," corresponding to the meridian of Ingolstadt: namely, 19 hours and 24 minutes. The second

<column-break/>

verification of the time is such that you strive to reduce the time to the native meridian, that is, of Ghent, which you shall do thus. When you have read "Ghent" in the table of regions under the heading of the aspects of Taurus and Libra, you see 0 hours and 39 minutes with the letter M; by subtracting 39 minutes from the time already equated, the final verification will result: namely, the 14th day, at 18 hours and 44 minutes <note>this calculates the precise time of the Full Moon before Charles V's birth, adjusted for his birthplace</note>.

## Example of / FERDINAND / the King.
<margin>The King's calculated birth</margin>
¶ In the King's birth, on the 25th day of February, the time of the mean conjunction was at 15 hours and 31 minutes. The Solar argument was 5 signs, 16 degrees, 34 minutes. Seek that on the left side by ascending, and on the line F G for the degrees of the ink <note>the printed lines</note>, and express them with the junction. Now, do not ignore the small circle that signifies the Solar argument; therefore, since both the Lunar argument and the circle itself are similarly inscribed with the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, etc.—although the cycle itself consists of such digits as 1, 2, <insert>13 minutes, 40 seconds was Mars. having been taken, let the thread be led through the same. Which being done, the bead will give the hours to be added in the area of the figure, namely 10, and 19 minutes, for thus the label ought to be taken. With the Solar argument in the small basket of the conjunction, namely 8 Lunar</insert> 3, 4, etc.—let it be used for the other because of its size; namely, having taken 5 degrees and 42 minutes, let the thread be led through the same. Which being done, the bead will give the hours to be added in the area of the figure, namely 10, and 19 minutes, for thus the label of addition near the center requires. From here, repeat the equation of days, which is 3 minutes and 40 seconds <note>original: ♂, the symbol for Mars, used here perhaps as a marker or error for seconds</note> through the 5th enunciation; if you add this, you have the time of the true conjunction at the Ingolstadt meridian: namely, the 26th day, at 1 hour and 50 minutes. If you still wish to have the equal or more suitable time for the city of Medina, examine Medina by the rule of the 3rd Enunciation; for there, under the heading of the Sun and the aspects, 1 hour and 12 minutes is offered with the mark M. Therefore, by subtracting 1 hour and 12 minutes, the time of the true conjunction remains: namely, the 26th day, at 0 hours and 42 minutes, which is what you had sought.

## An example from the time / before Christ borrowed / from the death of Alexander.
<margin>Example concerning Christ <note>This refers to the BC era</note></margin>
So that an example of this matter may also be brought forward from before Christ’s death, I have chosen the death of Alexander the Great, which occurred 311 years and 93 days before Christ was born. Now, if I wish to know whether a conjunction or an opposition most closely preceded this death of Alexander, and on what day, hour, and minute it happened, I subtract 311 years and 93 days from 400 years (namely, from the next larger century); there remain, therefore, 88 years and 272 days. If I count this number of days from the first light of January, it is seen to coincide correctly with the 29th of September. This being done, I take out the root of the 400th century from the table of roots for the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, by the aid of the 22nd enunciation. Once taken out, it offers 6 days, 1 hour, and 40 minutes. These are now sought in January, expressed with the index X, and this in the instrument of the dragons <term>Instrumentum draconum: a specialized astronomical tool for calculating eclipses and lunar nodes, often called "dragons" because the nodes were known as the Head and Tail of the Dragon</term>. Furthermore, as for the remaining 88 years (for eighty-eight years have already elapsed), after I consider them on the rim of the small wheel X and place the index Y upon them, imitating the twenty-second enunciation, then the next preceding conjunction is discerned on the 29th day of September, falling on the 20th day of that same month. It is established from the 22nd enunciation that this conjunction was only a mean one: namely, at 6 hours and 36 minutes in the afternoon. The 22nd enunciation, already mentioned often, instructed that I should fix the index Q to 1 hour and 40 minutes, just as the root of 400 years requires. I also fixed index P to the 89th year; moreover, I had passed the thread to the ninth conjunction (for that ninth conjunction had appeared in order from January), which on the rim reported 6 hours and 36 minutes (already mentioned a little before). Then, through the 25th enunciation, I investigated the Solar and Lunar arguments fitting for this day, hour, and minute. For the Sun, it was 3 Signs, 19 degrees, 8 minutes, the ratio of which was the apogee of the Sun, which had 2 Signs, 6 degrees, 20 minutes. For the Lunar argument, 4 Signs, 17 degrees, 54 minutes. With both of these prepared, I detected the distance between the true and mean conjunction through this instrument as follows. With the Lunar argument being less than 6 Signs, the Solar argument had to be received in the small circle, and the thread passed through it; having been passed through, the bead, which is now ratified next to the Lunar argument, showed in the area of the instrument 2 hours and 36 minutes to be added to the time of the mean conjunction. It is therefore elicited that this opposition appeared at the Ingolstadt meridian around 8 hours and 52 minutes. This time of conjunction, if you please, you may accommodate to any other meridian through the aforesaid instructions.

IMPERIAL

# ASTRONOMICAL
## TWENTY-SEVENTH PROPOSITION.

Having already examined the possibility of a lunar eclipse—so to speak—that is, the time at which it might happen, using the instrument of the twenty-third proposition; we shall now further perceive through the present figure whether it will certainly occur, and how great the future eclipse will be.

<margin>How a lunar eclipse is to be formed on a flat surface.</margin>
Once you have identified the true opposition <note>A "true opposition" occurs at the exact moment of the Full Moon, when the Sun and Moon are directly opposite each other from the Earth's perspective.</note> of the day on which you foresaw a possible darkening of the Moon, gather the **Arguments** <term>Argument: a mathematical value used as an input to find a celestial body's position on a scale or table.</term> of the Sun and Moon for that same day using propositions 12 and 25. Also, collect the true position of the Moon, its latitude, the argument of its altitude, and the true position of the **Dragon’s Head** <term>Dragon's Head: The "ascending node," the point where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path (the ecliptic) moving northward.</term> using propositions 17 and 18. By gathering these, you will have brought together everything pertaining to eclipses. Through the instrument of proposition 18, the possibility of an eclipse, both of the Sun and the Moon, can be determined—even better than in the previous one—in this manner: When you have properly placed the index of the Dragon's Head at the time of the true opposition or conjunction, you will also observe the Moon's place in the Zodiac. If the thread stretched through that point falls between **d** and **a** (with the Moon staying near the Dragon’s Head) or between **g** and **e** (with the Moon near the **Dragon’s Tail** <note>The descending node.</note>), you may boldly declare that the Moon will fail <note>i.e., be eclipsed.</note> at that opposition. Conversely, you will observe a failing of the Sun by this certain rule: mark the times of the true conjunction with the thread; if it passes between **b** and **c** near the Dragon’s Head, or between **f** and **g** near the Dragon’s Tail, a solar eclipse is possible at this conjunction. Truly, however, the darkenings of the Sun cannot be determined by us as precisely as those of the Moon without the labor of calculation, due to the differences in **aspects** <note>original: "aspectuum," referring here to parallax, the shift in apparent position depending on the observer's location on Earth.</note>; nevertheless, God willing, we do not despair of reducing these also to the form of an instrument in the future, as far as is permitted. 

Once the possibility of a lunar eclipse is recognized, mark a line on some flat surface, which you shall name **H D**, the midpoint of which shall be **A**. Let another line, perpendicular to this, be drawn and called **B F**. Now fix one foot of the compass on the letter **A**; let the other, extended, draw a hidden circle at your discretion, which is cut by the line **B F** at points **B** and **F**. This being done, consider the latitude of the Moon: if it is Northern, then its true Argument must be between 5 signs and 18 degrees at minimum, up to 6 signs, or even 0 signs and 12 degrees. Now, if the Argument is 0 signs, let the quarter **B D** be divided into 18 parts thus: first into three, then each of those into three more, and finally each into two, and you will have 18 portions, each containing 5 degrees. Mark the point nearest the letter **B** as **C**, and draw a straight line from the center **A** through **C**. If, however, the Argument of latitude is 5 signs, then divide the quarter **B H**; place the letter **M** at the first section after the letter **B**, and draw a line through **M** and the center **A**, as before. But if you see a Southern Moon, having an Argument of 6 signs and some degrees besides, then choose the nearest point from letter **F** toward **D**, marking it with the letter **T**. If the Argument is 11 signs, move from **F** toward **H** to such a point, and mark it **G**. In this part, do not be disturbed if you sometimes see degrees not joined to signs, provided you carefully observe the signs alone.

->These [rules] of all, etc.<-

Next, on the outer rim of the following figure (which hereafter shall be called the **Semi-diameter Instrument**), seek the Argument of the Sun. When you have placed the thread over it, note where it touches the inner rim (which measures the variations of the shadows in seconds <note>arc-seconds.</note>); take those seconds cut off by the thread separately. Then, seeking the Argument of the Moon, mark it likewise with the thread, which reveals to you two semi-diameters: namely, that of the Moon’s body and that of the Earth’s shadow. While the thread remains thus, fix the compass in the center, extending the other foot to the point where the darker area is touched by the thread; for that extension is the semi-diameter of the Moon's body, which you should keep unchanged. After this, fix another compass at the end of the semi-diameter already obtained, extending the other foot of the same compass to the boundary of the dark area; you will then have the semi-diameter of the Earth's shadow. You see this area is enclosed all around by a certain bright circumference, beyond which you see another surface, the width of a pen's stroke, which is distributed into 60 seconds. But since you have already learned the seconds of the shadow's variation, the

When you have fixed such a compass at **A** on the plane previously prepared for this, and described a circle, you see the true size of the shadow—the shadow, I say, of the Earth, which is formed during the Moon’s passage at the time of that opposition. Soon, in the instrument named the *Dispositorium*, observe the Moon’s Argument, whether it be on lines **A C**, **A M**, **A G**, or **A T**. Place the foot of the compass in the designated spot and extend the other to the point of the argument. Afterward, transfer the same extension of the compass to the prepared plane, and with one foot fixed at **A**, mark a point with the other on the line recently set aside for this purpose, and sign it with the letter **M**. Now take the compass extended according to the semi-diameter of the Moon's body; when you have fixed it at **M** and described a circle with it, consider that you have the body of the Moon. From these things, finally, you can be certain regarding the eclipse happening at this opposition and its magnitude. For if the entire body of the Moon passes under the shadow, it is a total eclipse; if partially, a partial eclipse; if not at all, no eclipse occurs.

->THE EMPEROR’S ASTRONOMY<-

## A flat representation of the ECLIPSE OF CHARLES.

<margin>What things are needed to predict eclipses.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental initial 'Q' containing a scene of an astronomer holding a quadrant, observing stars and the moon in the night sky.</image-desc>We shall now repeat this business even more abundantly and completely through a practical teaching method. Looking at the year 1500 of Emperor CHARLES, namely his birth year, it appears that a failure <note>original: "defectus"; referring to an eclipse</note> of the Moon could happen in that same year, on the fifth day of November. Therefore, I immediately investigate the time of true opposition <note>The "true opposition" is the moment of the Full Moon when it is exactly opposite the Sun.</note> and find it to be the 5th day, at 13 hours and 52 minutes of November. The position of the Sun I find to be 23 degrees and 22 minutes of Scorpio [♏]. The true position of the Moon is 23 degrees and 22 minutes of Taurus [♉]. The Argument of the Sun <term>Argument of the Sun: A technical value representing the Sun's position in its orbital path.</term> is 3 Signs, 4 degrees, 23 minutes, and 29 seconds. The true Argument of Latitude of the Moon is 5 Signs, 11 degrees, 24 minutes, and 39 seconds. The true position of the ascending node <note>original: "☊"; the point where the Moon's orbit crosses the Earth's orbital plane.</note> is 5 Signs, 1 degree, 28 minutes, and 51 seconds. I complete all things necessary for predicting the eclipse. Having seen these, I draw on a plane surface lines intersecting each other at right angles, as can be seen before you. In the present case, finding the Argument of Latitude to be 5 Signs and 11 degrees, I divide the circle F H into 18 portions according to the rule’s prescription. Marking the first point near F with the letter G, I draw a straight line through it and the center A, which I label with the three letters C A G. Next, when the Argument of the Sun is sought on the outer rim of the preceding figure and expressed with the thread <note>Apianus’s book famously included "volvelles" or paper instruments with moving parts and silk threads used as pointers.</note>, I see 51 seconds are cut off from the thread in the circle of the shadow, and I set these aside. Afterward, on that same outer rim, I repeat the True Argument of the Moon, namely 9 Signs, 22 degrees, and 59 minutes, also with the thread pulled across; I notice that the thread cuts the circles of the Moon's body at point B, and the shadow at point H. Keeping the thread thus, I fix one foot of the two compasses in center A, extending it to B, and I set aside the compass thus opened, which represents the semi-diameter of the Moon. I place the other compass at B and extend it to H to learn the semi-diameter of the shadow. I resume the 51 seconds previously collected from the shadow’s variation; having resumed them, I imagine the line at H divided into 60 parts, in which, counting 51 starting from H toward I, I add the letter R at the end of the count. I now contract the compass from I to R and declare that this contains the true diameter of the shadow. Keeping that compass unchanged, I place one foot at A on the previously prepared plane, and with the other I describe a circle, marking it with the letters O S Q R, and I thus know the true size of the shadow that occurred at the time of the Moon’s passage. Again, entering the layout device called the "dispositorium," I fix one foot of the compass at letter A and the other at the Argument of Latitude, which is 5 Signs, 11 degrees, and 24 minutes. I bring this same extension to the plane, placing one point of the compass at A on the line A G, and I mark the other point extended toward G with the letter M. Now, taking the first compass previously set to the size of the Moon, I place one foot at letter M and describe a periphery showing the size of the Moon itself. I mean the distinction between the Moon and the shadow—namely, how much it still shines and how much it is obscured—which is shown as 10 digits <note>original: "punctis"; astronomers divided the diameter of the sun or moon into 12 "digits" to measure eclipse magnitude.</note> and 50 minutes. You should judge this as if the whole diameter of the Moon were split into 12 digits; for whatever the number of those parts is, the eclipse is said to occur by that many digits. This matter will later be taught by a specific demonstration. Moreover, the bottom part, inclining toward the horizon, appears visible or bright, while the upper part is dark and gloomy. I wish to note in passing that this time of true opposition or middle of the eclipse matches our meridian—that is, the meridian of Ingolstadt—but by subtracting 39 minutes, it can be compared to Ghent <note>Charles V was born in Ghent.</note>. To see the Moon's path more fully and to know clearly from which part it began to be hidden, I raise a perpendicular from point M, extended sufficiently on both sides; then, taking the compass representing the Moon’s diameter and placing its foot at R, I mark point L with the other on the line A T. Soon, from center A through L, I draw a circle on both sides that touches the perpendicular on the right side at point N and on the left at point K. Placing the compass that expresses the Moon’s diameter at points K and N, I describe a circle around letter N, giving the beginning of the failing Moon. For it is clear where the Moon begins to be veiled by the Earth’s shadow. In the same way, I draw another small circle around letter K, signifying the end of that eclipse. This being done, it is clear how the Moon passed from N through M to K. Whatever has been said so far about the Imperial eclipse, the following figure can teach your eyes more clearly than light.

## HOW THE COLOR OF THE LUNAR ECLIPSE is to be predicted: A universal rule.

Having seen the magnitude of the eclipse, I predict its color by two factors: the Latitude and the True Argument. I first consider the Latitude in the following table, whether it be southern or northern, by which I immediately discover the color of the eclipse as desired. As in

<column-break/>

As in the Emperor's eclipse <note>original: "deliquio Imperatorio"; deliquium is a synonym for eclipse/failure of light.</note>, I take up the latitude of 29 minutes in the table; however, since that number is not in the table, I choose the one closest to it, namely 28, and I take the color written next to it—which is offered as black and red—as the one sought. Looking then at the Argument in the second table, the color of the distance produced by the Moon with the Earth is known. As in the same Imperial example, where the True Argument of the Moon is 9 Signs, 22 degrees, and 59 minutes; seeking these Signs, degrees, and minutes in the second table, they are not found exactly, but 9 Signs and 15 degrees are found. Therefore, because 22 degrees exceeds 15, they designate the color Gray. Once this is done, there remains the mixture of colors, by which, once conveniently performed, the true color of the eclipse will be forged. If you desire this more perfectly, mix these kinds of colors in the manner of painters, and you will have the matter before your eyes.

# THE CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY: THE COLOR OF THE ROYAL ECLIPSE.

<margin>
When he first showed himself in his mother’s womb, he had been in the womb for 40 days before the eclipse.
</margin>

Thus far, through the example of the Emperor <note>Charles V</note>, we have set forth the lowest transit of the Moon—that is, how the visible Moon traveled through the lower part of the shadow while hiding its own upper part. Now, however, we shall explain the "Royal" variation <note>referring to King Ferdinand I</note>, which is different: one where the Moon obscures its lower face but remains bright on its upper part, traversing the highest part of the shadow while tilted toward the Zenith. Indeed, throughout everything, from "head to heel" as the proverb says, right to the end of this book, one may see these two examples of the Caesars offering alternating turns to one another, so that whatever was missing in one was present in the other. In this way, nothing concerning the matters proposed has been left untouched or unsaid until now. When considering the year 1503, in which King **FERDINAND** was born, no nocturnal lunar eclipse is found; therefore, going backward to the day of conception (since this time must also be reckoned alongside the birth), an eclipse of the Moon is found to occur exactly in the middle of the period between conception and birth, namely on the 15th day of October in the year 1502. Now, following the rules of the previous instructions, for one seeking the time of the true full moon, it will be clear that the midpoint of this eclipse—that is, the space where it is usually greatest—occurred on the predicted day at 12 hours and 11 minutes in the afternoon, according to the meridian of Ingolstadt. To compare this with the clock of Medina <note>Medina del Campo, Spain</note>, one should subtract 1 hour and 12 minutes, and the final verified time will come out as 10 hours and 59 minutes. In this opposition:

> The Moon held 1 degree and 32 minutes of Taurus (♉).
> The Sun held the opposite position.
> The true <term>Argument</term> <note>A mathematical value used to locate a celestial body on its orbit</note> of the Sun: 5 [signs], 8 degrees, 12 minutes of Cancer (♋).
> The true Argument of the Moon: 5 [signs], 15 minutes, 33 [seconds] of Cancer (♋).
> The true position of the Head <note>The North Node, where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path</note>: 0 [signs], 21 degrees, 9 minutes of Cancer (♋).
> The true Argument of Latitude: 0 [signs], 10 degrees, 23 minutes of Cancer (♋).
> The Latitude of the Moon was 55 minutes.

Now let a plane be prepared as before, where orthogonal lines dividing each other at point A are drawn. Since the Argument of Latitude contains no signs <note>meaning it is less than 30 degrees</note>, let point C be transferred here from the figure called the *dispositorium* <note>a specialized calculating diagram</note>, and let the line A-C-G, which previously slanted to the right from B, be extended. From here, let the Argument of the Sun be sought on the outermost rim of the semi-diameters, and let the thread—which cuts 42 seconds in the circle of shadow variation—be placed upon it; these values must be set aside for later. Afterward, let the same thread be drawn through the true Argument of the Moon on the outermost rim. While it remains unmoved, let the compass be stretched from center A to B, and let this extension be called the semi-diameter of the Moon. Setting that extension aside, let the other compass point be fixed at B and stretched to Q; this interval of the compass would be the semi-diameter of the shadow, were it not for the fact that the varying shadow showed 42 <unclear>z</unclear> collected earlier. For that reason, line Q-R must be divided into 60 <unclear>z</unclear>, and the compass should be applied to 42 <unclear>z</unclear> toward R, starting from Q. That compass setting shall indeed be called the true semi-diameter of the shadow. With this compass gap, a circle thereafter drawn from center A of your plane will declare the shadow of the Earth, specifically the one that exists at the time of the passing Moon or at the moment of this opposition. Let the Argument of Latitude also be seen in the said *dispositorium* as follows: with the compass fixed at A, let it be stretched to the Argument of Latitude, and let the gap of the compass be placed on the plane thus: let one foot be fixed at A on line A-C, and let the second be marked with the letter M. Afterward, let the compass be adjusted to fit the semi-diameter of the Moon and taken up again; let one of its feet be placed at M, and with the other let the circle M-P be circumscribed, which represents the body of the Moon. Once this is done, it is clear how the Moon is usually veiled by the shadow. Furthermore, with the compass fixed at O, let it mark a point toward C to be labeled with the letter L. Then, from M, let a perpendicular line rise, somewhat long on both sides. With one foot of the compass fixed at A, let the other reach as far as L. Let that distance describe a circle cutting the perpendicular line on both sides at points K and N. Around points K and N, let the size of the Moon also be expressed, just as was done near point M. When these things are finished, the transit of the Moon through the shadow lies visible before the eyes. How many "points" the shadowing consists of will be known by dividing the line M-P ♋ into parts; for once this is done, it will be plain how many portions are contained between P and O. ¶ In this plane, which we have named the *Dispositorium*—because it prepares and arranges the work of the compass and makes it suitable for fully executing the eclipses of the luminaries—we have drawn certain parallel lines so that you may see how the Moon permeates the shadow in various ways. However, although points M and K require a further separation from the ecliptic, and M and N a closer one, such that they would constitute a slanted line with C-M-A, it would be a more burdensome task than is appropriate for this place to perform that. Nevertheless, in the following sections, the same will be provided more abundantly and perfectly in its own place, as soon as we have found a more suitable one.
<meta>Translator note: "Regij" (Royal) is a catchword for the next page.</meta>

<column-break/>

You may determine the color of the Royal eclipse in two ways, just as before with the Emperor’s records. In this manner: for the Moon, which obtained a latitude of 55 minutes, when you first enter the table with this value, you will see next to those same 55 minutes the color marked as "Grey with whiteness," and you affirm this to be the color of the eclipse. But the distance of the Moon from the Earth must also be considered here; for the closer the Moon is to the Earth, the blacker and darker it appears, which happens when it is at the opposite of its <term>auge</term> <note>Apogee, the point furthest from Earth</note>, just as when it is in the true auge of its epicycle, it is said to be most remote from the Earth. Therefore, the Lunar Argument must be examined: 5 [signs] 15 minutes 33 [seconds], which, when sought in the second table, signifies the color "Black and green." Thus, by mixing these two types of colors, it is easy for you to observe what mixture remains, which shall be the color of the present eclipse. You shall proceed in this way to find the colors of all eclipses.

# THE CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY: THE COLOR OF THE ROYAL ECLIPSE.

<margin>
When he first showed himself in his mother’s womb, he had been in the womb for 40 days before the eclipse.
</margin>

Thus far, through the example of the Emperor <note>Charles V</note>, we have set forth the lowest transit of the Moon—that is, how the visible Moon traveled through the lower part of the shadow while hiding its own upper part. Now, however, we shall explain the "Royal" variation <note>referring to King Ferdinand I, Charles's brother</note>, which is different: one where the Moon obscures its lower face but remains bright on its upper part, traversing the highest part of the shadow while tilted toward the Zenith <note>the point in the sky directly overhead</note>. Indeed, throughout everything, from "head to heel" as the proverb says, right to the end of this book, one may see these two examples of the Caesars offering alternating turns to one another, so that whatever was missing in one was present in the other. 

In this way, nothing concerning the matters proposed has been left untouched or unsaid until now. When considering the year 1503, in which King **FERDINAND** was born, no nocturnal lunar eclipse is found; therefore, going backward to the day of conception (since this time must also be reckoned alongside the birth), an eclipse of the Moon is found to occur exactly in the middle of the period between conception and birth, namely on the 15th day of October in the year 1502. 

Now, following the rules of the previous instructions, for one seeking the time of the true full moon, it will be clear that the midpoint of this eclipse—that is, the space where it is usually greatest—occurred on the predicted day at 12 hours and 11 minutes in the afternoon, according to the meridian of Ingolstadt <note>a city in Bavaria where the author, Peter Apian, was a professor</note>. To compare this with the clock of Medina del Campo <note>original: "Medina," referring to Ferdinand's birthplace in Spain</note>...

# CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY

## PLANAR FIGURE OF THE ECLIPSE during the coronation of Charles.

<margin>
The coronation of CHARLES performed at Bologna.
</margin>

I believe I have now sufficiently explained all the methods of eclipses, so much so that anyone, no matter the specific form, can immediately recognize them and depict them on a plane <note>original: "in plano"; a flat surface or piece of paper</note> before their eyes. However, to ensure that nothing is missing for the sake of total accuracy, I wish to add a "finishing touch" <note>original: "coronidem"; a Greek-derived term for a final flourish or appendix</note>, as they say. I choose the never-to-be-forgotten year of the coronation of CHARLES V, Emperor of the Romans, which was celebrated in Bologna, a city in Italy—though it is hard to say whether it is more excellent for its power or its abundance of every kind of learning. That year was 1530. While I was examining this year using the instrument, it appeared to me that an eclipse of the Moon could occur on a day in October. Re-examining the moment of opposition <note>The time when the Sun and Moon are directly opposite each other, required for a full moon and thus a lunar eclipse.</note>, it occurred at 12 hours and 31 minutes according to the meridian of Ingolstadt; however, for the meridian of Bologna, 10 minutes must be added (since Bologna is further east than Ingolstadt by that many minutes). Having found the time of the true opposition using unequated days <note>original: "diebus non æquatis"; referring to apparent solar time before adjusting for the Equation of Time.</note>, the motions necessary for the upcoming eclipse were then sought, which were as follows: The true position of the Moon was 22 degrees and 44 minutes of Aries. The true position of the Sun was 22 degrees and 4 minutes of Libra. The true argument of the Moon <note>A coordinate used to find the Moon's distance from the nodes of its orbit.</note> was 5 signs, 4 degrees, 15 minutes, and 19 seconds. The argument of the Sun was 5 signs, 3 degrees, 27 minutes, and 18 seconds. Preparing a plane for this—whether you prefer paper or wood—I erect two perpendicular lines meeting at center A. You see the argument of latitude at the beginning, 5 signs, 6 degrees and some minutes; therefore, from point T, as has been said, I draw a straight line called M A T. In the semidiameter instrument, when the thread marks the Sun's argument (which is 5 signs, 3 degrees, 27 minutes, 18 seconds), the little arc

<column-break/>

of the circle shows a variation of the shadow of 40 <term>z̈</term> <note>original: "z̈"; likely referring to scrupula or minutes of a degree</note> to be reserved. Then, placing the thread over the true argument of the Moon (5 signs, 15 minutes, 19 seconds), it intercepts the circle of the blackened area—the internal at point M and the external at point O. Now, by taking the distance of M from the center of the instrument, the true size of the lunar semidiameter is shown. The interval between M and O will be called the semidiameter of the shadow at the time the Moon passes through, except that the 40 <term>z̈</term> previously found must be subtracted by moving from O toward N, which occurs at point L. Let that span of the compass now form a circle on the plane; since this is the size of the shadow, let it be labeled with the letters O S R Q. After this, taking the distance of the latitudinal argument from the aforementioned table and extending it on the plane starting from center A, let it be marked with the letter M. Resuming the measurement that represents the semidiameter of the Moon’s body, let it describe a circle A P from point M; for that circle truly shows the true size of the Moon—I mean the Moon contained within the shadow. Therefore, extend that same lunar semidiameter from R toward T, placing the letter L at the end. From center A, let a circle be made through that same point L. Likewise, let a perpendicular be erected from point M, so that the circle just drawn from center A touches the perpendicular at points R and N. From these same points R and N, let circles representing the size of the Moon be described; from this it becomes clear how the Moon advances from N to M, and from M all the way to R, and that it stands further from the ecliptic at the end than at the beginning. Since it happens here that the shadow covers the Moon's body most broadly, and it was said previously that there are at least 12 points <note>original: "puncta"; a standard unit for measuring eclipse magnitude, where 12 points equals the full diameter of the eclipsed body.</note> of the ecliptic, we are compelled to repeat the same here.

<margin>
What is to be understood by these eclipses.
</margin>

The matter stands thus: Whenever the shadow is seen to exceed 12 sections of the Moon, it must be measured by how many points the excess occurs, while maintaining the proportion of the lunar dimension. Since the present figure shows the shadow exceeding the Moon by 6 parts, a total eclipse of 18 points is judged to occur. This is understood not as the Moon consisting of that many points, but that if it did consist of that many, it could be blackened by the shadow, a matter which is placed before your eyes in the present figure.

# THE CAESAREAN
## TWENTY-EIGHTH PROPOSITION.

To execute everything that has been presented so far concerning the obscurations of the Moon in a different way than the preceding ones, yet with a more succinct and expeditious method.

In previous sections, it was shown how the points of lunar eclipses could be found with the help of a circle. There, the shadow of the earth was drawn on a flat surface, and the body of the Moon was traced over it; as many points as the eclipse encompassed were clearly exposed to the eyes. Here, however, in the present instrument, one may more easily and promptly achieve five things simultaneously without the work of a compass, using only the application of a single "union" <note>An "union" refers to a joint or cursor on the moving parts of the paper instrument</note>. The first of these is what we have already mentioned: specifically, the points of the eclipse—that is, the twelve parts of the obscuration—are contained with precision. The second is how long the Moon remains thus obscured; that is, through how many hours and minutes it dwells in the shadows, which others call the "delay" <note>original: "mora"</note>. The third is the space of hours and minutes that comes between the beginning of a universal eclipse (if it be universal) or until the middle of it. The fourth is in how many degrees and minutes it completes this portion, which is otherwise called the "half-duration" (which the combination of the "time of incidence" <note>original: "tempus casus" — the time it takes for the Moon to enter the shadow</note>, as astronomers call it, and the "half-delay" constitute). The fifth is the path or transit—that is, that line which the Moon makes by its passage through the shadows—for the present instrument will show this much more perfectly than the preceding one.

<margin>Method of operation.</margin>
Therefore, anyone who intends to enjoy this instrument and intends to undoubtedly discover the five things already listed, should first of all collect the time of the true opposition, the degrees of the Sun and Moon, the Arguments <note>An "argument" is a mathematical value used as an input to find a planet's position on a chart or instrument</note> of the Sun and Moon, and lastly the latitude of the Moon—all the "fixed" data, so to speak; that is, those established for certain times. He should believe that, besides these, he will have no need for anything else at present. Although, in my judgment, there is an even closer way: first, an attempt should be made using the instrument decorated with dragons <note>Referring to the "draco" or nodal instrument used to determine if the Moon is near its nodes, which is the only time an eclipse can occur</note> to check the possibility of an eclipse, having examined both the day that precedes and the day that follows; for once the true locations of both are stated (namely the known meridians, that is, the positions of the Sun and Moon), I think it escapes no one during which noons the proposed opposition might insert itself. This matter having been noticed with precision, then collect the daily movements of the Moon taken from the noons of both days; through the daily movements, afterward hunt for the hour of true opposition with the help of the 26th Proposition, or by another method you have been taught. Once the hour of true opposition is recognized, seek the certain locations of the Sun and Moon by Signs, degrees, and minutes, and look up the true Argument of the Moon from the same, together with the lunar latitude, and likewise the true Argument of the Sun. Once these are collected, nothing will be lacking for the operator in general, even though nothing is needed here for the Solar and Lunar position except the Arguments of the Sun and Moon and the considered latitude of the same. Having the Arguments of the Moon and Sun, and its latitude, immediately seek the signs, degrees, and minutes of the Solar Argument in the upper limb from B toward C (if it is less than 6 Signs; but if greater, seek it in the interior limb from C toward B). Once the location of the Solar Argument is found, place the thread upon it and hold it immobile. After this, hunt for the signs and degrees of the Lunar Argument in lines F G or D E. Then adjust the thread from point S together with the bead <note>original: "margarita" — a small bead or pearl used as a marker on the string of the instrument</note> over the location of the Lunar Argument on line F G or D E, moving it until the bead touches the thread of the Solar Argument; mark that touch with the other bead hanging on thread A, and keep it unchanged; thus guard A.

¶ Now, if you labor to know whether the Moon is obscured and by how many points the overshadowing occurs, move thread A over the minutes of latitude on arc H I, and the bead in area H I N O indicates by how many points and minutes the obscuration of the Moon occurs. If the bead falls into the black area, a universal eclipse can be predicted, and it will be as much greater than a universal one as it sits more deeply within.

<margin>Second use.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, note the said minutes of Latitude in arc I K with thread A; while this is done, the bead shows the hours and minutes of the half-delay of the Moon in area I K O P.

<margin>Third use.</margin>
¶ Then, when the thread is placed over the latitude of the Moon in arc K L, the minutes intersected from the union in area K L P Q appear—if any are elapsed beyond an hour, or just minutes—up to the total obscuration, provided it becomes total. But if it is not total, meanwhile, from the beginning up to the middle of the eclipse, the same hours with minutes, or minutes only (both of which are called the "time of incidence"), are shown.

<margin>Fourth use.</margin>
¶ If the bead falls into area K P T V, then the time of incidence is always seen to be one hour and some minutes. But if the bead extends beyond line T V toward L Q, then it indicates only minutes, marked by ciphers.

<margin>Fifth use.</margin>
¶ The movement of the Moon during the time of half-duration is known thus: the minutes of latitude are sought in arc L M, upon which the thread is placed; once placed, the bead in area L M Q R shows most clearly to the eyes how many minutes of motion the Moon has tra-

<column-break/>

<margin>CHARLES</margin>
-versed from the beginning of the eclipse until the middle of the same (this time is called the half-duration). All of this, now proposed in general, will be elucidated by a special example. ¶ It has been repeated here several times that the Divine CHARLES <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor</note> was born in the year 1500; moreover, the possibility of an eclipse was seen to be contained in the 5th day of November of that same year; and although this matter has been demonstrated more than enough, we will repeat it even more clearly. Previously, a double method was shown by which both the hours and minutes of any opposition could be obtained: one which is provided from the daily motion (though that is double, i.e., of two days); the other, through the instrument assigned for conjunctions and oppositions, taught the same in its own place and proposition. Furthermore, you have been taught how the latitude of the Moon is to be found, not only at the opposition, but at all times, with the true position of the Moon and the head of the dragon <note>The ascending lunar node</note> already known. In this place, however, there is still a need for the Arguments of the Sun and Moon, equated precisely, and the lunar latitude; if you have these three, know that you have everything; if you complete the rest with these, they will occur in this order.

With the Solar and Lunar Arguments, and likewise the latitude of the Moon, having been inspected and now ready at hand, approach the following instrument. First, seek the true Lunar Argument, which is 9 Signs 22 m 59 in ♏ (Scorpio), on line D E, near the hanger of the ring; having found it, look over thread S, which is near letter A, and apply the bead to the already enumerated Lunar Argument. Then, place the other thread dropped from point A over the Solar Argument, 5 signs 6 degrees 23 m 39 in arc B C; hold this unmoved with the left hand, and with the right hand move thread S a little, and you will see it intersect thread A at point C; the bead of thread A is placed in that location, and thus you will have governed the bead for use. After this, count 29 minutes of Lunar latitude in arc H I; once counted, place thread A over it, which shows in area N H I O the 10 points <note>Digits of eclipse; 10 points means 10/12ths of the Moon is covered</note> in which the Moon is obscured (for these are parts of the entire body of the Moon); that same point is also marked with the letter C. The time of the Moon enclosed in shadows, which they call the delay, is not present in this instance, since the union does not yet fully reach 12 points. However, suppose someone hunts for the time of the delay through the obscuration and extends the thread over 29 minutes in arc I K; no time of delay will occur, as the bead is carried outside the line signifying this time, just as point C represents in this place written on line K P; for it lies flat and indicates no delay, as is evident to the eyes. ¶ When the thread is brought to 29 minutes in arc K L, the union shows 1 hour 35 minutes, which is called the time of incidence (and because this eclipse lacks a delay) also the half-duration. Whenever the bead falls into area K P T V, it must be known that one hour is perpetually to be added to the minutes, which hour is then added with the ciphers. ¶ Finally, bring the thread also into arc L M at 29 minutes, and you will see the bead cut 49 minutes, noted there with the letter C; namely, the time which the Moon completes from the beginning up to the middle of the failure. Now if you subtract the half-duration of the eclipse from the middle, the beginning of the failure is left at 12 hours 17 m. If you add the same amount—that is, the half-duration—to the beginning of the failure, you will have the end of it, which is 15 hours 27 m. In this way, therefore, you shall most perfectly know everything that is to be known in a failure <note>A "failure" (deliquium) is an archaic term for an eclipse</note>.

<margin>Example of FERDINAND</margin>
¶ Another example: that eclipse which happened near the time when King FERDINAND <note>Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V</note> had spent nearly half his time in the womb, in the year 1502, on the 15th day of October, at 12 hours 11 m after noon by the Ingolstadt clock, but corresponding to 10 hours 23 m by the meridian of Medina (understanding this as the middle time of the event); this was seen. The true location of the Moon here was 1 degree 32 m in ♈ (Aries). The location of the ☉ (Sun) was 3 degrees 32 m. The Argument of the ☉ (Sun) was 5 signs 4 degrees 2 m 12. The true Argument of the ☾ (Moon) was 6 signs 15 m 33. The true location of the ☊ (Node) was 0 signs 23 m 39. The Argument of the latitude of the ☾ (Moon) was 0 signs 10 m 23. The latitude of the ☾ (Moon) was 55 minutes North. When you have collected these, first look up the Solar Argument in arc B C, and the Lunar in line D E; according to these two, the ordered union rests on point R. Now if you act with the thread and bead as was demonstrated before, the individual items marked with the letter R will offer themselves, expressed in both hours and minutes, as they are written below.

THE EMPEROR'S ASTRONOMY

## ECLIPSES OF THE EMPERORS CHARLES & FERDINAND.

IN THIS place also, it is pleasing to teach a different way than before for how you may depict the path of the Moon. As soon as you have described the figure of the <term>eclipse</term> <note>original: "defectus"; literally a "failing" or "waning" of light</note> and the lunar body on a flat surface, and marked within it the <term>Argument of lunar latitude</term> <note>This is a technical term for the Moon’s distance from the "nodes" or the points where its path crosses the Earth's orbit, which determines if an eclipse occurs.</note>—which represents the distance of the Moon from the center of the shadow at the time of the maximum eclipse (called the "middle of the eclipse")—you should mark this point with the letter **M**. Soon after, subtract the Moon’s motion, which it completes in the time of half the eclipse's duration, from the Argument of latitude. Mark the signs, degrees, and minutes remaining from this subtraction in the required <term>layout</term> <note>original: "dispositorio"; likely referring to one of the moving paper instruments, or "volvelles," for which this book is famous.</note> with a specific point.

Then, taking the distance of this point from the center of the layout with a compass, transfer it onto the shadow on the line **A M L**, beginning at center **A**. You shall write this distance starting from **M**, wherever it may fall—whether toward the center or away from it. From that point, draw a straight line to the right, parallel to the line **M N**. Where this line touches the circle **L N**, mark it with the letter **X**; for there is the center of the lunar body at the moment the eclipse began. 

Next, add the motion of the Moon during the half-duration to the Argument of latitude of the middle of the eclipse. When this is done, the Argument of latitude corresponding to the end of the eclipse will result. Examine that same Argument in the Layout as well, and arrange its distance on the line **A M L** using your compass, marking it with point **d**. From there, draw a straight line to the left, parallel to line **M K**. Mark its junction with the circle **L K** with the letter **V** (for this is the center of the Moon as it is positioned at the end of the eclipse). 

Now, if you draw the circles around **V** and **X** with a proper rotation, and connect the letters **V** and **X** with a straight line, you will create the truest path of the Moon through the shadow. You can also obtain those two points, **c** and **d**, more easily in this way: choose any single degree in the layout and count within it as many minutes as there are in the Moon’s motion during the half-duration. Extend the feet of the compass to match those minutes. Then, with the compass held at that fixed width, place one foot on **M** and mark two points on either side; mark one with **c** and the other with **d**. From these two points thus prepared, according to what was said before, the parallel lines are to be drawn, and so forth.

Argument of the Moon's latitude in the Example of the Emperor, <note>Referring to Emperor Charles V.</note>

¶ At the beginning of the eclipse: 5 signs, 11 degrees, 24 minutes, 10 seconds
¶ At the Middle of the eclipse: 5 signs, 11 degrees, 24 minutes, 39 seconds
¶ At the end of the eclipse: 5 signs, 11 degrees, 25 minutes, 8 seconds
¶ Motion of the Moon: 29 minutes

Argument of the Moon's latitude in the example of the King, <note>Referring to Ferdinand I, King of the Romans (later Emperor).</note>

¶ At the beginning of the eclipse: 5 signs, 0 degrees, 9 minutes, 28 seconds
¶ At the Middle of the eclipse: 5 signs, 0 degrees, 10 minutes, 23 seconds
¶ At the end of the eclipse: 5 signs, 0 degrees, 11 minutes, 18 seconds
¶ Motion of the Moon: 55 minutes

## THIRD EXAMPLE

Let this third example be of a lunar eclipse <note>original: "Lunaris deliquii"; literally a failing or waning of the Moon</note> occurring in the year 1530, when the Imperial Crown was placed upon CHARLES at Bologna, while royal majesty was conferred upon FERDINAND at Aachen—both insignias of the Roman Empire, most worthy of these imperial brothers. If you prefer to treat this eclipse according to the method recently handed down, and wish to see the passage of the Moon through the shadows by the way just shown, and to know precisely the other factors considered in an eclipse, set before yourself these values written below, just as they are:

¶ Argument of the Sun: 3 signs, 27 deg. 18 min.
¶ True Argument of the Moon: 4 signs, 15 deg. 19 min.
¶ Latitude of the Moon: 14 minutes.

Therefore, if you direct the <term>bead</term> <note>original: "margaritam"; a small bead moved along a string on Apian's paper instruments to mark specific data points</note> according to the Arguments of the Sun and Moon, and have already plotted the path of the Moon in a straight line (as previously described), you will find all these subjoined values with the help of the lunar latitude:

¶ Ecliptic points <note>original: "Puncta ecliptica"; these indicate the magnitude of the eclipse—here, 16 points and 36 minutes indicates a total eclipse, as any value over 12 represents the Moon being completely immersed in the shadow.</note>: 16 min. 36
¶ Middle delay <note>The duration of the total phase of the eclipse.</note>: 44 minutes
¶ Time of the fall <note>The time from first contact with the shadow until the start of totality.</note>: 1 hour, 8 min.
¶ Half duration: 1 hour, 52 min.
¶ Motion of the Moon: 64 minutes.

THE EMPEROR'S ASTRONOMY

# THE EMPEROR'S ASTRONOMY
## TWENTY-NINTH PROPOSITION.
### That the passage of time in history, both before and after Christ, can be perfectly corrected through examples of eclipses, such as those added below.

<margin>A notable example of a lunar eclipse brought forth from Plutarch.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' within a circular frame decorated with stars, clouds, and celestial imagery.</image-desc>
To see thoroughly what power, excellence, and utility the knowledge of eclipses contains within itself, I have been compelled to add some examples from before Christ, from which the benefit may be seen more clearly than from previous ones. No one is unaware that recorders of events and histories, in numbering the years both of the world and of the founding of the City <note>The "founding of the City" refers to the traditional date of Rome's founding (753 BC), often used as a chronological anchor (Ab Urbe Condita).</note>, nearly "fall from heaven itself," as the saying goes <note>An idiom suggesting they are completely lost or profoundly mistaken.</note>. How much darkness, ignorance, doubt, and confusion this error brings into judging and understanding all other history is for the learned to judge. For from this it happens that if they remind the Christian reader of some event, at least a memorable one, which either preceded the founding of the City or followed not long after, they can by no means agree among themselves. Only the knowledge of eclipses can correct and improve such a great evil. For through eclipses, all things can be brought back to certain years—those preceding Christ no less than those following. Once a historian has found a certain time for a specific deed, he is able to gather the remaining spans of elapsed deeds, both forward and backward. All this will be made abundantly clear by examples.

<margin>Plutarch in the *Life of Alexander*</margin>
is the authority who states that in the month of June, when the mysteries were beginning at Athens, the Moon failed <note>original: "defecisse"; suffered an eclipse</note> in the same year that Alexander defeated Darius, King of the Persians. Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian and bishop, famous for his "Chronicon" which attempted to sync world history.</note> testifies that this happened in the seventh year of Darius's reign. But here there is doubt as to what year his reign began. Eusebius says Darius was defeated in the year of the world 4871; therefore, if you subtract 4871 from 5199 (for that is the total years Eusebius counts from the creation of the world to Christ), then 328 remains. Thus, according to Eusebius, Darius must have been conquered by Alexander 328 years before Christ. But this is found to be quite different. Let Eusebius, or any other chronographer you like, be off by 18 full years, or have wandered 12 years ahead of the truth regarding the death of Darius; however, I will never be able to err even by a single day (with this one point added: that near the death of Darius, the Moon suffered an eclipse in the month of June in that same year), as I trust is made clear enough from the following. Indeed, looking at the Eusebian year for the 

<column-break/>

present <note>original: "præsentia"; referring to the year under discussion</note>, namely 328 BC, you will recognize that no eclipse at all occurred in June; indeed, across many years, neither before nor after, did any failing of the light fall in June. But in the current and incomplete year 326 before Christ, a lunar obscuration occurred, specifically on the 28th of June, as is made evident. Therefore, regarding the same eclipse which Eusebius asserts happened in 328 BC, it is established that he deviates from the truth by two full years. Whoever wishes to understand this matter plainly should proceed as follows.

<margin>The Error of Eusebius</margin>
The "great hundred" of years is 400. The <term>Radix</term> <note>The "root" or starting value used for astronomical calculations.</note> of the conjunction of the Moon ☾ and Sun ☉ is 6 days, 1 hour, 40 minutes. Furthermore, the Radix of the Moon ☾ and the <term>Dragon's Head</term> ☊ <note>The ascending node where the Moon crosses the ecliptic; eclipses only occur near these "nodes."</note> has 19 days, 20 hours, 15 minutes. When one who is about to work has collected these and arranged the indices X and Z, and has surveyed the years with these, he will find no opportunity for an eclipse except in the aforementioned year 326, where the Dragon's Head, together with the Sun ☉ and Moon ☾, points to the 28th day of June. But this usually happens if the pointers are set according to the remaining years, namely 75 beyond 400. To one examining the <term>opposition</term> <note>The Full Moon, when the Moon is opposite the Sun.</note> of the true opposition, it appears that 11 hours and 25 minutes must be subtracted between the mean and true opposition. Once these are subtracted, the true opposition is seen to fall on the 28th day of June, at 8 hours and 39 minutes, near the <term>Dragon's Tail</term> <note>The descending node of the Moon's orbit.</note>. The remaining values now necessary to track the eclipse are these:

¶ Argument of Latitude: 5 signs, 6 degrees, 7 minutes, 20 seconds.
¶ Latitude of the Moon: 38 minutes, 15 seconds.
¶ Motion of the Dragon's Head: 5 signs, 2 degrees, 23 minutes, 56 seconds.
¶ True Argument of the Moon: 5 signs, 8 degrees, 27 minutes, 22 seconds.
¶ True place of the Sun ☉: 6 signs, 1 minute, 16 seconds.
¶ True place of the Moon ☾: 0 signs, 1 minute, 16 seconds.
¶ <term>Apogee</term> <note>original: "Aux"; the point in the orbit farthest from Earth.</note> of the Sun ☉: 2 signs, 6 minutes, 20 seconds.
¶ Argument of the Sun: 5 signs, 25 degrees, 51 minutes.
¶ Variation of the Shadow: 3 and a half signs.

From all these you gather that eclipse which is depicted below. It appeared to those in Ingolstadt <note>The Bavarian city where Peter Apian was a professor and printed this book.</note> at 8:39 PM. Anyone wishing to compare this to the meridian of the Assyrian city of Gaugamela <note>original: "Gangamelis"; the site of the Battle of Gaugamela where Alexander defeated Darius.</note>, where Darius was defeated, should add 3 hours and 12 minutes, found in the table of regions next to the city's name; and this is because it lies to the east <note>original: "ortui incumbit"; literally "it leans toward the rising [sun]"</note> by that many hours and minutes above Ingolstadt. By adding 3 hours and 12 minutes to the Ingolstadt time, the time when this failing was seen at Gaugamela will come forth as 11:51 PM. If you search for any of the necessary details of the failing according to the teaching of this present proposition, and assign the passage of the Moon correctly, you will find everything prepared in this manner, as follows:

¶ Beginning of Eclipse: 28th day, 10:26 PM ¶ <term>Points</term> <note>Magnitude of the eclipse measured in "digits" or points; 12 points signifies a total eclipse.</note>: 7 min. 15
¶ Middle of Eclipse: 28th day, 11:51 PM ¶ Time of the fall <note>The duration from the start to the middle of the eclipse.</note>: 1 hour 25 min.
¶ End of Eclipse: 28th day, 12:16 AM ¶ Motion of the Moon: 44 minutes.

<meta>This page continues the author's demonstration of how astronomical data, specifically lunar eclipses, can act as a chronological anchor to resolve discrepancies between historical accounts. Having established the principle on the previous page, Apian now applies it to the specific case of Alexander the Great's victory over the Persian King Darius III, comparing the dates provided by the historians Eusebius and Alfonso X of Castile against the movements of the heavens.</meta>

THE EMPEROR'S ASTRONOMY

<margin>Darius defeated by Alexander according to Alfonso.</margin>
Truly, as I said in the previous sections, no eclipse is found in June except in the 32nd year after the date given by Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea was a 4th-century historian whose "Chronicon" set the standard for Christian chronology.</note>; I wish for you to judge the matter thus. In the twelfth year after the Persian War, according to Eusebius, moving toward the time of Christ, a lunar eclipse of 6 points and 20 minutes <note>A "point" or "digit" represents one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body; 6 points indicates that half the Moon was obscured.</note> occurred on June 18th, at 11:32 PM. Alfonso <note>Referring to the Alfonsine Tables commissioned by King Alfonso X of Castile in the 13th century.</note>, however, established that same year of Darius’s defeat by Alexander as the starting point in his own eras. This is clear from this argument: Alfonso asserts that 311 years and 93 days elapsed from the death of Alexander until the birth of Christ. Now, since Alexander defeated Darius five years before his own death (as histories unanimously agree), if one adds those five years to the 311, it results in 316 years. Therefore, according to Alfonso, Darius was defeated by Alexander exactly that many completed years before Christ. But these twelve years mentioned before are more recent and closer to Christ, occurring later than the calculation Eusebius established. Thus, Alfonso and I approach the time of Christ nine years more closely than Eusebius does. 

But I ask you, which of these should you trust more? Alfonso? Truly, he nowhere produces a clear explanation for his calculation. Or Eusebius? He connects histories with such an accurate sequence that it seems incredible he could be mistaken by as many as twelve years. Nevertheless, even Eusebius falls short by three years, which were omitted through negligence (as is likely); I have correctly identified these beyond any doubt. For our eclipse is the closest to Eusebius’s account, since histories testify that Darius was defeated in June at the time of an eclipse. Even though Eusebius was a most accurate calculator, he nonetheless slipped from the true year; for a June eclipse did not occur in the year he assigns to Darius’s defeat, nor in the two following years, but in the third year, which we have identified. But perhaps I seem too eager to vindicate Eusebius from these errors; yet one should not think I am detracting anything from Alfonso, simply because he does not cite the reasoning for his calculation. He likely foresaw that such precision would never be demanded by anyone, thinking it safe enough if he took Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Almagest" was the foundation of the field.</note> as his guide, who also numbered his calculations from the death of Alexander the Great. For it was the custom of those nations to observe the reigns of their kings even after they were deceased, not 

aliter
<meta>catchword: otherwise</meta>

<column-break/>

otherwise than we measure the years from the birth of Christ our Savior. Indeed, Ptolemy seems to count 463 years after Alexander's death until the time of future observations, which began in the 152nd year after the birth of our Savior, in the third book of his *Great Construction* <note>original: "magnae suae constructionis," better known by its Arabic title, the *Almagest*.</note>. From this it is clear enough that Alfonso likewise derived his calculations along with Ptolemy from the death of Alexander, which was recorded as 311 years before Christ. If we wish to follow Ptolemy in this matter, as we certainly ought to—since his calculation is undoubtedly true as one who lived not so long after Alexander and because of his diligence in observation (for he directed all other times toward this temporal source or origin)—he could by no means be mistaken. If, I say, we wish to follow him, why should Alfonso not also be followed? 

But what do you do here in the third year after Eusebius? In that year, a lunar eclipse is found that is in no way dissimilar to the one that occurred previously under Alfonso’s time. It is of exactly the same magnitude (as both the preceding and following figures show) as the one which fell in Alfonso’s year, and it also happened at the same time. Truly, I cease to judge the matter further as it stands, since it is not my present purpose to fully correct the histories, but only to indicate and prepare a path toward accomplishing that. One day, if God grants life, we shall revise the histories in their entirety and firmly establish them by the calculations of eclipses, where we shall repeat both this and other examples. Let us therefore return to the proposal.
