THE EMPEROR'S ASTRONOMY

### THE THIRTIETH STATEMENT.

To judge historical errors even more clearly through another example of an obscured Moon—specifically one preceding the time of Christ.

<margin>
Livy reports the eclipse of Sulpicius Gallus as occurring one day later than it actually happened.
</margin>

<margin>
Perseus began to reign in the year 175 before Christ, according to Eusebius <note>Eusebius was a 4th-century bishop and historian whose "Chronicon" was the primary source for dating ancient events in the Renaissance.</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
Eusebius is clearly proven to be in error by six years in his assertion of the reign of Perseus.
</margin>

Livy writes in the fourth book of his fifth Decade that Gaius Sulpicius Gallus predicted a coming lunar eclipse to the army of Lucius Aemilius Paulus. This occurred when Paulus defeated Perseus, the last king of Macedonia, in Samothrace and led him captive to Rome. Gallus predicted it so that the soldiers would not be struck by terror <note>Ancient soldiers often viewed eclipses as divine omens of doom; Gallus used science to maintain morale.</note>, as the causes of lunar eclipses were not yet commonly known to the public. Plutarch, in his *Life of Nicias*, asserts that solar eclipses had long been considered no miracle, but the same was not true for the Moon. Livy claims that Gallus predicted the eclipse would occur on the night following the day before the Nones of September <note>In the Roman calendar, the "day before the Nones of September" is September 4th.</note>. However, it is possible to learn with absolute certainty that this was not the case. It actually occurred on the night before the third day of the Nones <note>September 3rd.</note>—as if you were to say the eclipse happened on the night preceding Monday, rather than the night preceding Tuesday. It is impossible for Livy's timeframe to admit an eclipse, nor can there be any other date than our own calculation. This is because in the nearest nineteen years, neither before nor after, has any eclipse of the Moon been seen to fall on this day. Pliny also mentions this same eclipse in the second book of his *Natural History*, chapter 12, but slightly differently, as he did not express the day precisely. Therefore, to predict the year and day of this eclipse, first observe when Perseus lived. According to Eusebius, he was made ruler of Macedonia in the year 5024 from the creation of the world, in the third year of the 151st Olympiad, which would be 175 years before the birth of Christ. But since Perseus held power for ten years, it is clear he was defeated by Lucius Paulus in the year 165 before Christ. Yet, even that is not correct. Rather, according to the occurrence of the eclipse, Perseus is found to have been captured in the year 172 before Christ. You shall calculate it in this manner: if you count backward 171 full and complete years from the birth of Christ,

<column-break/>

(noting that one must include the year of the Nativity in the count) and then add the months of December, November, and October, going backward to the third day of September, you will then hold the true year of Perseus's downfall. However, this kind of temporal reasoning will by no means satisfy those who strive to show the succession of historical annals based on the founding of the city of Rome <note>The Roman "Ab Urbe Condita" (AUC) dating system often conflicted with the Christian "Anno Domini" (AD) or "Before Christ" (BC) systems used by Renaissance scholars.</note>, as they disagree significantly. To understand the present example, let us first propose the year 165 in which Perseus fell, according to Eusebius. Whether that is the true year or not will not escape us by this method. From the greater century of 200 <note>Apian uses 200 AD as his "radix" or base reference point for his calculations.</note> we subtract 165, leaving 35. We now look at the "Radix" <note>A base value or starting point for astronomical tables.</note> of the Sun ☉ and Moon ☽ for the year 200, which is 14 days, 18 hours, and 21 minutes. We likewise inspect the Radix for the conjunction of the Dragon's Head ☊ and the Moon ☽, which has 7 days, 18 hours, and 50 minutes. We move the indices X and Z on the "Instrument of the Dragons" <note>Referring to the volvelle or paper computer in this book used to calculate the lunar nodes (represented by a dragon).</note> over these same base values. Similarly, we move V and Y annually until an opposition occurring in the Head or Tail of the Dragon appears. This ought to happen on the second, third, or fourth day of September. Truly, as we do this, no year other than 29 years after our base date presents itself as having an eclipse on these days. Therefore, subtracting 29 years from 200, 171 years remain; if we add the remaining months going backward to the third day of September, we announce the true year of the eclipse. Indeed, if you very diligently examine 20 or 30 years before or after, you will never find that same lunar eclipse occurring on that day. I say on that specific day, including the night, for as has been said, the Moon is not said to suffer an eclipse during the day. Therefore, after the base year of 200, seeking the mean opposition of the 29th year in September, you find 2 days, 17 hours, and 6 minutes. Between the true and mean opposition, you see 4 hours and 25 minutes must be subtracted; with those subtracted, you see that 12 hours and 41 minutes remain as the time of true opposition. The remaining values required for the eclipse are these:

<margin>Eusebius’s error in determining the end of the Macedonian Empire.</margin>
<margin>How Livy is to be understood regarding the hours of the eclipse.</margin>
Finally, the time of the true opposition <note>The moment of the Full Moon.</note> for the Macedonian event (specifically when Perseus was defeated) should be referenced to the local meridian. Since he was captured in Samothrace, we have preferred the meridian of Samothrace. Therefore, using the table of regions, we find 1 hour and 32 minutes; by adding this to the time of true opposition in Ingolstadt, the result is 2:13 PM <note>Apian is adjusting for the longitude difference between his home in Ingolstadt and the site of the battle.</note>, which was the mid-point of the eclipse at Samothrace. From this, it is clearly evident that Eusebius is six years too late in his assertion of Perseus’s capture and the end of the Macedonian Empire. As for what Livy says—that this eclipse was seen from the second hour of the night until the fourth—we must consider that the hours were not counted exactly. In this passage, Livy begins counting not from sunset, but more likely from twilight, as is common among the general public. He perhaps imitated the popular opinion, especially that of the soldiers, whose observation is more focused on slaughter than on the heavens, their minds more intent on the spear than the pole <note>A play on words in Latin: "pilo" (spear) versus "polo" (the celestial pole/heavens).</note>, and their contemplation of salvation placed in fortresses rather than the stars. Therefore, let the errors committed here by military negligence not move us at all; instead, let us take 12:29 AM <note>original: "horam 12... cum minus 29"</note> as the true beginning of the eclipse.

### ANOTHER EXAMPLE OF CORRUPTED HISTORY taken from Plutarch,

<margin>Nicias’s mind seemed most troubled during the siege.</margin>
<margin>When the war of Nicias was waged.</margin>
<margin>The translator of Plutarch is censured first.</margin>
Plutarch, in his *Life of Nicias*, the leader of the Athenians, relates that Nicias—having been somewhat surrounded by the Syracusans whom he had been besieging for some time—decided to depart with his men by night. This was exactly thirteen days before he and Demosthenes were captured, as can be gathered from the history. But by chance, it happened that the Moon was eclipsed on that same night. Because of this, Nicias and all the soldiers were violently disturbed; due to their ignorance of the cause, they feared it portended some great evil for them. For at that time, Anaxagoras had only just begun to teach the true reasons for the Moon's movements, which were not yet known to the public. But it remains to be investigated when this darkening of the Moon occurred, for this is the point of infinite debate. Eusebius, in his chronicles, writes that this war was waged in the year of the world 4782; this number demonstrates it was the year 417 before the incarnation of Christ, or the second year of the 90th Olympiad. Reality itself shows that this is not the case at all, but rather it happened in the third year after this—specifically 414 BC—on the 8th of September. At that time, not long after its rising, the Moon was shadowed by a fourth part of itself (that is, to three points). The year cited by Eusebius contains no eclipse, nor do several years after or before it; thus, there can be no other date but ours. Furthermore, Plutarch mentions that Nicias was captured shortly after by the Syracusans near the Asinarus River with these words: "It was the 24th day of the month, which they call Carneios, and the Athenians call <term>Metagitnion</term> <note>original Greek: μεταγειτνιῶνα; an Attic month roughly corresponding to late summer.</note>; but I believe the Latins call it May." In this place, the translator of Plutarch forces me to be more wordy, as he stumbles twice quite seriously, introducing irrelevant side-notes that do nothing for the text and which, unless refuted, greatly overturn our purpose. ¶ The first error is in saying "It was the twenty-fourth day of the month," where it should read the twenty-seventh, not the twenty-fourth. The Greek text uses the phrase <term>tetarta phthinontos</term> <note>original Greek: τέταρτη φθίνοντος</term>, which signifies the fourth day, but specifically the fourth day *before the end of the month*. The Athenians were accustomed to count the last ten days of any month (for they divided every month into three decades) backward, calling them <term>phthinontos</term>, that is, "of the waning" Moon or month. Thus, the last day was called <term>ene kai nea</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνη καί νέα</note>, meaning "old and new"; the second-to-last was "the second of the waning," the third-to-last was "the third," and the day before that was called "the fourth of the waning." From this, it is established that <term>tetarta phthinontos</term>, which

<column-break/>

<margin>The translator of Plutarch is argued against a second time.</margin>
Plutarch calls the "fourth," is actually the twenty-seventh day of the month, not the twenty-fourth. ¶ The second error is where it is said, "I believe the Latins call it May." For those are not the words of Plutarch, but a completely fabricated commentary by the translator, and if we concede to it, it is most contrary to our work. In my judgment, the reason that drove that translator to call *Metagitnion* "May" is this: Aristotle writes in the sixth book of the *History of Animals* that bears mate in the month of *Elaphebolion*, carry their young for 30 days, and then emerge from their dens in the third month after birth, when spring is already present (for the words sound like <term>ede tou earos</term> <note>original Greek: ἤδη τοὺ ἔαρος; "already of the spring."</note>). Pliny likewise, in the eighth book of his *Natural History*, chapter 36, reports that the mating of bears occurs at the beginning of winter and the birth on the 30th day. If they mate at the beginning of winter, as Pliny writes, it must be that the month <term>Elaphebolion</term> <note>original Greek: Ελαφηβολιῶν</note> is the first of the winter months. Therefore, if one follows Aristotle and Pliny and examines all the Greek months in order, one finds *Elaphebolion* in the ninth place, corresponding to the Latin December (which is itself the beginning of winter). Consequently, *Hecatombaeon* would coincide with April, and *Metagitnion* with May. But in the comparison of Greek and Latin months below, the translator behaved as if this war had been waged in our own time. In our age, the Sun enters Capricorn (near where we calculate the true beginning of winter) on the 10th day of December. For this reason, the translator compared the ninth Greek month, *Elaphebolion*, to December, *Munichion* to January, *Thargelion* to February, *Scirophorion* to March, and so on. But it was far different in Aristotle's time; to estimate it by the present is a mistake. For in the age of the war or of Aristotle (which were nearly the same), the Sun entered Capricorn not on the 10th, but in the final days of December. Thus, January should rather have been chosen for the start of the year and called *Elaphebolion*. If he had done this, he could have seen that the beginning of the Attic year extended even into June. Furthermore, if he had considered that the Athenians began their years at the new moons, and that it happened (as it did during the war) that the start of the year sometimes progressed into July, he would have easily understood that the second month, *Metagitnion*, could coincide with August and September.

<margin>He deduces from Aristotle what kind of beginning of the year the Athenians established.</margin>
Indeed, Aristotle himself supports this in the eighth book of the *History of Animals*, where he treats deer, which he openly testifies celebrate their mating in the months of *Boedromion* and *Metagitnion*. This happens for us at the beginning of September, with the Sun occupying the fifteenth degree of Virgo, near the star called the Lion's Tail <note>Denebola.</note>. But considering Aristotle’s era, it appears to have happened around the middle of September, since the Sun reached the first degree of Virgo at the beginning of September. Therefore, the month of *Boedromion* was something further along—indeed, extended from September into October—and by similar reasoning, the month of *Metagitnion*, having begun in August, finally ended in September. Furthermore, it is so clear that Plutarch intended *Metagitnion* to mean September that it requires no other proof than to weigh his own words more sincerely. For he says: "At the time when Nicias prepared his departure, he proposed this as the greatest reason for his journey: namely, that the beginning of Autumn was already weighing heavily, and the air, becoming corrupt, was bringing a sudden plague" (for not a few of the soldiers were already dying). Indeed, a few lines later the same author adds: "Since they had been left (specifically after the slaughter) in a low-lying place, they were failing first from the Sun and heat in the open air. Then, with the frost of the autumnal nights coming upon them, they contracted illness from the very change of opposites." Add to this that Thucydides, the most accurate writer of Greek history, holds the same view as Plutarch regarding this war, which was waged during Thucydides’ lifetime. I have added his words here, lest anyone think this a deception. When he speaks of Nicias fleeing and being besieged near the hill of Lepada in the seventh book of the *Peloponnesian War*, near the end, he writes: "But when they were struck by so many men from a high place—for missiles were more easily hurled from above—and could not break through, they retreated and rested, especially as there were thunders and rains, such as usually happen in the time of year turning toward autumn. From this arose <unclear>fear</unclear>, and all the more vehemently, because they thought all these things were happening for their destruction."

<margin>By Plutarch's Metagitnion, however, September must be understood.</margin>
After these words, what is more manifest than that the time of the war was autumnal, as Plutarch also asserts? I believe it is sufficiently proven that in this passage, *Metagitnion* should not be taken as May, but more truly as September. When it is written that Nicias was captured on the twenty-seventh day, it is conjectured to have happened on the thirteenth day after the eclipse; for the Athenians, as will be said a little more fully below, were accustomed to number the days of their months according to the ages of the Moon. Furthermore, *Metagitnion* was the second month for the Athenians, from which anyone can readily understand that the beginning of that year commenced with the new moon closest after the summer solstice. At that time, the summer solstice occurred on the last day of June or the first of July. The beginning of Autumn, the entry of the Sun into Libra, was established on the second-to-last day of September. Therefore, since that eclipse occurred near the beginning of Autumn (for it was seen on the 8th of September), if you count back 15 days from that day, you will have the beginning of *Metagitnion*; counting back 30 days from there, you encounter the head of the month *Hecatombaeon* (the first month), which is the 26th of July. That day was usually the first New Moon following the summer solstice. Now, if the 27 days on which Nicias surrendered are counted within the month of *Metagitnion*, that same day is found to be the 20th of September. Finally, the Athenian numbers of their months...

<meta>This page continues Apian’s technical and historical analysis of chronology. Having corrected Eusebius’s dating of the fall of the Macedonian Empire on the previous page using the eclipse of 168 BC, he now shifts to the Greek calendar. He aims to prove that the Greeks used a lunar-based system by reconciling literary accounts from Plutarch and Thucydides with astronomical reality, specifically focusing on the ill-fated Athenian expedition to Sicily.</meta>

THE EMPEROR'S ASTRONOMY

It should be known that [the Greeks] adapted their months to the ages of the Moon—that is, they arranged them according to the new moons. This fact requires no proof, for the same author, Plutarch, testifies more than once that the Greeks accommodated their Calends, Nones, and Ides <note>The Roman divisions of the month, which Apian is using here to explain the Greek system</note> to the Moon, especially in his *Life of Romulus* when he says: "Now, therefore, the Roman Calends in no way agree with the Greeks." Furthermore, they rightly claim that the day on which Romulus laid the foundations of the city was the thirtieth day, on which the Moon failed <note>original: 'defecisse'; meaning eclipsed</note> from its meeting with the Sun, etc. From these accounts, it is clearly established that the Greeks numbered their days according to the phases of the Moon. I wish to warn in passing, however, that an error lies beneath the text where it is said "the Moon failed from the meeting of the Sun"; it should instead read "the Sun failed from the meeting of the Moon." For the Greek words clearly imply this, which read: <note>original: 'καὶ σύνοδομ ἐλλήνικἡ ἐν αὐτῇ γενέσθαι σελήνης πρὸς ἥλιον'</note> "and that an ecliptic conjunction of the moon with the sun occurred on that day." 

<column-break/>

If you interpret these words, they mean nothing other than that the Moon joined with the Sun in an eclipse on that same day. From this it is clear that it must have been the Sun, not the Moon, that was veiled, since the sphere of the Moon is far lower than that of the Sun. Thucydides also speaks in support of the former opinion in the second book of the *Peloponnesian War*, where he says: "In that same summer, at the Lunar Calends—that is, the new moon <term>interlunium|The period of the moon's invisibility during its conjunction with the sun</term> (the only time it is believed such a thing can happen)—the Sun failed at midday, with some stars appearing." Plutarch follows this with even more detail in his *Life of Solon*, saying: "The day which follows they call the *noumenia* <note>original: 'νουμηνίαν'</note>, that is, the Calends," etc. He reports similar things in many places. However, whatever has been said up to this point regarding the months and the beginning of the ancient Archons <note>The chief magistrates of Athens, used for dating years</note>, this entire matter can be taught to your eyes clearer than light in the following daily record.

# THROUGH EXAMPLES OF THIS KIND
I have intended to show, with these few examples thus far, how it is possible—with the help of lunar eclipses—to rescue historical accounts from the errors that frequently occur in them due to an incorrectly assigned reckoning of years. By a similar path at some point, God willing, I intend to treat the failings <note>original: 'deliquia'; meaning eclipses</note> of the Sun as well in a specific volume set forth for that purpose. In that work, diligent effort will be given so that the times of the founding of the city <note>Rome</note> may be truly recognized, without the guesswork by which we have long been left in the dark. For eclipses of the Sun are especially desired for understanding this; indeed, nothing is truer than the infallible sequence of the celestial movements. Finally, as a sort of side-task, I shall teach how the eclipses I have described so extensively may also be observed and examined with the eye. While there are many who use various instruments for seeing in different ways, they all use them incorrectly. For some are accustomed to observing eclipses in a basin filled with water, others with mirrors, others with simple perforated paper, and others in different ways. However, so far are these people from discerning the true magnitude of the defect <note>The extent of the eclipse</note> that, moreover, they severely damage their eyesight by their methods. Therefore, when you are about to observe a solar eclipse, take no more than two fragments of glass—the thicker kind used for windows—about the width of a palm, but of two colors: one being red, and the other green, yellow, purple, or sky-blue. Experience itself will teach you the differences between the colors. Then, insert a sheet of very white paper, perforated with a very thin needle, between the two glasses, and glue them together with wax or bitumen. Then, at the time of the eclipse, hold this before your eyes and aim your line of sight directly through the hole at the failing Sun. In this way, you will behold the Sun harmlessly, no differently than if you were looking at the Moon. This method can be proven daily, but especially when you have noticed from the above instructions that the Sun and Venus, or the Sun and Mercury, are joined bodily <note>A transit of a planet across the Sun</note>. For if you observe that same conjunction through the glasses at the proper time, you will clearly see the planet beneath the body of the Sun, in whatever part it may be hiding, without any obstacle and without harm to your sight.

## THE THIRTY-FIRST PROPOSITION

To depict the forms of eclipses at will, making the images now smaller, now larger.

<margin>
The eclipse of C.S. <note>Gaius Sulpicius Gallus</note>
a higher
method, the matter
<unclear>acted</unclear>
</margin>

The current structure of the instruments seemed to require figures a little larger than what might perhaps be approved by everyone. For one who wishes to depict these same figures according to their own purpose—now smaller, now larger—and so that no one might find me lacking in total reliability, I have added the method by which one can form individual figures at will: small, large, and medium. This is done through the figure of the eclipse that we previously predicted was observed by C. Sulpicius. Having set forth this description of the eclipse, first stretch a straight line on a plane as long as you like; mark one of its ends with Y, and the other with A and M. Next, from point A or M, erect a perpendicular line called A R. Then, with one foot of the compass fixed at A (the center of the eclipse), move the other to R or O; since this compass span is the semi-diameter of the shadow, place the same on the perpendicular, which is named A R. Again, with the compass fixed at the letter A and the center of the shadow, extend it to M; place this compass space (because it represents the distance between the centers of the Moon and the shadow) likewise upon the perpendicular. Do the same with points *c* and *d*. Furthermore, transfer the lunar semi-diameter, namely M P, onto the perpendicular. Once these tasks are completed, mark point Y anywhere you like on line Y A, and from that point, send lines to each of the points on the perpendicular A R. Afterwards, choose another point Z on line Y A, from which, if you draw a perpendicular upwards, you will see that it cuts all the lines drawn from point Y. Indeed, the closer this line is to point Y, the narrower the figures it produces; for the lines that meet at Y measure increasingly shorter diameters for both the shadow and the Moon, which is exactly what the true distance of the lunar center from the shadow's center does. According to this proportion of division, therefore, paint the figures of the eclipse by repeating the previous steps. But if you desire figures larger than the present ones, prolong the lines from Y beyond the line A R, and move point Z further away from A; for in this way, the lines meeting at Y will show even larger diameters on the perpendicular.

## THE THIRTY-SECOND PROPOSITION.

To investigate "Great Conjunctions"—that is, the meetings of the three superior planets, Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, and Mars ♂—at any time, whether before or after Christ, with wonderful ease.

<margin>
The powers of
Great
Conjunctions.
</margin>

PTOLEMY TESTIFIES THAT THE PLANETS are certain ministers of human generation and corruption, or rather, of this world. Since they wander now upward, now downward, now forward, now backward, now far from and now near to the ecliptic, they produce the most diverse effects in things placed below them, bringing about various causes in their rising and setting. He teaches that the wanderings or courses of the three superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, which are further from the Sun than Earth is</note> are especially to be observed, for the most significant effects on affairs are usually produced by them—such as the transfers and changes of Kingdoms, Religions, Wars, and Powers, etc. Regarding this matter, as one who judges all things most deeply, in his fiftieth "word" <note>Aphorism 50 of the "Centiloquium," a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>, he warns the Astrologer not to observe them lightly, saying: "Do not overlook the one hundred and nineteen conjunctions, for in these is placed the knowledge of those things which happen in the world, both of generation and corruption, etc." Since such a great judge of the stars, and likewise the entire assembly of other astrologers, holds these conjunctions in such high regard, we also have deemed that they should not be overlooked at present; indeed, we have been compelled to teach something about them for that reason. Great Conjunctions are fourfold: Greatest, Major, Minor, and Mean. The Greatest is of Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, and Mars ♂. Major is of Saturn ♄ and Jupiter ♃. Minor is of Jupiter ♃ and Mars ♂. Mean is of Saturn ♄ and Mars ♂.

<margin>
The names of
Conjunctions.
</margin>

He who would now search out the great conjunction of some future year must first collect the "roots" <note>the base positions of the planets</note> of the planets whose conjunction he seeks from the nearby subordinated table—whether he chooses two or three planets. These should correspond to the centuries of the specified years in this manner: for a year following Christ, let the Root correspond to the nearest century; for a year preceding Christ, let the Root of the next larger century be chosen, which will happen if a century that is not complete is made complete by the addition of more years. In that case, however, the "complement" must be guarded. For in this place, we shall call that the remainder, or the remaining years. When this is duly performed, let the index M of the lower wheel be placed over the Root of Saturn, and let the number of the remainder be sought on the rim. After a thread is drawn through that point, let the index M be substituted again. One should act in exactly the same way with the remaining indicators, moving them first to the Root and then to the remaining years. Finally, therefore, move the thread to the first day of the month of January in the Calendar for Saturn, and lead the same all the way to the end of December. If the thread falls on the same day of all the Calendars in the wheels of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, it is certain that on that same day there will be, or has been, a mean conjunction of the three planets, which is called "Greatest." ASTRO. CAESA. <note>Imperial Astronomy</note>

If the thread <note>Referring to the silk thread attached to the center of the paper instrument to measure degrees</note> for Saturn and Jupiter expresses the same day, it is a Great Conjunction. Sometimes it aligns for Saturn and Mars, which is called a "medium" conjunction, just as sometimes the thread joins Jupiter and Mars, and it is called "minor." Everything will be clearer from the following examples.

<margin>Example of CHARLES, the Emperor.</margin>
The Emperor Charles <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, born 1500</note> was born in the year 1500, as is often stated; you will know whether or not a great conjunction occurred in that year in this way. Choose the Root <term>Root: The starting astronomical position for a specific date, used as a base for calculations</term> of Saturn for the century 1400 (since 1500 is not yet complete), which is Sign 9, 32 degrees, 38 minutes. Likewise, take the Root for Jupiter, which has Sign 5, 3 degrees, 29 minutes. Also take the Root of Mars, which is Sign 6, 3 degrees, 31 minutes. Next, if you join the indicator for Saturn to the Root of Saturn and pull the thread through the remaining 99 years, place the indicator under the thread again. Working in the same way with the other pointers, draw the thread through the first day of January in the wheel of Saturn. Then, moving the thread little by little through each day, you will see the first day of January. You will also see the first day in the Calendar of Mars cut by the same thread; therefore, you can affirm without doubt that a medium conjunction of Saturn and Mars occurred on that day in the 23rd degree of Aquarius <note>original: ♒</note>. Because Jupiter does not fall under the thread, it is said to have no share with the others in this present conjunction. Having found the "mean" <note>average or calculated position</note> conjunction, it is easy to find the true one from the earlier instructions; it follows on the 10th day of February. Although the mean conjunction is sometimes earlier and sometimes later, the true one is customary.

<margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin>
The birth of King FERDINAND <note>Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V, born 1503</note> is recorded in the year 1503. The root for his century, 1500, is Sign 2, 6 degrees, 6 minutes, 34 seconds for Jupiter. For Jupiter <note>original: ♃uis</note>, it is Sign 0, 3 degrees, 47 minutes; for Mars, however, Sign 5, 8 degrees, 5 minutes, 5 seconds. With the indicator of each planet properly connected to its own root and the thread sent through the 2 remaining years, and each indicator brought back under the thread, no conjunction of the three superior planets is seen to have occurred in this year 1503. Therefore, moving the indicators further into the full year of 1503, a mean coupling of Saturn and Mars is immediately offered in the succeeding year, 1504, occurring on the 8th day of January. But the true conjunction of those planets seems to have already passed, having occurred in the King's birth year, 1503, on the 25th day of October. It is clearly seen there how the mean conjunction follows the true one, whereas in the previous example it was seen to precede it.

<margin>Method for working before Christ.</margin>
But so that the method of operating even before the time of Christ is not unknown, let the third rule be of this kind. It is said that in the year 24 before the Flood <note>The Biblical Deluge</note> a great conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter occurred in Aries <note>original: ♈</note>; you will know whether this is true or not by this path. Setting down 3105 years (for the Flood was that many years before Christ), I add 24 to them, from which we get 3129, the running years in which this occurred. Therefore, taking this number with 75, I assume the larger century, namely 3200. I track the Root of Saturn, which has Sign 5, 13 degrees, 6 minutes. I likewise take the Root of Jupiter, which is Sign 7, 11 degrees, 35 minutes. Then, arranging the individual indicators and pulling the thread through the remaining 75 years with the subjugation of the pointers, I find with the most certain faith that a mean conjunction occurred on the 18th day of March, at about the 11th hour of the afternoon, and this in the sign of Aries.

<header>ASTRONOMY FOR THE EMPEROR</header>

### PROPOSITION THIRTY-THREE.

*From the known hour of Birth, to find the time of the infant's Stay in the womb, and consequently to know the hour of conception.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'R' featuring a seated figure and floral ornamentation.</image-desc>

REASON AND EXPERIENCE alike have proven that some infants are born in the seventh, others in the eighth, others in the ninth, and others around the tenth month after the time of conception; births do not occur before these times, nor are they extended beyond them. For those born within these limits act much like ripe fruits that fall from the womb. However, births earlier than seven months are like raw and imperfect fruit, or like immature apples torn from their branches by some violence, rushing out from the womb; thus it happens that an infant born before the seventh month very rarely survives to see the light of day. Those who were conceived during New Moons or Full Moons, or on the day following them, are also said to be born in the seventh month. Since astrologers saw that nature possessed such limits for birth, and thinking more carefully about the time the fetus is enclosed in the womb—from the sowing of the seed to the birth—they chose to divide this time into three parts, calling them "stays" or "dwellings."

<margin>
Greater Stay: 288 days.
Mean Stay: 258 days.
Lesser Stay: 273 days.
<note>In the original Latin text, the "Mean" (258) is numerically smaller than the "Lesser" (273). This may be a typesetting error or a specific astrological convention of the time.</note>
</margin>
Thus, the first is called the **Greater Stay** (consisting of 288 days). This occurs for one about to be born when the Moon has set slightly below the horizon shortly before, still clinging to the end of the Sixth House. The second dwelling is called the **Mean**, which is completed in 258 days; for after just as many days the birth is produced in this case, with the Moon holding exactly to the Ascendant <note>original: "horoscopum"</note>. The third dwelling contains 273 days and is called the **Lesser**. In this, the infant is born when the Moon has already set below the horizon on the western side. Whenever the position of the Moon at the offered hour of birth does not match any of these cases, it is easily understood that the Stay must be different from the previous ones, as will be explained below.

<margin>Miscarriages are excluded from this rule.</margin>
We declare that all miscarriages <note>original: "Abortiuos"</note> born in the seventh month are not bound by this doctrine of ours, by which we teach how to seek the stay in the womb. Rather, it applies to those who are brought forth in the 9th or 10th month, as is clear and as rightly tends to happen. If, therefore, we trust Hermes, that most ancient reporter of celestial things, the degree of the sky which held the Ascendant at the time of the estimated birth (I call it "estimated" when one has not reached the exact point or minute) is the same degree which the Moon occupies at the moment of conception. Conversely, the degree of the Moon which exists at the time of birth was the rising degree (Ascendant) at the hour of conception. Not a few of the Arabs were of this opinion, boasting that they had sufficiently confirmed the matter by the testimony of experience.

<margin>Various opinions on finding the stay.</margin>
Ptolemy, however, seems to disagree with them in the 51st aphorism of his *Centiloquium* <note>The "Hundred Sayings," a collection of astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note> with these words: "In whatever sign the Moon is at the time of birth, make that the Ascendant at conception; and in whatever sign she was found <insert>at</insert> conception, make that or its opposite the Ascendant at birth." In this, it is certain that Ptolemy speaks of the *sign*, not the *degree*. There are some, however, to whom it seems that not only was the sign the Moon inhabited at the time of birth the Ascendant of conception, but that the same sign or its opposite occupied the Ascendant of the conception. Leaving aside this controversy, whatever its nature, we shall follow the common way of investigating the infant's stay in the maternal womb—first ratifying the Ascendant for each birth, through which practitioners of horoscopes <note>original: "genethliaci"</note> are accustomed to scrutinize the symptoms or accidents of bodies.

<margin>Common method of inquiring into the stay.</margin>
I wish to advise anyone who will use the following figure and establish the estimated Ascendant, or quickly learn the stay of the newborn in the womb, that they should first study to inquire after the hour and minute of birth with as much diligence as possible. This is called the "estimated hour of birth." For midwives and others, when asked about the sixth or seventh hour, usually respond: "between the sixth and seventh," or if about the third or fourth, they report: "it happened between the third and fourth," and similar things. Therefore, the celestial figure must be erected for the question; so that if someone says "between 6 and 7," the figure should be built for 6 hours and 30 minutes. If they say the time was closer to 6 o'clock, the figure should be set for 6 hours and 20 minutes; but if the answer is closer to 7 o'clock, let the figure be set for 6 hours and 40 minutes. But if you hear a perfect account of the time, you may erect it for that without further worry. Once erected, first observe the Ascendant, then the place of the Moon. Seek the degree and minute of the Ascendant in the Zodiac of the accompanying instrument, and place the index **Q** (which is inscribed **ASCENDANT**) upon that find. After this, draw the thread through the Moon's place in the Zodiac, and the thread will show the day and hour of the stay on the outer rim of the lower small wheel. Hold that thread unchanged, and substitute the day of the stay on the upper wheel, and the index **R** of that wheel will give the day of conception in the Calendar. There, strive to know both the day and the hour of conception. You will hunt for the day of the stay on the upper wheel among the thirty days (since the days of the smaller stay from 258 to 288 are marked) under these words: **DAYS OF STAY** <note>original: "DIES MORÆ"</note>. Each of the days carries four parts, each of which denotes 6 hours, except on the edge of the movable and lowest wheel, where each day contains 24 parts. Therefore, careful attention is needed here to see which hour the thread of the lowest orb touches; for you will seek that same day or hour on the upper wheel and place it under the thread.

Hour

<column-break/>

<header>ASTRONOMY FOR THE EMPEROR</header>

<margin>Example of CHARLES.</margin>
Once the hour and day of conception are found, look for the corresponding position of the Moon at that same hour or minute if you can, which will be known from the instrument of the Moon. That place of the Moon is called the "True Ascendant" of the birth time. Having obtained the Ascendant, finally construct the second figure of the heavens (which shall be named "The Figure of the Heavens Verified by Conception"). Let the following be the demonstration of the preceding rule: Since the divine Emperor Charles was born in Ghent, erect the celestial theme <note>A birth chart.</note> suitable for that meridian or polar elevation of his location, and corresponding to the time of birth, namely 15 hours and 44 minutes after noon. <note>February 24, 1500, at 3:44 PM.</note> Here, the time requires no adjustment at all. The Ascendant of this birth is Gemini 31 minutes 30 seconds <note>Signs only have 30 degrees; the OCR "31" is likely a misread of a specific degree, perhaps 21 or 13.</note>. Attaching the pointer **Q** to this, direct the thread through the place of the Moon, which is Cancer 7 degrees 7 ½ minutes. In the extremity of the rim, it will show a **Stay** of 272 days, 19 hours, and 12 minutes. When you have sought these same days and hours on the upper wheel, bring them immediately under the thread; having done this, index **R** in the Calendar of the lower wheel points out the 27th day of May, at 8:32 AM, of the preceding year 1499, for the Imperial conception. At that hour, you see that the Moon possessed Cancer 7 degrees 7 ½ minutes. That is the true Ascendant for this birth.

<margin>Another method of finding the stay, different from the common one.</margin>
This is called the "common" way of operating. Now I will add what I think, as a friend and not a critic. To me, it seems far more advisable if we consider the latitude of the Moon, and borrow that place of the Moon from the ecliptic which, at the time of birth, produces the same circle of position along with the Moon, but not the degree of longitude. For in this way, the Moon comes precisely to the Ascendant, and the Horizon also constitutes the same circle of position. Likewise, since the average is exactly 273 days, just as was done before, it falls on the 27th day of May, at 3:44 AM; the Moon is found in Cancer 28 degrees 30 minutes, which you shall recognize as the Ascendant.

<margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin>
For King FERDINAND <note>Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V.</note>, the birth took place in the city of Medina, as has been said often already. At the birth hour, namely 8:47 AM, the Moon occupied the 20th degree of Pisces. The Ascendant itself was the degree 45 of Gemini <note>OCR error: likely 4 degrees 5 minutes.</note>. Now, when the **Q** index is brought over the Ascendant and the thread is drawn through the position of the Moon, it will indicate on the rim of the wheel **Q** the King's **Stay**, namely 280 days, 12 hours, and 50 minutes. When you have sought this Stay on the upper wheel and substituted it under the thread, you will immediately see pointed out by index **R** the 2nd day of June, at 11:37 AM, in the year 1502, which is the certain time of the King's conception. The position of the Moon corresponding to this time, which is 25 degrees 42 minutes of Pisces, was entirely the Ascendant of the birth. Although the majority of astrologers follow this method, I would nevertheless think it safer to accept and imitate the true place of the Moon (since the stay of the birth and the hour of conception are sought through the mean motion of the Moon). In this way, even if a lapse of half an hour occurs, it does not happen to err by more than half a minute in the position of the Moon. Therefore, having the day of conception, place the degree of the Moon as the Ascendant for the estimated hour. Seek the hour through the degree of the Sun—namely, the hour at which it happens that the degree of the Moon is in the Ascendant—and having sought that to the minute, consider the place of the Moon at that same moment. For in my judgment, you will rightly use this degree for the Ascendant, which in the Imperial birth was Gemini 11 degrees 44 ½ minutes, and in the Royal birth, the degree was Pisces 27 degrees 55 minutes.

### PROPOSITION THIRTY-FOUR.

*To know the parts of Fortune, as they are called, and of all things pertaining to astrology, by means of the present figure.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' with floral motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>What the Part of Fortune is.</margin>
IN THIS PLACE, A PART is nothing other than the distance between two significators of a certain matter in the Zodiac, numbered according to the order of the signs, and its secondary dimension repeated through the Zodiac starting from the horizon. By "significators," I mean the planets that preside over whatever matter is to be judged. If both of these agree in qualities or names, as in Heat, Cold, etc., or Masculinity, day-ruling, etc., then the lordship or "part" is granted to the more excellent one, which must be borrowed from it, and not from the inferior. If these are unequal in significance, as one being diurnal and the other nocturnal, then the part is taken from the diurnal by day, and from the nocturnal by night; although Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Abumasat"; a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> denies that a part should be chosen unless from two things signifying something together. The wiser astrologers have observed those things pertaining to the "parts" with a certain sanctity and the greatest veneration, judging that it ought to be done so, since all things that protect our life are usually derived mostly from the place or parts of Fortune. For they wished the Sun and Moon to be the parents of nature, not without merit, since they hold all actions, places, and times nearest to us. They asserted with the firmest reasons that the Moon prepares the matter, the Sun induces the form; the former governs the night, the latter the day; the one vitalizes the body, the other the soul. Furthermore, it was observed by the ancients that the Ascendant is owed to the Sun by the same reasoning, since the Ascendant or horoscope protects human life no differently than the Sun.

<meta>This page continues the practical application of the astronomical instruments described by Apianus. # THE ASTRONOMICAL CAESAREUM

A similar judgment is held concerning the Moon. For the ancients also assigned to her a proper **horoscope** <note>In this context, the "horoscope" refers to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> or **Ascendant**, as she shares no small communion with the Sun and stands just slightly below the Sun in her rising. Indeed, they distinguished the Moon’s Ascendant from the Sun’s Ascendant on the ecliptic by the same distance that the Moon differs from the Sun, so that the Ascendant for each would differ by the same interval by which the Sun and Moon are separated.

<margin>By "Part of Fortune," the Moon’s Ascendant is to be understood.</margin>
This Ascendant of the Moon they called the **Part of Fortune**, for because it belongs to the Moon, it signifies the body, wealth, appearance, and similar physical circumstances. When the place of the Part of Fortune enjoys a more fruitful aspect along with the favorable placement of the **luminaries** <note>The Sun and Moon</note>, it is an excellent omen; the same logic applies to discerning the other Parts. Indeed, the Part of Fortune excels all others, just as the luminaries themselves, which preside over it, surpass the remaining planets. The symbol for this Part is <image-desc>Symbol for Pars Fortunae: a circle with an inscribed cross</image-desc>. However, the investigation of the Parts is threefold: first of the planets, second of the houses, and third of other various matters.

<margin>The method for finding the Part of Fortune.</margin>
The latter we use in the revolutions of the years of the world, from which we foreknow the high price of grain, or its cheapness, abundance, scarcity, and the like. Therefore, to determine the Part of Fortune at present, consider the subordinate members of the instrument. First, you see the lowest and movable wheel, upon which is an index inscribed **ASCENDANT**; on that small wheel, the twelve Signs are written, through which the distances between two places in the Zodiac are taken, if the index is joined to that degree from which you wish to compute the distance. Then there is another wheel, movable and above the first, carrying a pointer <image-desc>An arrow-shaped pointer</image-desc> and the symbol <image-desc>Symbol for Pars Fortunae</image-desc> which represents not only Fortune but also the Parts of other things; for this reason, it is inscribed **INDEX OF PARTS**. This is placed over the location from which the counting begins. The use of this instrument is clear: if you seek the location of the Part for a day birth, first look at the degree of the Sun in the Zodiac, to which you apply the **ASCENDANT** index; then move the pointer to the Moon’s location in the Zodiac. Afterward, move both indices together without changing their distance until the **ASCENDANT** index touches the actual Ascending degree of the Zodiac <note>The degree rising at the moment of birth</note>, and the Index of Parts will immediately show the location of the Part of Fortune. If you wish to have the location of the Part for a night birth, place the index of the lower wheel over the Moon’s location, and the upper one over the Sun’s location. Then rotate both together, preserving the distance, until the first one holds the Ascending degree in the Zodiac; thus the upper index gives the location of the Part. Although the Arabs and the majority of astrologers promote this method for the night Part, Ptolemy, in the 88th section of the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note> and especially in the book *Apotelesmatum* <note>Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos, the foundational text of Western astrology</note>, seems to reject it. For he maintains that one should always proceed from the Sun to the Moon, and not the reverse, whether choosing Parts by day or by night. I wish to mention this difference in passing, not to disprove the efforts of the Arabs—whom I always respect—but to leave it to the reader to judge what Ptolemy thinks in this matter.

<margin>Example of CHARLES, the Emperor.</margin>
The horoscope of the Emperor <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor</note> at birth had the Ascendant at 9 degrees, 31 minutes of Scorpio <note>original: "♏"</note> at the horizon of Ghent, while the Sun <note>original: "☉"</note> was at 14 degrees, 34 minutes of Pisces <note>original: "♓"</note> and the Moon <note>original: "☽"</note> was at 7 degrees, 7 minutes of Pisces. To calculate the Part of Fortune from this, move the lower index of the wheel to the location of the Moon (for it was a nighttime birth); from there, the upper pointer demonstrates the location of the Sun. Move both afterward, maintaining the same distance (which you can easily do if you connect them with a bit of wax), until the index of the Ascendant holds the degree of 9 Scorpio 31, which is the horoscope of the birth. There, the pointer of the Parts will immediately present the Part of Fortune at 6 degrees 36 minutes of Scorpio before your eyes; and this is according to the Arabs, but following Ptolemy, you will see it at 3 degrees 4 minutes of Scorpio. But perhaps this is not quite satisfactory unless you also see a daytime birth.

<margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin>
Therefore, let us propose King Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V</note>, born under the Ascendant 2 degrees 45 minutes of Scorpio at Medina, Spain, at 8 hours 47 minutes before noon. On this account, one must go from the Sun to the Moon with the Part. Accordingly, set the lower index (the one for the Ascendant) at the Moon’s degree, which is 28 degrees 55 minutes of Pisces. Set the upper index to the Sun’s location, namely 5 degrees 20 minutes of Scorpio. Having done this, rotate both wheels with your hand until the Ascendant index touches the King’s horoscope, which is 2 degrees 45 minutes of Scorpio. And the pointer will indicate the location of the Part of Fortune, namely 6 degrees 35 minutes of Scorpio. A little while ago we said the finding of the Parts was threefold, and it is now timely to show their "tongues" <note>Their methods or definitions</note>. Since the Part of Fortune, which can also be called the Part of the Moon, surpasses all others in dignity and is in more frequent use than all the rest, it rightly claims the first place here, to serve as a model for dealing with the other Parts. But since the **Part of the Future** <note>Also known as the Lot of Spirit</note>, which is called the Part of Jupiter or of the Sun, offers itself immediately in every business (for if you investigate the Part of Jupiter, the Part of the Sun or of things to come must be known first), I wish to declare this one prior as well, to make the use of this instrument clearer through it.

<margin>Finding the Parts of the Future.</margin>
The Part of the Future <note>Lot of Spirit</note> in the day is taken from the Moon to the Sun; at night, the opposite. I want you to understand this once and for all for all Parts in general: that you proceed from the degree of the Moon to the Sun, following the order of the signs, and add just as many degrees to the Ascendant; at the end of these, you establish the Part of the Future. This way of extracting the Part is entirely contrary to the previous one. For in the previous one, the index stood from the Sun toward the Moon; the first was connected to the Sun's degree, whereas the present one does so with the Moon; and just as it is numbered at night in the present from the Sun against the Moon, so in the previous it was done from the Moon to the Sun. The remaining business of the pointers and the duty of operating is the same as described, provided that the starting point—whether Sun or Moon—is carefully observed.

<column-break/>

The Parts of the other planets, or the locations of the Parts in the Zodiac, are found as follows:

The **Part of Saturn** <note>original: "♄"</note> is sought from his location to the Part of Fortune by day; at night the opposite is taken. The **Part of Jupiter** <note>original: "♃"</note> is taken in the day from the Part of the Future to the location of Jupiter; at night the opposite, and it is added to the Ascendant; for this is what it means, in simple terms, to "project the parts."
The **Part of Mars** <note>original: "♂"</note>, or the Part of Boldness, is taken during the day from Mars to the degree of the Part of Fortune; at night conversely, and it is added to the Ascendant.
The **Part of Venus** <note>original: "♀"</note> is taken in the day from Venus to the Part of the Future; at night the opposite, to be joined to the Ascendant.
The **Part of Mercury** <note>original: "☿"</note> is taken during the day from the Part of the Future to the Part of Fortune; at night from the other direction, and is joined to the horoscope.

## HOW THE TWELVE HOUSES
-> of the heavens are to be numbered in the Zodiac. <-

### Parts of the First House
The **Part of the Ascendant or of Life** is taken in the day from Jupiter to Saturn; conversely at night, and is applied to the Ascendant. This is because the difference between Jupiter and Saturn is the same as between the Ascendant and its Part, or because Jupiter and the Ascendant are separated by the same space (counting according to the order of the signs) as Saturn and the found Part. And this is a certain general rule for all Parts.
The **Part of Hilech** <note>original: "Hilech," the Giver of Life</note> is taken in the day from the conjunctional degree (if the birth was at a New Moon) or from the preventional degree (if the birth was at a Full Moon) to the degree of the Moon, and is projected from the Ascendant.

### Parts of the Second House
The **Part of Substance** (Wealth) is taken day and night from the Lord of the House of Substance <note>The ruler of the 2nd House</note> to the degree and minute of the House of Substance, and is projected from the Ascendant.

<margin>added to the Ascendant.</margin>
### Parts of the Third House
The **Part of Brothers** is taken in the day from Saturn to Jupiter, at night conversely, and is added to the Ascendant.
The **Part of the Benevolence of Brothers** is taken in the day from the Sun to Saturn, at night conversely; but if Saturn should be under the Sun's rays <note>Combust, or very close to the Sun</note>, it is taken in the day from the Sun to Jupiter, at night conversely; always understand this as an addition to the Ascendant.

### Parts of the Fourth House
The **Part of the Father** in the day from the Sun to Saturn, at night conversely.
The **Part of Death** in the day from Saturn to Jupiter, at night conversely.
The **Part of Grandfathers** in the day from the Lord of the Sun's House to Saturn, at night conversely.
The **Part of Parents or Kindred** in the day from Saturn to the Sun, at night conversely.
The **Part of Inheritances**, both day and night, from Saturn to the Moon.
The **Part of the Nobility of the Native** in the day from the degree of the Sun to the degree of his exaltation.

### Parts of the Fifth House
The **Part of Sons** in the day from Jupiter to Saturn; at night from Saturn to Jupiter.
The **Part of the Knowledge of the Son**, day and night, from Venus to Jupiter.

### Parts of the Sixth House
The **Part of Azemene** <note>Degrees associated with physical defects or "falling" sickness</note> in the day from Saturn to Mars, at night conversely.
The **Part of Servants** in the day from Mercury to the Moon, at night from the Moon to Mercury.
The **Part of Sickness** from the Lord of the 8th House to the degree of the Lord of the Ascendant, and add it to the degree of the 8th House.

### Parts of the Seventh House
The **Part of Marriage of Men**, day and night, from Saturn to Venus.
The **Part of Marriage of Women**, day and night, from Venus to Saturn.
The **Part of Contentions** (Disputes) in the day from Mars to Jupiter, at night conversely.

### Parts of the Eighth House
The **Part of Death**, day and night, from the Moon to the degree of the 8th House; and add from above how far Saturn has traveled in his sign, and compute it from the beginning of the sign in which Saturn is located.
The **Part of the Killing Planet** in the day from the Lord of the Ascendant to the Moon.
The **Part of the Year in which death, affliction, or impediment is feared**, day and night, from Saturn to the Lord of the House of the preceding Conjunction or Prevention <note>The New or Full Moon prior to birth</note>.
The **Part of Imprisonment** in the day from Saturn to the Part of Fortune, at night conversely.

### Parts of the Ninth House
The **Part of Peregrination** (Foreign Travel), day and night, from the Lord of the 9th House to the beginning of the 9th House.
The **Part of Travel by Water** in the day from Saturn to 15 degrees of Cancer, at night conversely.
The **Part of Religion** in the day from the Moon to Mercury, at night conversely.
The **Part of Travel by Land** from the Lord of the 9th House to the beginning of the 9th House.

### Parts of the Tenth House
The **Part of Region or Kingdom**, and what work the native shall do, day and night, from Saturn to the Moon.
The **Part of the King and Kingdom**, in the day from Mars to the Moon, at night conversely.

### Part of the Eleventh House
The **Part of Friends**, day and night, from the Moon to Mercury.

### Parts of the Twelfth House
The **Part of Enemies**, day and night, from the Lord of the 12th House to the degree of the 12th House.
The **Part of the Election of a King** is taken at the hour of election; in the day from Jupiter to Saturn, at night conversely, and is computed from the Ascendant of the year's revolution.
The **Part of Armies**, day and night, from the Moon to Mercury.

# THE ASTRONOMICAL CAESAREUM

A similar judgment is held concerning the Moon. For the ancients also assigned to her a proper **horoscope** <note>In this context, the "horoscope" refers to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note> or **Ascendant**, as she shares no small communion with the Sun and stands just slightly below the Sun in her rising. Indeed, they distinguished the Moon’s Ascendant from the Sun’s Ascendant on the ecliptic by the same distance that the Moon differs from the Sun, so that the Ascendant for each would differ by the same interval by which the Sun and Moon are separated.

<margin>By "Part of Fortune," the Moon’s Ascendant is to be understood.</margin>

This Ascendant of the Moon they called the **Part of Fortune** <term>Pars Fortunae: A mathematical point in a birth chart calculated by adding the Moon's position to the Ascendant and subtracting the Sun's position</term>, for because it belongs to the Moon, it signifies the body, wealth, appearance, and similar physical circumstances. When the place of the Part of Fortune enjoys a more fruitful aspect along with the favorable placement of the **luminaries** <note>The Sun and Moon</note>, it is an excellent omen; the same logic applies to discerning the other Parts. Indeed, the Part of Fortune excels all others, just as the luminaries themselves, which preside over it, surpass the remaining planets. The symbol for this Part is <image-desc>Symbol for Part of Fortune: a circle with an inscribed cross</image-desc>. However, the investigation of the Parts is threefold: first of the planets, second of the houses, and third of other various matters.

## THIRTY-FIFTH PROPOSITION.

How to perceive without any difficulty, by means of this following instrument, the Golden Number, the dates of movable feasts such as Easter, Pentecost, etc., and the "Key" (as they call it) or, if you prefer, the root.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a scholar or astronomer holding an armillary sphere or globe, seated in a study with books and a window.</image-desc>

<margin>
Who the inventor of the Golden Number was.
</margin>
**THE GOLDEN NUMBER OR THE** Decennal Cycle <note>original: "cyclus Decennalis"; This refers to the 19-year Metonic cycle, which aligns the phases of the moon with the solar year.</note> was first discovered by the Chaldeans, and later sent by them to Rome. When the Romans realized how useful and easy it was to use, they transferred it into their diaries and calendars, writing it in golden letters; thus it came to be called the "Golden Number" by all posterity. It contains 19 solar years, because after that span of time, all the conjunctions and oppositions of the Moon and Sun usually return to the same places. However, when later observers noticed that this Golden Number could not perform exactly what was believed, they began to call it not so much "golden" as "silver" or "leaden," and some even judged it worthy of being abolished entirely. Yet, even if it is somewhat unsuitable for this business of conjunctions and oppositions, it should not be cast aside immediately, as it remains useful in other matters. Likewise, the cycle called the "Cycle of Keys" <note>original: "cyclus clauium"; a number used to find the date of Septuagesima Sunday and other movable feasts.</note> also encompasses 19 years, though their order is changed every year and does not proceed in a standard progression. Through this cycle, the times of future movable feasts are drawn out year by year with the help of the Golden Number.

<margin>
Method of operation.
</margin>
For anyone wishing to know the Golden Number or the Cycle of Keys for a given year, first take the century of the designated time from the table described here (choosing the century that is less than or equal to the total year). Having found this time after the birth of Christ, look for the alphabetical letter found right next to it in the following wheel, which contains letters from A to T, and mark it with the pointer X. After this, read the specific years past the century in the spiral circle (which bears years from 1 to 100). Once this is read, follow the lines drawn from the center through the rims; the Cycle or Golden Number will be seen on the outermost rim, and the Cycle of Keys will be revealed on the inner return of the centers. If you desire the same for a time before Christ, act thus: look in the small table for the thousand and century that exceeds your proposed year. Subtracting your year from that, look for the remainder in the spiral revolution; by moving straight between the lines to the outer rim, the Golden Number will appear, and in the inner rim, the Cycle of Keys.

<margin>
Example of the Emperor CHARLES.
</margin>
Take a certain method for this matter. The Divine Emperor CHARLES the Fifth was born in the year 1500 after Christ. Taking 1500 from the table, it is seen to have the letter A. The index for the letter A is joined to it (which precisely denotes that century), showing the Golden Number to be 19 and the Cycle of Feasts <note>original: "Cyclum festorum"; here referring to the Cycle of Keys.</note> to be 38. This imperial example seems a little obscure because it falls precisely on the century mark; therefore, another more manifest example should be given.

<margin>
Example of King FERDINAND.
</margin>
We have heard that King FERDINAND <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), the younger brother of Charles V.</note> was born in the year 1503 from Christ. The lesser century 1500 in the table indicates the letter A. If the index is joined to this, and the 3rd year is inspected in the voluminous circle as the remainder, the Golden Number 3 will appear on the outermost rim, and the Cycle of Keys 34 on the innermost. This cycle is kept as it is suitable for finding the movable feasts shortly thereafter.

<margin>
The Golden Number in the time of JULIUS Caesar before Christ.
</margin>
For a third example: when JULIUS Caesar ruled the Roman Empire, the 45th year before our Salvation was passing. When I desire the Golden Number and the Cycle of Keys belonging to this time, I first take from the table inscribed "Before Christ" the century greater than the proposed number, which is 100. Seeing the letter E next to the century 100, I mark it with the index of the movable disk. Then, ascending directly from the 45th year, 3 is offered in the first rim (that is, the Golden Number), and 34 in the second (the Cycle of Keys). These two could have existed at that time, even if one of them was not in use. If you now seek the Golden Number for the year 100 in which Christ was born to the world, the value of one will result, which was then held for the decennal cycle.

## THIRTY-SIXTH PROPOSITION.

To find the Cycle of the Roman Indiction <note>A 15-year cycle used in the Roman Empire and later by the Church to date documents.</note> belonging to any year faster than it can be said.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'K' featuring a scholar sitting at a desk writing in a book, with a library in the background.</image-desc>

**"CYCLE" IS A GENERAL** word for a space [of time] that returns in a circle. This Cycle of the Indiction includes fifteen years, which constitutes three *lustra* <note>original: "lustra"; a five-year period.</note>. It is still used by the Romans no less than it was in the past, as can be seen everywhere in the "Chancery" (as they call it) or better, the offices of scribes, and in the instruments or documents of notaries. The origin of this cycle is as follows: When the Romans ruled almost the entire world, and because of that the various nations were hardly able to bring annual tributes to Rome, three distinctions of time—that is,

<column-break/>

boundaries for the paying of tributes—were appointed. Each space of time comprised 5 years. Thus, at the end of the first *lustrum*, gold was brought to the city by everyone, clearly to assert and signify the majesty of the Roman people and the splendor of the Empire. When the second *lustrum* was finished—that is, in the tenth year—silver was brought as pay for the soldiers' expenses. When the third *lustrum* reached its limit, it demanded copper and iron for the repair of weapons. Therefore, that Roman edict spread among the nations that the year's Indiction must be inserted into all documents and books (plainly so that a clearer and more abundant memory of the Indiction would be returned to the nations). To this end, any individual instruments lacking the Indiction number were held to be void or deprived of all trust, just as our own documents are invalid without seals. Toward the end of every five-year period, when the tax was brought to Rome by the nations, the Romans were accustomed to purify the world <note>original: "orbem lustrare"; a ritual of purification performed after a census.</note> with every kind of sacred pomp. To find the cycle for any year, I add 3 to the proposed number of years (for according to Abbot Dionysius <note>Dionysius Exiguus, the 6th-century monk who established the "Anno Domini" era.</note>, Christ was born in the third indiction) and divide the collected sum by 15; the cycle will appear in the remainder. I wish for you to understand this with a clearer guidance.

<margin>
Method of operation.
</margin>
**The Emperor CHARLES** was born in the year 1500. To this, 3 is added, resulting in 1503. This, divided by 15, gives a quotient of 100. Discarding that, the 3 that remains is set as the true Cycle of the Indiction.

<margin>
Example of the Emperor CHARLES.
</margin>
**For King FERDINAND**, we know the birth year was 1503. When 3 is added to this and the remainder is divided by 15, the Indiction 6 will come forth (ignoring the 100 in the quotient). Likewise, to have the cycle for this year 1539, I add 3, giving 1542. Dividing this by 15, I find 102 in the quotient, which I omit as I said before, since it indicates nothing other than that 102 Indictions have passed since the birth of the Lord (specifically, fifteen times one hundred and two years). The 12 remaining indicates that the Indiction belonging to this year is 12. It must be noted that the cycle is always 15 when nothing remains from the division. The beginning of any Indiction is the first day of September, because they thought that time was best for bringing things to Rome, as the labors and works of cultivating the earth are then more relaxed and fewer among all nations, the harvest for everyone having already been completed.

<margin>
Example of King FERDINAND.
</margin>

How to perceive without any difficulty, by means of this following instrument, the <term>Golden Number</term> <note>A number from 1 to 19 indicating a year's position in the lunar cycle.</note>, the dates of movable feasts such as Easter, Pentecost, etc., and the "Key" (as they call it) or, if you prefer, the root.

Who the inventor of the Golden Number was.

**THE GOLDEN NUMBER OR THE** <term>Decennovennal Cycle</term> <note>original: "cyclus Decennalis"; Although the transcription reads "Decennalis" (ten-year), the text describes 19 years, making "Decennovennalis" (nineteen-year) the intended technical term for the Metonic cycle.</note> was first discovered by the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers/astrologers.</note>, and later sent by them to Rome. When the Romans realized how useful and easy it was to use, they transferred it into their diaries and calendars, writing it in golden letters; thus it came to be called the "Golden Number" by all posterity. However, when later observers noticed that this Golden Number could not perform exactly what was believed, they began to call it not so much "golden" as "silver" or "leaden," and some even judged it worthy of being abolished entirely.
