### THE THIRTY-SEVENTH STATEMENT.

->To quickly find the Solar Cycle, the Dominical Letter, Leap Years,<-
->the Interval and the Concurrents, by means of the present instrument.<-

<margin>Why it is called Solar.</margin>
The Solar Cycle <term>Solar Cycle: A 28-year cycle used to determine the day of the week for any date in the Julian calendar.</term> encompasses 28 years. It is called "solar" not because the sun completes its course through the zodiac in that timeframe, but because within 28 years, all the variations occurring in the Solar Letter (that is, the <term>Dominical Letter: A letter from A to G assigned to Sunday for a year; used to calculate the days of the week.</term>), the Leap Year, and the <term>Concurrents: Numbers (1-7) representing the day of the week on which the 24th of March falls, used to sync the solar and lunar calendars.</term> return to their original starting point and state. In this cycle of years, Leap Years combined with common years occupy every day of the week; that is, over this span of time, every letter of the calendar becomes a Dominical Letter, and from the leap days, two full weeks are eventually composed. The Solar Year consists of 365 days, as first observed by Julius Caesar. If you take the beginning of this year at noon, the beginning of the following year will start in the evening after noon of the same day it previously began. The second year will begin at midnight of that same day, moving forward a bit more. The third year will claim the following dawn for its start, and in the fourth year, noon of that same day will again provide the beginning. For this reason, an entire day is intercalated <note>inserted into the calendar</note> every fourth year. This happens on the 6th of the Kalends of March <note>February 24th</note>, and the year begins again at noon on that same day as before. This intercalation can be done nowhere more conveniently than in February, because that month is the shortest of all; for this reason, it is customary for this to happen on the Sixth Kalends of March, which is the 24th day of February. <margin>What a Leap Year is and why it is so called.</margin> It is written as "the sixth Kalends" twice, and the letter F is repeated twice, which is why the intercalary year is also called <term>Bissextile: From the Latin "bis" (twice) and "sextus" (sixth), referring to the doubling of the sixth day before the Kalends of March.</term>, as if having "twice six" Kalends of March. Those two days are usually counted as one. Such a necessity for this intercalation exists that, if it were not done, the feast of the Nativity of the Lord <note>Christmas</note> would eventually fall on the day of John the Baptist <note>Midsummer</note> over a span of 728 years, and the rest of the feasts would vary across half the year. Although the intercalation is repeated every four years, nevertheless, because the year is not exactly 365 days and 6 hours, the ephemeris or Calendar remains uncorrected for us, as will be discussed more fully in the following sections. From the Solar Cycle, we hunt for the Dominical Letter, both Common and Leap years, and the Concurrent days. <margin>Method of operation.</margin> For those who wish to investigate using the frequent figure <note>the diagram</note>, one should first select the smaller century number after Christ from the table provided here. The number aligned with this century will be called the Solar Cycle; find this same number on the outermost or larger rim of the instrument and mark it with index X. After this, seek the proposed year in the spiral circle; draw a straight line from that find to the outermost rim, where you will find the number of the Solar Cycle and, on the inner part, the Dominical Letter. If only one Dominical Letter is found, you call it a common year; if double, the year will be called bissextile. The first or upper Dominical Letter will be from the beginning of the year until the 24th day of February; the second or lower one from the 24th of February until the end of the year. Just as in the year of the birth of our Redeemer, the root is found to be nearly 9 (which was the Solar Cycle at that time, if we trust the Abbot Dionysius, surnamed Exiguus <note>Dionysius Exiguus, the 6th-century monk who established the AD dating system.</note>). The Dominical Letters were D and C, of which D indicated the Sundays until the feast of Matthias <note>February 24th</note>, and C until the end of the year. <margin>Example of CHARLES, the Emperor.</margin> The centenary of the birth of Emperor CHARLES <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor</note> is 1500; looking this up in the table, the Solar Cycle nearby shows 25. Seeking the number 25 on the outer rim, the Dominical Letters E and D are offered, indicating that CHARLES was born in a Leap Year. <margin>Example of KING FERDINAND.</margin> We know King FERDINAND <note>Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V</note> was born in the current year 1503; the 1500 centenary gives 25 in the table as before. When searched for on the rim, index X marks it; finding 3 in the remaining years in the spiral circle and moving directly to the outer rim, the Solar Cycle 28 is found there, and the nearby Dominical Letter A is discovered. <margin>The solar cycle, dominical letter, interval, etc., that existed at the founding of Rome.</margin> By this method, the 753 complete years of the founding of Rome are said to have occurred before the Savior. Therefore, the greater centenary 800 is taken, and examined in the table it gives 21 as the coordinate. Finding this on the rim, index X is placed beneath it. Then, 753 subtracted from 800 leaves 47 as the current year in which the city began to be built. Seeking 47 in the spiral circle shows above it the Solar Cycle 12 and the Dominical Letter G, corresponding to this number. You may also know a Leap Year by another very quick method. If you divide the proposed number of years by 4 and nothing remains, the proposed year is a Leap Year; but this applies to years numbered after Christ. For years before Christ, you act in this way: subtract the proposed year from the larger century, then divide the sum of the remainder by 4, as is clear in the previous example of the founding of the city, in which Rome appeared to be founded in the third year after a Leap Year. For when you subtract the 753 years elapsed from the founding until Christ from 800, 47 remain; when these are divided by 4, 3 are left over, which indicates it was the third year after a Leap Year. Therefore, counting backward from Christ, 754

<meta>The catchword "anni" indicates the first word of the next page is "years".</meta>

<column-break/>

complete years occur. The cause of the Dominical Letter being changed is twofold. One is that in a Leap Year, on the 24th day of February, the letters *f, f* are repeated twice in succession, from which it necessarily happens that all following letters are transposed by the space of a full day, as in this example: we have accepted that the Emperor CHARLES was born in a Leap Year; on February 24th, the day on which the Dominical letters begin to diversify or change. For on the twenty-fourth day the letter *f* appears, referring to Monday, since the Dominical E was used until the 24th day. However, since by the name of intercalation the letter *F* is also assigned to the 25th day, *f* in this place will be called Tuesday, even though *g* had been the sign for Tuesday until now. Because the year now proceeds with one extra day added, it is not unpleasantly called by the Germans a *Schalt iar* <note>original: "ain Schalt iar"; a leap year.</note>. For the Germans properly call *Schalten* what the Latins, speaking circuitously, call "to move or push forward with the hand," or as I might say, "to drive forward"; *fur schiben* <note>original: "fur schiben"; to push forward.</note>, *Schalt ein* and *fur schiben* are the same thing among these nations. The other cause is the end of the year and the beginning of the next, both marked by the letter A. Indeed, the sequence of two A letters (A A) makes it impossible for the Dominical letter not to vary, as appears in a Leap Year. For example, in the year of our Lord 1502, the Dominical letter was B; it was therefore necessary for the letter A to have possessed Saturday, and A is the letter for the 31st day of December. Since therefore the very last day of December became a Saturday, it follows that the first day of the following year (in which King FERDINAND was born), which always begins from A, was a Sunday. Therefore, the letter A, which should have been the Dominical letter in FERDINAND's year, was changed. Since we have already mentioned many things about the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>, it will not seem out of place if we now treat more clearly the same Sunday festival which will be used more frequently in what follows. Thus the Christian church named the Lord's Day what the Jews call the Sabbath; it moved from Saturday to Sunday not rashly, for since Christ was both born and the victor over death on the day of the Sun, and triumphing on that same day restored us to life, who would wonder? Should we not worship on this day rather than the Sabbath? Why should we share a festival with the Jews, in which nothing of the sort happened for us? From whom all our religion ought rightly to shrink. By the Jews, however, the day of the Sun was called the first of the Sabbath or the first day, and by us it is called Sunday <note>original: "der Sonnen tag"</note>, just as the Jews call the second of the Sabbath what the ancients called the day of the Moon and we call Monday <note>original: "den Montag"</note>. It now remains for us to speak briefly of the Interval. The Interval is the space of time and days that falls between the feast of the Nativity <note>Christmas</note> and the Sunday of *Esto mihi* or Quinquagesima <note>The Sunday before Ash Wednesday</note>. The remaining days from the Nativity until the next Sunday are called the CONCURRENT DAYS. However, although I prescribe the method of inquiry in this place, and whereas until now the Interval and Moveable Feasts were usually found through the Dominical letters, I will teach another way. **Rule:** While the Dominical Letter offers itself to the seeker without trouble, I will teach how to find the Concurrents only through a rule. **Rule:** Look at the Dominical letter; if it is A, know the concurrent is 0. If it is B, then the concurrent is 1, and so on, as is clear in this verse:

->A 0, B 1, C 2, D 3, E 4,<-
->F 5, G 6.<-

With this added concerning a Leap Year: the first Dominical letter must be carefully taken and the second neglected. As for what pertains to the Moveable Feasts and the Interval, that will be dealt with in the following statement, where words will be spoken concerning Easter.

### THE THIRTY-SEVENTH STATEMENT.

->To quickly find the Solar Cycle, the Dominical Letter, Leap Years,<-
->the Interval <note>The "Interval" refers to the number of weeks and days between Christmas and the start of the Lenten season (Septuagesima Sunday).</note> and the Concurrents, by means of the present instrument.<-

<margin>Why it is called "Solar."</margin>
The Solar Cycle <term>Solar Cycle: A 28-year cycle used to determine the day of the week for any date in the Julian calendar.</term> encompasses 28 years. It is called "solar" <note>original: "Ciclus Solaris"</note> not because the sun completes its course through the zodiac in that timeframe, but because within twenty-eight years, all the variations occurring in the Solar Letter (that is, the <term>Dominical Letter: A letter from A to G assigned to Sunday for a year; used to calculate the days of the week.</term>), the Leap Year, and the <term>Concurrents: Numbers (1-7) representing the day of the week on which the 24th of March falls, used to sync the solar and lunar calendars.</term> return to their original starting point and state. 

In this cycle of years, Leap Years combined with common years occupy every day of the week; that is, over this span of time, every letter of the calendar becomes a Dominical Letter, and from the leap days, two full weeks are eventually composed. 

The Solar Year consists of 365 days <note>The author is referring to the Julian year of 365.25 days; the following text explains the cumulative effect of the extra quarter-day.</note>, as first observed by Julius Caesar. If you take the beginning of this year at noon, the beginning of the following year will start in the evening after noon of the same day it previously began. The second year will begin at midnight of that same day, moving forward a bit more. The third year will claim the following dawn for its start, and in the fourth year, noon of that same day will again...

# THE THIRTY-EIGHTH STATEMENT.

## To identify Easter and the rest of the moveable feasts, having obtained the Cycle of Keys and the Dominical Letters.

<margin>Exodus ch. 12</margin>
<margin>Leviticus 23</margin>
<margin>Numbers 28</margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 16</margin>
<margin>Ezra 3; 2 Chronicles 35</margin>
<margin>Josephus, Book 3</margin>
<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
WE READ IN EXODUS, chapter 12, that the Lord said to Moses and Aaron in Egypt: "This month shall be to you the beginning of months; it shall be the first in the months of the year. Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them," etc., and a little later: "For it is the Phase <note>original: "phaſa"; another term for Passover, from the Hebrew 'Pesach' meaning 'to pass over'.</note>, that is, the passage of the Lord." In Leviticus 23 as well: "In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, is the Lord’s Phase, and on the fifteenth day of this month is the solemnity of the unleavened bread of the Lord." And in Numbers, chapter 28: "In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, shall be the Lord’s Phase, and on the fifteenth day the solemnity. For seven days they shall eat unleavened bread, of which the first day shall be venerable and holy," etc. Deuteronomy 16: "Observe the month of the new fruits, and of the first time of spring, that you may perform the Phase for the Lord your God, because in this month the Lord your God led you out of Egypt by night," etc. And in Ezra, chapter 3 and chapter 6: "The children of the transmigration performed the Passover <note>original: "Paſcha"</note> on the fourteenth day of the first month." In 2 Chronicles, chapter 35: "And Josiah performed the Phase to the Lord in Jerusalem, which was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month." Josephus also, that most famous writer of history, in Book 3 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 12, left it written in this manner: "In the month of Xanthicus <note>original: "Xantico"; a Macedonian month name used by Josephus.</note>, which among us is called Nisan, that is, the beginning of the year, on the fourteenth Moon opposite the Sun in Aries—in which month we were liberated from the servitude of the Egyptians—the sacrifice which they then performed when departing from Egypt, we are commanded to sacrifice every year, which is called the Passover," etc. "On the fifteenth follows the festivity of unleavened bread, which is celebrated for seven days, in which they eat unleavened bread." Thus far Josephus. The Evangelist Matthew testifies in chapter 5 that Christ did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it; therefore, as the time of his Passion approached, he did not neglect to celebrate the lawful Passover, which the law commanded for the 14th day of the first month and at evening, when the day of unleavened bread begins; rather, he celebrated it most opportunely and truly with his own. The holy Evangelists, as advocates of the truth, testify to this. Matthew, in chapters 6 and 20, where he says: "On the first day of the unleavened bread," etc., "the disciples came to JESUS saying, 'Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?'" etc. "And when evening was come, he sat down with his disciples." Mark likewise, as well as Luke and John, show the time of the Passover clearly enough. But you may ask, why all this? So that, good reader, you may understand that the Paschal feast for both the Jews and for some time thereafter in the primitive church was on the 14th moon of the first month—which for us is by no means the case, for a certain reason. For Eusebius, the compiler of the *Ecclesiastical History*, relates in Book 5, chapter 23, that a most severe dispute arose among the Asian bishops and those abroad, those who established the first Synod in Caesarea in Palestine (the first, I say, after that one whose apostolic acts they remembered), namely, whether the Passover should be celebrated on the 14th of the first month according to the Law of Moses. There, Theophilus, the Bishop of Caesarea, with Victor the Roman Pontiff thus commanding, firmly concluded that the Passover should no longer be celebrated with the "Sabbatarian" Jews on the 14th day of the first month, but rather the Sunday Paschal feast should be honored by Christians. Therefore, the same Theophilus, presiding over the Council of Caesarea, because this had been equally approved by all, publicly promulgated a decree to all the churches, namely, that it was established that Easter should be celebrated between the 12th of the Kalends of April and the 11th of the Kalends of May <note>Between March 21 and April 21 in the old style; this defines the 'Easter Limits'.</note>, and that no power was granted to anyone to overstep these boundaries either before or after. And this was rightly done, because at that time the equinox fell on the 11th of the Kalends of April, that is, the 21st day of March; after which, if the 14th Moon occurs, the Paschal festivity can be transferred all the way to the 20th or 23rd day of April, in this manner: if the opposition (that is, the 14th Moon) falls on the 13th or 12th of the Kalends of April, then the time of the next 14th Moon must be awaited, which does not happen before the 19th or 20th of April, which is also the limit set by Theophilus. Regarding the Moon, the precept is not to be neglected by which the Jews were commanded to observe the 7 moons after the 14th with a continuous consecration of holidays. Therefore, when between the 11th of the Kalends of April and the 12th of the Kalends of May the full moon or the fourteenth is offered (at least after the equinox), then the next Sunday after that opposition is chosen for Easter. But if it happens that the full Moon falls on a Sunday, the next Sunday after it is taken, as if it were still being sacrificed, by that reasoning in which Moses affirmed 7 perpetual lights were sanctified. This is done so that we do not venerate the same Passover with the Jews, who adore it on that same day. And it becomes a holy day for us as well, for from one Sunday to the next only seven days are counted, so that we too honor the Passover on one of the 7 Mosaic sacred days. You see now that commonly the Latins, Greeks, and Hebrews decreed the Passover should be celebrated after the equinox. Following this decree, the fathers of the Nicene Synod established the equinox on the 12th of the Kalends of April, and Easter on the 11th of the Kalends, that is, the following day after, proceeding as far as the 5th of April. For if the 11th of the Kalends of April happens to be a Sunday, then Easter will be prolonged to the next Sunday, which will be the 5th of the Kalends of April, namely the 28th day of March. After these, the assemblies of Antioch, Caesarea, and Alexandria established and confirmed the same. Therefore, let the calculation of the equi-

<column-break/>

nox be added, which was reported on March 21st; Dionysius <note>Dionysius Exiguus, the 6th-century monk who devised the AD year numbering system.</note>, that Roman abbot, laid the foundation of his Calendar, as if the time of the equinox were fixed and never variable in the future. For that reason, the feast of Easter has not been celebrated before the 21st of March thus far, as was once the custom, nor will it be celebrated in the future (and this is against the decrees of the Nicene Council, unless the custom of the Church—now made more depraved by a multitude of errors—is corrected and the true reckoning of the equinox is entered upon). Although holy scripture makes no mention of the equinox, but only of the first month, nevertheless it is given to be understood that the first month is that whose opposition, that is, the full moon, coincides with or closely follows the equinox; since that opinion of the apostles was long ago read and approved, for whom it was a sacred rule that no one is allowed to celebrate the Passover before the spring equinox. However, the equinox that occurred at the time of the aforementioned Synod is now shown to differ from ours by 11 days; since that one occurred on March 21st, our present one occurs on the 10th, and after a few years it will also be on the 9th day.

<margin>The error of the Paschal celebration is demonstrated through the example of King FERDINAND.</margin>
You will learn most completely the causes of error in celebrating Easter, from which follows the confusion of the entire Roman Calendar, from the birth of King Ferdinand, proposing the year 1503 as an example. For you see there, on the day following his birth, which is March 11th, the equinox; and on the 12th, the full moon; and that the Sunday fell on that very full moon. On which occasion the feast of Easter, according to the statute of Theophilus, ought to have followed on the next Sunday, which is March 19th. But by the judgment of the Church, you see it delayed by 29 full days and sanctified on April 16th. From this, one may perceive with their own eyes the manifest error of the Calendar, and how Easter was celebrated in the time of King Ferdinand not according to Moses after the 14th of the first month, but after the full moon of the second month (which can clearly be seen as foreign to the law); and what is even more, it was celebrated at that time when the sun occupies the 5th degree of Taurus, which is called "unclean." <note>By "unclean," the author implies the date has drifted so far into spring that it no longer aligns with the symbolic requirements of the first month, Aries.</note>

<margin>Various observations on the length of the year.</margin>
The reason the equinox continually anticipates <note>i.e., occurs earlier each year.</note> is the trepidation of the eighth sphere and the length of the Solar year, which to this day is not yet sufficiently known. For Hipparchus declared the year to have 365 days, 25 minutes, and 12 seconds. Julius Caesar said 365 days and 6 hours exactly, which is far from the truth. Ptolemy asserts that 365 days, 5 hours, 55 minutes, and 22 seconds make a year. Alfonso pronounced that 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes, and 16 seconds are in it (if you follow him, I do not see how you would intercalate a day every four years). The anticipation of the equinox varies by approximately one day in 132 years. The immediate cause of the corrupted Calendar is that the conjunctions and oppositions of the luminaries are assumed according to the Cycle of Dionysius, although they cannot retain their certainty over such a long passage of time.

<margin>How the Paschal feast is to be investigated.</margin>
Following the custom of the Church, I have provided cycles through which you will now learn to investigate Easter, which you can always use as long as the present rite of the Church is preserved as it is now. The Cycle of Keys <term>Cycle of Keys: A sequence of numbers (1-35) used to find the "Easter Limit" or the earliest possible date for moveable feasts.</term> from Statement 35 and the Dominical Letter from the preceding Statement have taught the foundations through which the Paschal feast will now be learned. Therefore, look at the "Number of Keys" in the inner rim, which is held in capital letters near the text NVME RV S CLAVIVM, as is clear. Mark that number with the pointer of the rotating wheel Z that carries the flag. Then, in the outer rim, look for the previously found Dominical Letter occurring next after the pointer according to the order of days, and join the pointer to it in such a way that the letter is not hidden by the pointer, but the "line of trust" <note>the fiducial line or reference edge</note> of that same pointer only falls in the middle between the present Dominical letter and the next preceding one, counting against the order of days. For the Christian constitution protects that day as the Paschal day by a certain general observation. After this, the moveable feasts appear in their places in order. Let this be an ocular demonstration:

<margin>Example of Emperor CHARLES.</margin>
The divine CHARLES, forever Augustus, was born in the current year 1500, whose Dominical Letter was E D and the Cycle of Keys was 38. Now, let 38, which is the second to last number of the inner rim, be marked with the pointer. Because E has already ceased to be the Dominical letter in February (as the logic of a Leap Year requires), the pointer must now be moved not to the letter E but to the letter D near the 19th day of April. Thus, let it divide the letters C and D, and the days 38 and 39, through the middle. Once this is done, the Paschal feast with the rest of the feasts will be clear, expressed in their names around the circle. Only Septuagesima <note>The ninth Sunday before Easter, marking the start of the pre-Lenten season.</note> must be noted for itself, which in a Leap Year is not celebrated on the day that the name Septuagesima reaches, but on the day that follows it.

<margin>Easter is to be celebrated in Aries</margin>
...for then, at that Paschal time, the Sun occupied the 8th degree of Aries <note>♈</note>, even though that feast must be observed by us when the Sun is in Aries) it would have fallen.
<margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin>
¶ The birth year of King FERDINAND <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), Holy Roman Emperor and brother of Charles V.</note> is 1503; the Dominical Letter for this year is A, and the Cycle of Keys is known to be 34. Now, if you set the index Z to 34 on the inner rim, and then align the pointer to the Dominical Letter A that follows next on the outer rim, the 16th of April will be shown as the day. Meanwhile, take care that the letter A is not covered by the index. Once this is completed, a circular description of all the movable feasts appears.

->SUCH IS THE SEQUENCE OF THEM<-

| | | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

<note>These dates represent the liturgical calendar for the year 1503. Many are named after the first words of their Latin introits (opening chants).</note>

Easter is here again inserted a second time in the mind, because the equinox occurred a second time after the birth of King FERDINAND. Thirdly, after the opposition <note>☍; the full moon</note> (indeed, the true opposition, not the mean opposition, ought to be observed in the Paschal celebration), which therefore would now have to be sanctified on the 12th of March according to the Church Fathers, or on the 19th of March according to Theophilus and the sound logic of the equinox. But because ecclesiastical custom chooses the 16th of April, imitating Dionysius <note>Dionysius Exiguus, whose 6th-century calculations fixed the equinox on March 21.</note>, whose equinox is the 21st day of March, it happens similarly that Easter is extended 35 days beyond its proper limit, and is celebrated while the Sun is in the degree of Taurus <note>♉</note>, which is called "impure" <note>This refers to the Sun having moved too far past the equinox point, losing the symbolic purity of the exact start of Spring.</note>. <margin>The error of the Jews in the celebration of Passover.</margin> ¶ Nor indeed are we alone deceived here, since the ignorance of the equinox also imposes upon the Jews themselves, although they seem to themselves to be remarkably wise in this matter. For they do not worship the Passover in the first month in obedience to the Law, but in the second month, contrary to Moses and their own edicts. For while they set the equinox on the 13th or 14th of March, it happened in this present year of 1539 that they were free for the Paschal solemnity on the 11th of April; whereas if they followed a precise calculation of the equinox, they would have performed those Paschal ceremonies more agreeably to their own law on the 12th of March. Thus, by overstepping the truth by 30 whole days, they are in error. <margin>How the Paschal feast varies by reason of the diversity of meridians.</margin> There can also be another cause for variations of Easter occurring at a less fixed time across the whole world, beyond the Mosaic tradition and that of the Church. For the diversity of meridians <note>Differences in longitude.</note> introduces to us the final occasion for the variation of Easter across different regions. For the globosity of the Earth ensures that the whole Earth cannot be illuminated by the Sun at once and in a single moment, which is what causes the day. Indeed, for only half the part is it day, for the other it is night, and vice versa; thus, by no small chance, a variation in this venerable feast can occur. For to one part of the earth the opposition of the luminaries <note>the Full Moon</note> may be visible, to another not at all; to one after midday, to another after the middle of the night. From this it happens that one person observes the opposition on a Sunday, and another sometimes on a Saturday. For him to whom it appeared on Saturday, the feast is imminent on the following Sunday; for him to whom the opposition is seen on Sunday, he soon proceeds to the sacred solemnity on the eighth day following. This matter would hold true if a certain universal constitution of the Church were not promulgated throughout the world. But since I remember that these and similar things are not obvious in themselves, let it suffice to have touched upon them with a word.

<column-break/>

<margin>How the day of the equinox is to be investigated annually.</margin>
...they correspond to the time of the equinox. That number of hours is written in our customary way in the third space toward the center, 3 by 3, from midday to midnight, and again from midnight to midday. The fourth area of this rim contains within itself the number of days together with their names, so that it may be known whether the day is in February or March. Meanwhile, on a part of the rim, certain markers occur with the years of Christ noted individually from one century to another, the first of which carries the year 1300, and the latest the year 3000 (all being understood from the birth of Christ). After all these, a rotating wheel <note>a volvelle</note> is seen embracing five pointers; the first pointer is marked with the letter B, the second C, the third D, the fourth E, and the fifth F. Each of these contains 20 years under it, so that the sum of all constitutes 100, which is a complete century. In the belly of this instrument, moreover, a thread extends, suitable for universal use. And these things suffice for the parts of the instrument. One who is about to inquire which day of a pre-established year the vernal equinox claims should look at the index of the fixed wheel, bearing the century number of the proposed year or years. Then, having found this, placing another upper mobile index over it, he will find the proposed current year in the rectangular surface beyond the century of the lower index. And thus he will have this wheel aligned to the meridian of Ingolstadt <note>The location of the author's university in Bavaria.</note>. Having done this, he will seek the proposed year in the area of numbers, where, extending the thread over the small line placed next to it, he will find the month, day, and hour of the vernal equinox on the lower rim of the wheel, occurring or about to occur before or after midday. But if you choose some precise century or an exact hundredth year for which to investigate the equinox, no more labor is needed. For the indices distinguished by centuries are hidden from no one; through these, a thread drawn from the center manifests the time of the equinox, either past or future, more quickly than can be said. <margin>How the Equinox corresponds to a meridian other than Ingolstadt.</margin> If you desire the equinox corresponding to another meridian or another place, take the place from the table of regions placed in the third statement; if it is further east than Ingolstadt, count its found hours and minutes on the present instrument, beginning from the meridian line—that is, from 12 (I mean the line marked with the letter M) toward the R—and direct the thread through the found hours or minutes, with the pointer of the upper circle fixed under the same. And again, bring the thread over the line of the current year beyond the century, and immediately on the rim of the wheel below, the day, hour, and minutes of the time of the vernal equinox will stand forth. Now, if you add only these three days and 0 hours, 42 minutes— <margin>Below: days and hours of longitudes, the day and hour etc.</margin> —to the number of days in March (in which the equinox occurs), you will have the day, hour, and minute of the Autumnal equinox, which happens in September. But if a place more westerly than Ingolstadt is offered, count its hours and minutes found through the table of regions toward the C, if they require it, with the thread and pointer arranged as has been said. All this will emerge much more clearly through examples. <margin>Example of Emperor CHARLES.</margin> ¶ The birth year of Emperor CHARLES the Fifth <note>Holy Roman Emperor (1500–1558)</note> is written as 1500. Because this number is a century in itself, it will require less work. You therefore immediately place the thread over the pointer M of the lower wheel (where 1500 is held), which reveals on the rim the tenth day of March, at 6 hours and 28 minutes after midday (namely, for the meridian of Ingolstadt). However, since Ghent <note>Gandavum</note> was the Emperor's birthplace, as stated above, Ghent must now be sought from the table of regions through the third pronouncement. It is found there to be 39 minutes further west than Ingolstadt; therefore, you will bring pointer B over the marker M, and it will count 39 minutes backward toward the setting <note>the west</note>, through which the thread is drawn; it will immediately indicate on the rim the 10th day of March, at 5 hours and 49 minutes in the afternoon, at which the vernal equinox occurred for those living under the meridian of Ghent.

SINCE HITHERTO I HAVE DEALT WITH MANY THINGS regarding the errors of Easter in the name of the equinox, it now seems appropriate to show how you can at any time recognize with great certainty that which is occurring. However, so that this may be more successfully accomplished, I have provided the figure through which it is possible to perform this according to days, hours, and minutes computed in our manner; beginning from the year of Christ 1300 up to 3000, the instrument embraces the equinoxes. Nor indeed because we believed it would be necessary to do so...

<column-break/>

<margin>A summary description of the parts of the instrument.</margin>
...but so that I might make it plain that in such a great space of time the vernal equinox will retreat back into February, and so that at least in this way a more timely desire for amending the calendar might be induced in the Church. Therefore, first receive the parts of the instrument, and afterwards its use. The lowest and immobile wheel of this figure consists of one rim, crowded with many closed loops, each of which is divided into 14 parts marked with transverse lines. Each of the sections refers to the 14th day, which are the 27th and 28th of February, <margin>not allowed by the lines to them</margin> and twelve of March. The extremity of this rim bears white and black spaces in turn, of which the white denote days and the black denote nights. Next to the line crossing the shining space, you see the letter M added subsequently, which is the mark of midday <note>Meridies</note>. The line bisecting the black signifies midnight, with the letter N opposite. In that darker space, the letters C and R are found, C indicating the setting <note>Occasus/West</note> and R the rising <note>Ortus/East</note>. Under the said color twelve degrees are always held, signifying the twelve hours of the night; similarly, under the white, 12 hours of the day are contained, in turn now white, now black. For the night shares equal hours with the day, because those days...

<column-break/>

<margin>The island of Yucatan in the west.</margin>
...to these days, hours, and minutes, if one adds three days, 0 hours, and 42 minutes, there will come forth the 13th day, 6 hours, and 31 minutes of September, the time of the Autumnal equinox. ¶ Another demonstration for the sake of clearer understanding is this. The island named Yucatan, found under the auspices of the divine CHARLES and converted to the sanctity of the Christian faith <margin>found by the name and auspices of the divine Charles for the [advancement] of the Christian faith etc.</margin>, is distant from Ingolstadt toward the west by 6 hours and 40 minutes. If you work skillfully to find when night becomes equal to day there in this year 1539, then connect the pointer of letter B to M; counting 6 hours and 40 minutes from that B toward the setting <note>West</note> on the outer rim of the mobile wheel, and drawing the thread through them, you will see on the outer rim of the immobile wheel the 10th day of March, at 10 hours and 12 minutes before midday, as the time of the equinox in Yucatan. <margin>Example of King FERDINAND.</margin> ¶ For King FERDINAND, the birth year was 1503, being born in the city of Medina in Spain; the century is 1500, wherefore B is brought over M, by reason of the setting, because Medina exceeds Ingolstadt by 1 hour and 12 minutes; 1 hour and 12 minutes toward the west from B will have to be sought on the rim of the mobile wheel, through which the thread will be drawn, and index B will be brought back under the same. But the thread directed through the line closest to three years <note>to represent 1503</note> shows on the rim of the immobile wheel the 11th of March, at 10 hours and 43 minutes before midday. At that very minute, therefore, the Sun can be said to enter the beginning of Aries for the inhabitants of Medina. <margin>How the equinox is to be found in more easterly regions.</margin> ¶ But lest you be able to complain that anything is missing, I will also open the way for understanding a more easterly place. Jerusalem is further east than Ingolstadt by 2 hours and 24 minutes; in which place, if you wish to know on what day and hour the equality of day and night occurred in the birth year of the aforementioned king—namely Ferdinand, which is 1503—then place B, as you know, over the letter M, counting 2 hours and 24 minutes toward the east from B, and do this on the rim of the mobile wheel, drawing the thread through them, with index B moved. Now if you bring the thread to the line of three years, then it will reveal on the rim of the fixed circle the 11th of March, at 2 hours and 19 minutes in the afternoon, corresponding to the clock of Jerusalem. Since, however, we have used only the letter B so far, it will not be out of place to make the matter clearer with yet another teaching. Let it be such: if you wish to know the vernal equinox for the year of Christ 1598 for the meridian of Ingolstadt...

### THE INTERNAL SCALES
Inside the octagon, the rings track numerical data across centuries and relative positions:

*   **The Year Scale:** The outermost color-coded ring displays centuries from **1300** to **3000**.
*   **The Positional Scale:** On the right-hand side, the instrument tracks the displacement of celestial bodies:
    *   **Westernmost** <note>Latin: "Occidentaliores"</note>
    *   **Easternmost** <note>Latin: "Orientaliores"</note>
*   **The Central Disk:** At the very heart of the instrument sits a rose <note>The rose is the personal emblem of the author, Petrus Apian.</note>, surrounded by four small white circles. 
    *   <note>These four circles represent the "Medicean Stars"—the four largest moons of Jupiter discovered by Galileo. Apian’s inclusion of these in a 1540 publication is a testament to the cutting-edge nature of this book.</note>
    *   The edge of the disk is marked with increments: **.20.**, **.40.**, **.60.**, **.80.**, and **.100.**

...readily available, you find 98 years at indicator F; therefore, apply the letter F to the indicator M for the 1500th century, and direct the pointer over the line for 98 years, which will indicate on the rim of the instrument the 13th day at 3 hours and 37 minutes <note>original: "M 37"</note> on the 55th of September <note>This likely refers to a specific degree or minute marker on the instrument's scale rather than the 55th day of the month.</note> in the afternoon. If you add three days, 0 hours, and 42 minutes to this number, there will remain 13 days, 1 hour, and 37 minutes of September, at which time the **Autumnal Equinox** <term>Autumnal Equinox</term> <note>The moment when the sun crosses the celestial equator heading south, making day and night approximately equal in length.</note> will occur. Thus, unless I am mistaken, you are now abundantly instructed in how the double equinox is to be tracked every year, as well as the date of Easter according to the rite of the Church. However, since it seemed proper to the Councils that we Christians should not celebrate Passover <note>original: "pascha"</note> with the Jews, it seems not ill-advised to mention a few things regarding this matter as well. The Mosaic Law prescribes to the Jews that the festival of Passover must be honored on the fourteenth moon of the first month; however, because of their ignorance of the equinox—

<column-break/>

—which they have moved to the 13th or 14th of March, they are in no way able to fulfill this. Regarding this equinox, although it suggests nothing doubtful, they are nevertheless usually entangled in their own traditions. For if the 14th moon falls on the second day of the week, that is, the day of the Moon <note>Monday</note>, they are then accustomed to carry out Passover on the day of Mars <note>Tuesday</note>. And if the full moon occupies the day of Mercury <note>Wednesday</note>, they receive the day of Jove <note>Thursday</note> for Passover. Or if the 14th moon occurs on the day of Venus <note>Friday</note>, they then cross over into the day of Saturn <note>Saturday</note> with their Passover. No scripture orders or compels them to do this, unless they were so strictly devoted to their own constitutions; for they labor under I know not what superstition in fleeing the days of the Moon, Mercury, and Venus, lest they should ever become paschal days. But so that you may perceive with your own eyes the annual Passover of the Jews, I have arranged the following method below, examined by certain calculation for 160 years.

## CONCLUSION OF THE FIRST PART

MAY YOU SEE, friend Reader, that I am entirely devoted to your true cultivation; for the closing of this first part of the astronomy, I have subjoined a certain theorem, in which, as if in an arena present before your eyes, you may discern toward what purpose the movements of the stars—which have been handed down so extensively throughout this entire part of the work—contribute. Such a matter is one that may be of the greatest possible benefit to humanity, for whose sake I am perpetually prepared to undergo anything. It skillfully teaches how to find the **Critical Days** <term>Critical Days</term> <note>original: "Dies Criticos." In historical medicine, these were specific days during an illness when a change or "crisis" was expected, often determined by astrological calculations of the moon's position.</note>—that is, judicial days, whose principal use among physicians exists in treatments—not when they are already present, but when they are imminent. Whence, unless I am mistaken, it can be sufficiently clear to the prudent how the science of astronomy is accustomed to serve not only for pleasure but even for human utility. Although this theorem is succinct, I should think that nothing is desired by anyone in it for a better declaration of astronomy.

### FORTIETH AND
### final enunciation.

To find the Critical Days—that is, judicial days—necessary for physicians in judging illnesses, by means of this subjoined instrument, without the labor of calculation.

It is confessed among all that certain stars are instruments of divine power, through which we believe that entire universe is governed. For who is there who would deny that the works of the constellations, whether you call them effects, or inclinations, or influences, are certain proofs of divine providence? Since we see that nothing in this world is unaffected according to the dispositions of the stars, although all things are accustomed to be referred back to God.

<column-break/>

Just as you would not attribute the structure of any work to the tool, but to the craftsman who uses it, so we ought to ascribe the effects of the stars, which follow their movements, not to the stars themselves, but to God, the primary cause who rules and governs them. Since the Best and Greatest God reveals such various courses and movements of the stars to us, and unlocks the heaven itself as if it were an open book in which future things are signified through the transits of the stars and luminaries, we have resolved to say a few things about those matters which have been collected by us from that book, and especially about those things which seem to pertain to human health. Although in part we may be able to be of service especially to vigilant physicians, it is my intention to be of use not only to these, but also to others who will have at least some regard for their own health. Although, for the sake of those physicians especially who are unskilled in the stars, it was done...

# CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY

...someone might think this [method] was devised by us, and not without merit; for we confess that those who follow our counsel will be able to heal the suffering more certainly and effectively. For no learned man is ignorant of the great power of the judicial days, which they call **Critical Days** <term>Critical Days</term> <note>From the Greek 'krisis,' these were specific days during an illness when a patient's condition was expected to change decisively for better or worse.</note>. How great a necessity lies upon the physician to observe the **Crisis** <term>Crisis</term> is encouraged by many, especially by Ptolemy, that most knowledgeable author of nature, in the 60th aphorism of his *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Claudius Ptolemy.</note> in these words: *In the case of the sick, look to the critical days and the movement of the Moon through the angles of the figure [the 16 angles]. For where you find those angles well-disposed, it will be well for the patient; conversely, it will be ill if you find them afflicted.* Thus far Ptolemy, whose words, since they contain some obscurity and are not immediately obvious to beginners in astronomy, I shall make clearer and more plain. First, it must be known 
<margin>what it is.</margin> 
what the word **CRISIS** signifies: *krisis* in Greek, *iudicium* <note>judgment</note> in Latin. It is a swift and violent movement in a disease toward health or toward destruction. It is called "violent" because it happens due to severe symptoms. For at that time, a most bitter struggle is excited between the disease and nature, and no other time of sickness is more grave than the Crisis. However, no crisis can be perfect in which there is no sensible expulsion of the offending matter, from which it is established that in diseases occurring without physical matter <note>referring to "spiritual" or purely energetic imbalances</note>, no crisis occurs. There are four differences in the days pertaining to the judging of diseases: they are **Critical**, **Indicative**, **Intervening**, and **Empty**.

<margin>Critical and announcing; intervening or interpolated</margin>
¶ The **Critical day**, which is also called the Decisive, Radical, or Judicial day, is that time when nature rises up for either the expulsion or the transformation of the offending humors <term>Humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament.</note>. ¶ The **Indicative** or **Indiciary day** is that which gives a sign of the future crisis; it shows on which day and hour, and of what kind it should be. For in it, some sign of the future judgment appears entirely, through which we are certain of the health or the danger of the following crisis.

¶ **Intervening days** are those which are also called "interpolated" or "provocative," in which the harmful humor provokes nature to a fight. They are called intervening because they fall between the critical and indicative days. A crisis sometimes happens on these days, but only by accident—for instance, by reason of the strength of a medicine or some other symptom.

<margin>The day which is called medicinal.</margin>
¶ The **Empty** or **Medicinal day** is said to be that in which nature rests entirely, and nothing is decided between the disease and natural strength; so much so, that during an empty day, one may safely labor at a cure. But before we approach the practice of the crisis itself, other things seem necessary to mention. First, every sign claims for itself a certain peculiar part of nature, insofar as it pertains to the four qualities. **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius**, because they are hot and dry, govern **yellow bile**. **Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn**, because they are cold and dry, correspond to **black bile**. **Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius**, hot and moist, imitate **blood**. **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces**, cold and moist, are assimilated to **phlegm**. Next to be known is that a planet rules over each sign, from which it takes the name "Lord"; as **Mars** is lord of Aries and Scorpio, **Venus** of Taurus and Libra, **Mercury** of Gemini and Virgo, **Jupiter** of Sagittarius and Pisces, **Saturn** of Capricorn and Aquarius, the **Moon** of Cancer, and the **Sun** of Leo. Furthermore, each of the signs claims a peculiar part of the human body, as do the Houses of Heaven, which the following figure indicates:

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

At this point, it should be noted in passing that no part of the body should be violated with iron <note>original: "ferro," meaning surgical tools or bloodletting lancets</note> in any way whenever the Moon is traveling through the sign of that part. According to Ptolemy’s testimony: *The divisions of the limbs through the signs should be studied diligently, for in whatever place of the figure a sign may be, it nonetheless retains the genuine property of the part it signifies.* A similar thing is also done with the planets, for each of these also expresses natures or temperaments according to the four qualities:

<column-break/>

In addition to this, the twelve signs are commonly said to be three-fold: **Movable**, **Fixed**, and **Common** <term>Modalities</term>. For when the Moon is in one of the movable signs at the beginning of some disease, it happens that the disease is terminated quickly; conversely, if the Moon is in a fixed sign at the onset of the disease, we see the same disease prolonged; just as when the Moon is in a common sign at the start of the affliction, the disease is mostly changed and passes into another.

| Movable Signs | Fixed Signs | Common Signs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Aries | Taurus | Gemini |
| Cancer | Leo | Virgo |
| Libra | Scorpio | Sagittarius |
| Capricorn | Aquarius | Pisces |

Nor do the individual planets tend to indicate individual members of the human body and various diseases any less:

> ♄ **Saturn** looks upon the bladder, the spleen, and the right ear; its afflictions are Cancer, Gout, Elephantiasis, and all such melancholic conditions.
> ♃ **Jupiter** holds all diseases that arise from overly abundant or scorched blood.
> ♂ **Mars** signifies the gall, the private parts, the testicles, the left ear, and the liver; also acute fevers, Erysipelas <note>a skin infection</note>, Morphea <note>discolored skin patches</note>, and very hot internal abscesses.
> ☉ **The Sun** possesses the brain, sight, nerves, the heart, the right side, the right hypochondria, and every hot affliction, such as burning fevers and types of tertian fevers.
> ♀ **Venus** observes the kidneys and the nape of the neck, and indicates any diseases of the private parts, especially those caused by cold.
> ☿ **Mercury** regards the lungs and the tongue, any afflictions of the mind, phantasms, dreams, mental alienation, and the like.
> ☽ **The Moon** dwells in the womb and female parts; she indicates menstruation, catarrhs, and cold and moist diseases such as apoplexy, paralysis, types of convulsions, epilepsy, etc.

<margin>When planets are said to be combust.</margin>
¶ It is further to be noted that a planet is called "under the rays" until it is found between 15 and 12 degrees from the Sun; but approaching within 12 degrees of the Sun, it is then said to be **Combust** <term>Combustion</term> <note>When a planet is so close to the Sun that its own influence is "burnt up" or hidden by the Sun's light.</note>, and its effect is most weak—and the closer it becomes to the Sun, the weaker it is; indeed, it is called "impeded" in a term not unusual among astrologers. 
<margin>Retrograde.</margin>
Likewise, know that a **Retrograde** planet is destitute of all power. 
<margin>The Combust Way.</margin>
When the Moon is in what is called the Milky or **Combust Way** <term>Via Combusta</term> <note>A notoriously unlucky stretch of the zodiac, typically defined here as from 19 degrees of Libra to 4 degrees of Scorpio.</note>, then its power seems nearly cast down.

¶ Any of the wandering stars <note>planets</note> exercises the greatest power if it holds the 10th, 11th, 7th, or 5th houses, provided it is free from the more hostile gaze or commerce of others, as has been said. But the same are said to be weak when they occupy the 12th, 6th, or 8th house.

¶ Likewise, regarding the 12th, 6th, and 8th houses: in whatever place of the figure they may stand, they nonetheless bring damage to all things with which they participate by their aspect.

# CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY

<sig>tt iiii</sig>

### CONCERNING THE HOUSES OF THE HEAVENS

<margin>Where the Crisis should be anticipated.</margin>
¶ The **first house of the heavens** and its ruler always represent the sick person, the inquirer, or the consultant. The **Seventh house**, together with the ruler of the Disease, represents the illness. The **Tenth house**, together with its ruler, represents the Physician—specifically, what kind of doctor he is and with what fortune he will encounter the disease. The **Fourth house** and its ruler signify the Medicine <term>Medicamen</term>, specifically what benefit it will bring to the afflicted person. The **Sixth, Eighth, and Twelfth houses** represent the locations or sources of the diseases. Therefore, whenever a better planet <note>A "benefic" planet like Jupiter or Venus.</note> occupies any of the four angles <term>Angles</term> <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses.</note>, or if the ruler of any of those angles is fortunate, free, powerful, and not hindered, then a more favorable judgment follows for that angle; if less so, the opposite will occur.

<margin>Preparation of the instrument for investigating the Crisis.</margin>
¶ Time now calls us to the **Crises**. For now, we shall teach what they are, how they may be foreknown as they occur, and how the **Indicative**, **Empty**, and **Intercedent** days <note>Indicative days (often the 4th day) show how the crisis on the 7th day will go; Intercedent days are secondary points of change.</note> may be recognized. Therefore, you must most studiously fish out from the suffering patient the exact moment they felt they began to feel worse; this will henceforth be called the "beginning of the disease," or elsewhere the "hour of invasion." It is the time when the sick person perceives they are suffering—for instance, when they feel their usual activities are hindered—which is indeed easy to notice in acute diseases and those that attack suddenly. But since a certain struggle between the disease and our own vital power usually arises on the 7th, 14th, and 21st days, Astrologers have called these **Critical days**. Others, however, scattered between the Critical days, in which a similar but weaker struggle is seen to happen, they have called **Indicative days**. They noted still others, distinct from those Judicial and Indicative days, in which a very weak contest between nature and disease was imminent; these they named **Intercedent**. By scrutinizing the lunar motion in these matters (as they perceived that the humors <term>Humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to control health.</note> and all these lower things are most violently affected by its occasion), they discovered 16 lunar angles in the Zodiac. When the Moon stays in these angles, it brings assistance to nature to overcome the disease. There is no reason for you to be moved by the fact that the Arabs are mentioned here, who establish this partition of angles in the celestial equator rather than the Zodiac, and this according to Ptolemy (as they think), when in truth Ptolemy never dreamed of such a thing, let alone felt it. If you do not believe me on this point, reread Pontanus and others. Each of the angles contains 22 ½ degrees, as the following figure distinctly reveals. In this figure, first, a certain index appears with the sign **X**; this is moved to the degree of the Moon at the beginning of the affliction. From there, a certain white line is drawn through the center of the instrument, where it forms right angles with another line and proceeds to the outer rim. These two lines cut the instrument into 4 parts and show the locations of the Crises in the Zodiac. Those Crises, to distinguish them from the others, are painted black. In the middle of any two Critical points, there is another named **Indicative**. Then, between a Critical and an Indicative point, another is always placed, called **Intercedent**. Thus, each of these four quarters is partitioned into 4 angles, which you will see as 16 connected points, each separated from the other by an interval of 22 ½ degrees; this interval is called **Empty** while the Moon travels through it. ¶ Therefore, for the days already mentioned, let him who desires to know what is to come join the index **X** to the location of the Moon (as exactly as it can be given), in the place, I say, which the Moon occupied at the time the disease began. By doing this, he will see all the remaining days—Critical as well as Indicative and Intercedent—marked before his eyes in the Zodiac by degrees and minutes (by applying the thread to the lines of the pointer).

<margin>By what reason the Crisis occurs.</margin>
Nature is quite precise in this regard; it does not attack the disease before the time of assistance is at hand, which the squares <term>Quadratures</term> <note>A 90-degree angle between planets, often considered stressful.</note> and oppositions <term>Oppositions</term> <note>A 180-degree angle between planets.</note> are most accustomed to bring. For the fourth and opposite aspects truly tend to effect a Crisis because, at these times, the Moon is no longer present with the humor that was "offending" from the beginning, but is positioned as an adversary to it. It stimulates nature and acts as a truer attacker of the disease. You shall observe not only those aspects of the Moon—namely the square and the opposition—but also the others that cause the Indicative and Intercedent days, always understanding such aspects as being made from the degree where the disease began. For then the Moon shows what will happen regarding the Crisis—that is, whether it will turn out healthy or not—which will be judged more perfectly if you examine the celestial figure constructed for that time. If you wish to know the Critical, Indicative, or Intercedent time after this, see on which day the Moon will enter those degrees shown by the lines of those days. Thus, look at the noon of that same day to see where it has the Moon; this matter can be known equally through the Moon-instrument or through the Ephemerides <term>Ephemerides</term> <note>Tables showing the daily positions of celestial bodies.</note>. Taking the position of the Moon at noon, notice whether it exceeds the Critical or Indicative degrees, etc., or not. If it exceeds them, then the hour of the Crisis or Indication will occur after noon. Therefore, one must note by how many degrees it exceeds: for every degree, calculate 1 hour and 52 minutes—or more simply, 2 hours; and for half a degree, one hour (or 4 minutes less if you wish to be exact). In this way, you will find, either approximately or perfectly, the hour in which nature will begin its contest with the disease.

<margin>How the hour of the Crisis is to be sought.</margin>
If, however, the location sought on the instrument at noon is found to be less [than the required degree], similarly divide the number of degrees into hours before noon, attributing two hours (or 1 hour and 52 minutes) to one degree, and you will have the hour of the Crisis or Indication, etc., close to the truth, and this according to the Moon's average motion. If you desire it even more exactly, seek the daily motion of the Moon due for the proposed day, from which you will most easily find the hour by the rule of proportions in this manner: In the first place, put the daily motion; in the second place, 24 hours; and in the third, the distance of the Indicative place from noon. As in: "the daily motion gives 24 hours; what does the distance give?" A perfect rule, as often as it re-
<meta>The catchword "mittit" connects to the first word of the next column.</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>How to know from the figure whether the Crisis is healthy or unhealthy.</margin>
-mits <note>original: "mittit"</note> hours and minutes. This caution being observed meanwhile: if the distance is before noon, let it be subtracted (as if they produce the 3rd hour before noon, let it now be subtracted from 12, and it be said that the hour is 9 in the morning). But the afternoon result stands by itself and is named from noon. Since, however, the Moon does not perform an equal motion every day, it is necessary that the days of the Crises also vary among themselves, and do not always fall certainly on the same day. Most frequently, however, the second Crisis appears on the 7th and 14th day. The reason is that the square <note>indicated by the symbol ◻</note> and opposition <note>indicated by the symbol ☍</note> indicate concerning diseases (especially acute ones) so frequently, one of which occurs on the 7th and the other nearly on the 14th day. There is also a third Crisis, which happens more often on the 20th or 21st day because of the other square aspect. Therefore, having obtained all the Critical days (and what I say of the Critical, I wish to be said of the others, the Indicative and Intercedent), erect a figure of the heavens with the planets and fixed stars, especially the more notable ones located in the Zodiac or near it, collected in the same chart. This being done, look above all at the position of the Moon, committing each of its "accidents" to memory: namely its aspects and its "passions" <note>Astrological conditions or afflictions.</note> according to the motions of all the other planets, whether it undergoes benevolent or malevolent influences. Make a similar judgment regarding the fixed stars. For if all these have obtained suitable places, they will portend a healthy Crisis and that nature will prevail over the disease. If you see the Moon more hindered, you shall judge all things contrary and ill-omened, and that nature will succumb to the disease. Unless the matter of the disease fights against the present judgments, or the misfortunes of the aspects consist in "Hartz"—that is, in their similarities <note>original: "similitudinibus"</note>. This is usually a sign of health, though by accident. For instance, if the affliction is phlegmatic (that is, cold and moist), but the Moon by a certain radiation communicates with Mars, a hot and dry planet—or vice versa. Or if, in a bilious disease, the Moon occupies a colder and moister star. For though a planet might normally be harmful to a sickness by itself, its nature may be so contrary to the disease that it rather assists the natural power against it. Something similar is determined regarding the more prosperous stars, both fixed and wandering. For if any of these "cools" <note>original: "in frari"</note> the disease—that is, its nature is mismatched to the disease's temperament—the crisis seems to be disturbed, though because of the star's genuine goodness, the crisis is not altogether removed. Furthermore, there is a judgment in all 16 angles of the figure at a glance: namely, that more violent struggles tend to arise in the Critical angles than in others because of the evident discord of the signs, which they have by reason of their qualities and gender in the squares and oppositions. But I find there is no such distinction in the Indicative or Intercedent days, which is why the provocation of nature and disease is felt most lightly on these latter days, unless perhaps some accident brings a cause for a more serious struggle. Just as if the Moon were weighed down by increasingly unfavorable planets and surrounded by a dejected and ill-omened place through such an Intercedent day, while the Indicative figure again showed a more benign Moon in all respects; for then, why could this day not be more fortunate than the other? In reality, the Indicative and Intercedent aspects cannot be named [as separate things], but because they are aspects closer than other places, therefore when they are traversed by the Moon, it is not uncommon for it to stir nature against the illness, accustomed to ripening them by digesting and "cooking" them <note>In ancient medicine, "coction" or cooking was the process by which the body's heat matured and neutralized the disease-causing humors.</note>. This also must not be overlooked: that on a Critical day, the patient often dies when the Moon is joined with a more malignant planet or participates in an unhappier aspect, and especially when the planet is very similar in temperament to the disease. Conversely, if it is joined with more fruitful planets and fixed stars, the opposite occurs. And sometimes a Crisis happens on the 5th day with the Moon occupying an opposition, whence there is also a trine <note>indicated by the symbol Δ</note> of the Moon on the 10th day. But these occur mostly for the reasons we have already enumerated, namely by "accidents." Nor is that of Hippocrates contradictory: "The fourth is the index of the seventh," where Hippocrates names the fourth and not the fifth. For since he wished to hand down the rules of Crises in a certain regular method to those less skilled in the stars (so they would not be entirely ignorant), and since he endeavored to express the 7th and 14th as the more notable markers of a Crisis, he judged it safe to proceed by fours. Therefore, it was done that he wished to insert the 4th rather than the 5th among the Critical days, just as also the 11th rather than the 10th for the same reason, although the trine aspect falls on both the 10th and 11th, and consequently so does the crisis. In the same way, you might think Hippocrates said 20 and not 21, even though judgments occur no less on the 21st than the 20th. Furthermore, Crises are accustomed to change not only by reason of the stars, as we have heard, but also by other things, which for physicians are six in number, which a couplet of this sort encompasses:

->Matter, Strength, Physician, Symptom, Attendant,<-
->And Stars: so many things are accustomed to vary the crises.<-

<margin>Causes of the variation of Crises.</margin>
¶ But how each of these occurs is not the purpose of the present work to teach, where we promise nothing besides astronomical matters. Returning to the proposal, therefore, let us run through the rest. If the Moon at the beginning of the disease or in any Crisis lacks any other aspect, it signifies simply neither good nor evil. But if at such a time it is seen by any of the planets, it usually follows the nature of the same (whether fair or unfair), bringing whatever it may to the sick person. But if the beginning of the disease finds the Moon sharing in some aspect, know that in the following Critical day, the crisis happens to be hindered. If at the start of the illness the Moon occupies any of the four angles, then it establishes a certain judgment in whatever sign it may be.

### CONCERNING THE HOUSES OF THE HEAVENS

The **Tenth house**, together with its ruler, represents the Physician—specifically, what kind of doctor he is and with what fortune he will encounter the disease. The **Fourth house** and its ruler signify the Medicine <term>Medicamen</term> <note>From the Latin for remedy or drug.</note>, specifically what benefit it will bring to the afflicted person. Therefore, whenever a better planet <note>A "benefic" planet, typically Jupiter or Venus, believed to bring positive outcomes.</note> occupies any of the four angles <term>Angles</term> <note>The four most powerful points in an astrological chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses.</note>, or if the ruler of any of those angles is fortunate, free, powerful, and not hindered, then a more favorable judgment follows for that angle; if less so, the opposite will occur.

Indeed, if the Moon undergoes an eclipse at the time of a **crisis** <term>crisis</term> <note>The critical turning point of a disease, traditionally occurring on specific days like the 7th or 14th.</note>, it is a sign of evil. At that same time, if the Moon should look upon a planet positioned under the **Solar rays** <term>under the rays</term> <note>When a planet is so close to the Sun (within roughly 15 degrees) that its influence is thought to be "burnt up" or hidden.</note>, nothing can be determined, because such an aspect possesses little more than nothing—indeed, no power at all. Judge similarly in Crises unless **Saturn** or **Jupiter** are beheld, for they can show their power when they are 15 degrees distant from the Sun and **oriental** <note>Rising in the east before the Sun.</note>; the same applies to **Mars**, though he must be at least 10 degrees distant from the Sun and oriental, while the rest must be at least 15. For if any of them forms an aspect with the Moon while further than 15 degrees from the Sun, it is usually a sign that things will not go well. Those three, if they are **occidental** <note>Setting in the west after the Sun.</note> (that is, they set after the Sun) and are more than 15 degrees distant, similarly testify to something perverse. **Venus** and **Mercury**, when they are oriental and less than 15 degrees from the Sun, are more unfavorable indicators. If at this time the ascending sign is **Aries** or **Libra**, and the Moon occupies one of the **angles**, she will bring a most certain crisis when she progresses to a **square** $\square$ or **opposition** $\text{☍}$ <note>A "square" is a 90-degree angle; an "opposition" is 180 degrees. Both were considered stressful or challenging aspects.</note>. Likewise, if the Moon is increasing in light at the beginning of the disease and is seen by the Sun or Mars at the same time, it signifies that the sick person will be in lethal danger when the Moon reaches the square or opposition of that degree. But if she looks upon Saturn while increasing in light, then being seen later in square or opposition, the illness will increase, yet in such a way that the patient is likely to escape death, though with difficulty. But if the Moon looks upon Saturn while increasing in both number and light, no change in the infirmity will follow when she forms that square or opposition. One must also not neglect the fact that the sick person is often burdened on whatever days the Moon beholds some more unfortunate light; they are affected more heavily if it happens that the Moon stands at the boundary of an unfortunate aspect, just as that same patient may later be saved and find relief again when the Moon approaches a second, more favorable aspect. If the Moon is waxing at the beginning of the illness, it is a sign that the disease will be ended at the square or opposition if only health-giving rays are present; but if unfortunate rays approach, the sick person will be altogether lethally affected. # THE SECOND
# PART OF THE
# IMPERIAL AS-
