# PETER APIAN,

THIS SECOND PART OF THE ASTRONOMY encompasses the advantages or uses of the whole *Primum Mobile* <note>original: "primi mobilis". In the Ptolemaic system, this is the outermost sphere of the heavens that carries all others in its daily rotation.</note>, all of which are first demonstrated through the instrument called the plane **meteoroscopion** <note>A specialized instrument for measuring celestial altitudes and solving problems of spherical trigonometry.</note>, and are afterwards very firmly confirmed by geometric demonstrations, aided by the calculation of sines and chords. However, I wish to advise the pious reader here not to assume that all uses of the present meteoroscopion are delivered at once; indeed, he will see cosmographical matters more abundantly in their own volume. There he will also learn that not only through this and similar plane meteoroscopion-type instruments can any matter of this business be grasped, but also through a certain numerical meteoroscopion added furthermore. Nevertheless, if anyone desires the structures or construction of the meteoroscopions discovered and published by me, I refer him to our **planisphaerium** <note>A map of the celestial or terrestrial sphere projected onto a plane.</note>, where besides that and other things worth knowing, he will find the structures, or compositions, so to speak, of nearly all astronomical instruments. But although no one of the more sensible readers would fail to sufficiently draw the remaining advantages of the *Primum Mobile* from the immediately following statement on triangles, I nonetheless, desiring the matter to be even clearer to the less experienced, have subjoined certain observations of **comets** as a finishing touch <note>original: "colophon". Traditionally the final inscription in a book; here it refers to the concluding section of the work.</note>.

### THE FIRST ENUNCIATION

To summarize the parts of the instrument and to gather all its uses in the briefest possible way.

<meta>catchword: Instrument</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>
The entry into the instrument is twofold:
Areal,
Lateral.
</margin>
THIS INSTRUMENT, TO WHICH THE name **meteoroscopion** is given—because we place those things which are considered on high <note>original: "in sublimi". Referring to celestial bodies.</note> before our eyes in this, as it were—consists of four parts: two sides, the **limb** <note>The graduated outer edge or arc of the instrument.</note>, and the **area** <note>The inner grid or surface of the quadrant.</note>. Through these four, the whole business, use, and universal advantages of the spherical triangle are precisely revealed. I shall clearly show each advantage of this triangle in five quadrants, and I shall confirm the same with the most evident examples as soon as I have declared the members of the instrument. It must be known, therefore, that the instrument lies open to a twofold entry: the first is called "areal," and the second "lateral." The **Areal** entry is completed in the area of the instrument; the **Lateral** is completed on the line A-B or on the limb B-C. Two things are required for an entry of this kind, through which two other things, as if still unknown, are drawn out. To this end, because in every right-angled spherical triangle five necessary things present themselves, a twofold entry is needed when the same cannot be accomplished by a single one.

<margin>
The first twofold mode of entering laterally.
</margin>
The lateral entrance can be had in two ways. First, if one lateral number found on the line A-B is marked with a **pearl** <note>original: "margarita". A sliding bead on the instrument's string used to mark a specific value or intersection point.</note>. Then, let the thread, moved along the limb, be suspended at another lateral number; for thus the pearl shows the areal number, which is contained between the transverse lines. It likewise indicates the fundamental number, so to speak, or the **base** on the line A-C, falling through a circle from the letter B, and extended through the pearl all the way to A-C, as is clear in the example. Let one lateral number be 40 and the other 50 degrees; let the pearl hold 40 on the line A-B at point E. Let the thread, however, express the other side, namely 50 degrees on the limb, which should be at point L; and the pearl will have given the transverse circle of 30 degrees at point G—though if you treat it more precisely, 29 degrees and 30 minutes will occur. The third quadrant will exhibit a most open demonstration of this matter. The second mode of entering is this: let 50 degrees be sought on line A-B, upon which the pearl is placed; afterwards, if the thread is stretched through 40, just as before, 30 degrees are seen to be cut off by the pearl, which is suggested in the first quadrant by the letter *h*.

<margin>
What the Areal entry is.
</margin>
Furthermore, I have proposed in the fourth quadrant how the areal numbers, which are signified by the transverse circles, may be more truly known. Even more, when one lateral and one areal number are already known, the entry is called **arcal** <note>Related to the arc.</note>, which is also to be completed in two ways. First, by seeking the lateral number on line A-B and moving the pearl to it, and moving the thread back and forth on the limb until the areal circle is touched by the pearl; then the thread designates the other lateral number on the limb, which the second quadrant shows. Second, the already known lateral number is taken, and where the thread is passed through it, the place where it cuts the arc of the areal number is observed, for the pearl is fixed there. Afterwards, when the thread is brought down over the line A-B, the other lateral number is shown by the pearl, which one may also imagine in the second quadrant if point *e* were unknown. Now, through two known numbers, you have learned to find a third unknown. Therefore, so that you may have the fourth likewise, look at the first quadrant, in which all numbers, both known and unknown, are contained, where also the fourth is found, which in the same triangle is called the **base**.

<margin>
Nomenclature of the parts of the triangle.
</margin>
Now we must come to the nomenclature of the numbers. The first of these is that which represents the **hypotenuse** <note>original: "ὑποτείνουσα" (hypoteinousa). The longest side of a right-angled triangle.</note> of the triangle, indicated by the line A-B. One of the lateral numbers is always to be sought on the line A-B, being a partner to line A-C. The second number is usually signified by the arc C-B, which is to be considered nothing other than angle A of triangle H-A-M. The third is called the **areal** number, found on the transverse arc D-I, representing the side H-M, which signifies the **perpendicular** <note>original: "κάθετος" (kathetos). The vertical side of a right-angled triangle.</note> of the triangle. The fourth is called the **base** of the triangle, that is, the foundation, and it is sought on line A-C; this base is carefully recognized through point H, for line H-D contains as many degrees as line A-M. To these numbers you can now add a fifth, to be understood by the angle H of that triangle; if you should perhaps prefer to find this, it is necessary to invert the triangle, so that you establish the base from H-M, and the perpendicular from A-M; for once this is done, angle H falls back upon point A. And the arc R-G exhibits the quantity of angle A. Therefore, by this method and by these rules, you will be able to examine the business of the whole *Primum Mobile* with precision, provided you do not entirely lack common sense. Be intent on this one thing: that you fashion a triangle suitable for a spherical surface according to your purpose.

<margin>
How one must deal with triangles.
</margin>

Next, I shall enumerate the non-right spherical triangles <note>A triangle drawn on the surface of a sphere, where every side is an arc of a great circle.</note> and teach how they are to be imagined on this plane **meteoroscopion** <note>Apian’s specialized analog computer for solving astronomical problems.</note>. These kinds of triangles can be formed in three ways, as we mentioned before. For either all sides correspond to each other (equilateral), or only two do, with the third being smaller or larger (isosceles), or all sides differ from one another at once (scalene). When all sides are equal, one must be cut in the middle; if one half is taken along with another side, two known sides are obtained, with which you may then investigate the remaining features of this meteoroscopion from what has been said before. For any half of such a triangle is a right triangle. If two sides of the triangle are equal, but the third is narrower or wider, that third side must be divided into two parts. Thus, the whole triangle is also cut into two other right-angled triangles. From there, one must proceed according to the rules, for two sides of each resulting triangle are now known. 

When all sides of the triangle are unequal but known, proceed as follows. Look for the two shorter sides on line A B along with their numbers; then draw one thread over line A B and place the **pearl** <note>original: "margaritam". A sliding bead used as a marker on the instrument's strings.</note> over its number; afterward, extend the second thread again over line A B and add the **bead** <note>original: "unionem". Another term for the sliding marker.</note> to the other number. After this, take each thread in each hand and move them up and down on the **rim** <note>original: "limbo". The graduated outer scale of the instrument.</note> until both beads fall upon one and the same arc in the central area; however, move them proportionately—I say proportionately because the joined bases of both must equal the largest side of the triangle. For then the arc in the area upon which the pearls rest represents the "common arc," namely the one that splits this triangle of unequal sides into two other triangles, each of which contains different bases. 

For example: Let B H D be a triangle of unequal sides, of which B H comprises 36 degrees, H D 42, and B D 50 degrees and 20 minutes. Through this instrument, the common side is found, which divides this triangle into two right-angled ones, specifically 30 degrees and 34 minutes, which is represented by H F. The base of the smallest triangle, A M, is said to include 20 degrees, while the base of the largest includes 30 degrees and 20 minutes. L C represents the quantity of angle H B F of the smaller triangle, while K C provides the quantity of the larger triangle H D F; in this way, that triangle of unequal sides is reduced to two other right-angled triangles, each of which contains two known sides. Now, if you wish to investigate anything further, it will be possible if the previous instructions are recalled. Whatever has been handed down concerning right-angled triangles, the following figures repeat more clearly.

<margin>
How a non-right triangle can be resolved into two right triangles by another method.
</margin>

You can also resolve the same non-right triangles into two other triangles by another method, namely through a quarter-part of a circle—or call it a **quadrant** if you prefer—so that all their sides are established, as an example shows. Let the first triangle be taken again, in which all sides are equal. Let each be set at 42 degrees. I therefore establish the quadrant A B C, in which I immediately count 42 degrees for the base of the proposed triangle (which shall be called B F D), starting from B toward C, and mark it with the letter D; at the same time, I draw a straight line through D from point A. Because the sides are equal to each other, I in turn drop a perpendicular from letter D onto line A B, ending at point K. I draw a similar perpendicular from B onto A D, ending at point I, so that both divide each other at point H. Now, therefore, a straight line drawn from center A through letter H touches the arc of the quadrant at F and cuts the arc B D into equal parts. After this, I again raise a perpendicular from H toward D, and I see this line divide the arc of the quadrant H F at point L; thus F L is now the common side of the two partial triangles (which was previously called H F), being 17 degrees and 15 minutes. Similarly, I see that B F and F D contain 21 degrees, as the first and third figures among the following will show. 

Where two sides of the triangle agree, but the third is smaller: Let the example be the figure above, for in that one, two sides were 42 degrees and the third was 20. Therefore, place 30 degrees <note>The text here shifts to a 30-degree example.</note> on the rim of the quadrant, letting the start be marked by letter M and the end by D from whichever part you please. After this, draw two straight lines from the center A, one to M and the other to D, for these <meta>catchword: within</meta>

<column-break/>

enclose 30 degrees within themselves. Then divide the arc M D at point F, and extend a line to that same F from the center A; also count 42 degrees from M toward C and mark it L, and mark the same degrees counted from D against B with N. Now, a perpendicular drawn from N meeting point I on A D, coinciding with another perpendicular raised from L on A M and ending at letter K, should meet with the former at point H. From there, another perpendicular sent toward L should touch the circle at letter O, comprising 30 degrees and 42 minutes; here H F is the common side, as the second and fourth figures below teach.

What should be done with a triangle that has three unequal sides.

But if a triangle has all sides dissimilar, or indeed two similar but the third larger, execute the matter by this kind of example. # THE SECOND PROCLAMATION

->To recognize all the benefits of the First Motion through geometric demonstration, and that by the easiest means.<-

<margin>Euclid's Proposition 4, Book 6.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "C" containing a landscape scene with two figures and a starry sky.</image-desc> **Since** the course of the planets has been explained by us, along with the uses of the First Motion, with the greatest ease and with a fidelity never before produced (as far as I can see), it remains for me to present the contemplation of that same First Motion with equal ease, and to confirm it with the clearest demonstration. For when this is done, I hope it will come to pass that no one can complain that anything at all is missing from this astronomical work. I ask everyone to forgive me if I am more succinct in this part and do not bring forth a cumbersome heap of numbered propositions, as is customary in mathematical demonstrations. Indeed, my intention is to settle the matter as briefly as possible; for this reason, I shall be content with only one induction from **Euclid** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Geometry."</note>. But if I were to attempt to enter deeply into the treatment of the **First Mover** <note>The mechanical or divine cause of the heavens' rotation.</note>, I fear I would make it unpleasant for many, especially those who are less skilled in geometric certifications. But because I want the matter to be plain to all, and since I promised it would be delivered in very few words, I shall endeavor to provide it meanwhile by a single axiom of Euclid. This is the 4th proposition of Euclid's sixth book, which holds thus: *In all pairs of triangles whose angles are equal to the angles of the other, the sides facing those angles are proportional.* I shall briefly clarify that proposition using two proposed triangles in this manner: Let the first be A B C, and the second D E F. Let all the angles of both these triangles match each other perfectly, so that angle A corresponds to angle D, angle B to angle E, and angle C to angle F in every respect. Since these angles are similar to each other, it is necessary that the sides are also proportional. Thus, side A B of the first triangle corresponds to side D E of the second triangle, just as line A C of the first to line D F of the second, and again B C of the former to E F of the latter triangle. Furthermore, line A B is to line B C as side D E is to side E F. This will be even more obvious to any student imagining those two triangles placed one upon the other in this fashion:

<image-desc>Two similar right-angled triangles labeled ABC and DEF positioned next to each other to show proportional sides.</image-desc>

<margin>What must be done by him who is to understand the use of the First Motion.</margin>
Therefore, anyone about to investigate any benefit of the First Motion should first conceive in his mind a certain right-angled spherical triangle. For example, if he is to calculate how far the beginning of **Leo** <note>The zodiacal sign.</note> is distant from the **ecliptic** <note>The sun's annual path across the sky.</note>, he should first form a spherical triangle there. Since the ecliptic is closest to the beginning of Leo near the start of Libra (where it crosses the equinoctial), that same quadrant of the arc G L K must be compared, just as the nearest quadrant of the equator must be assigned the letters G Q H. Furthermore, with the letter L representing the beginning of Leo and G the beginning of Libra, the arc G L must be declared as 60 degrees, and the maximum **declination** <note>The angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator.</note> of the sun, K H, must be said to be 23 degrees and 30 minutes. The angle L G Q, which includes side K H, is of the same quantity as K H. It should be known that every triangle consists of no more than three angles and three sides, of which if two are known, the rest will also be established by this method. It is clear that the surfaces of the ecliptic M K L G and the equinoctial M H Q G cut each other through the diameter G N M, and therefore constitute a uniform angle from M toward G. From this, if you now draw a straight line from letter K to the center of the sphere M, and similarly draw a straight line from L to the diameter G M, cutting it orthogonally at point N, you will see that lines M K and N L are parallel. Furthermore, if you drop a perpendicular from K onto the base M H, it will fall on point O, just as

<column-break/>

a perpendicular dropped from point L falls upon the surface M H G at the letter P. Thus, two triangles are created, one M K O and the other N L P, with proportional sides and angles. <margin>Path of the first demonstration.</margin> Now, therefore, let us inspect the arc of the declining Leo, namely L Q, as was proposed, by saying: the **total sine** <note>original: "sinus integer". The radius of the calculation circle, used as a base for trigonometric ratios.</note> M K produces K O, the sine of the maximum declination; what does N L, which is the sine of arc G L, create? For someone proceeding according to the rule, <margin>By what ingenuity the tables of the First Motion are calculated.</margin> the result will yield L P, the sine of arc L Q which you were seeking. And in this manner, the tables of **Regiomontanus** <note>Johann Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), the most influential astronomer of the 15th century, famous for his table of sines.</note> serving the First Motion were calculated. Consequently, let us also inquire into the remaining angles and sides of this spherical triangle, from which all the benefits of the First Motion receive light. <margin>Second demonstration.</margin> Let us therefore assume arcs G L and L Q are known; thus, if I proceed to find angle L G Q, which is signified by arc K H, I say: N L (the sine of arc G L) produces L P; what does the sine M K produce? Here, if I compare the result following the rule, I find the quantity of line K O. Seeking its arc, namely K H, I learn the true capacity of the entire angle L G Q. <margin>Path of the third demonstration.</margin> Now let arc G L be unknown, but angle G and arc L Q be known. To obtain arc G L, you will say: the sine of angle G (namely K O) produces K M (the total sine); what then does L P (the sine of arc L Q) produce? Operating according to the rule, you will recognize the quantity of line N L; if you take the arc of this line, you will have settled the matter according to your wish as before.

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram showing a sphere with the North Pole ("POLVS ARCT"), the celestial equator ("COELVM AQVINOCTIALE"), and the Ecliptic. Points are labeled with letters K, L, M, N, O, P, Q, H to illustrate the trigonometric proofs described in the text.</image-desc>

<margin>Fourth Demonstration.</margin>
Suppose the angle G L Q and arc G Q are hidden, which we are to find by a similar path. Since the arc G Q H is one quarter of a circle and contains 90 degrees, we must seek arc Q H. Once found and subtracted from 90 degrees, the remainder leaves us arc G Q. To demonstrate this visually again, I imagine two surfaces as before: the **solstitial colure** <note>The great circle passing through the celestial poles and the solstices.</note> I K H along with its radius M H and axis I M forms one surface; while the quadrant I L Q with axis I M and radius M Q forms the other. Therefore, take a triangle such as you have above, distinguished by letters I L K, whose two sides we suppose are known to us, such as L K (which is the **complement** <note>The difference between an angle and 90 degrees.</note> of arc G L) and I L (which is the complement of arc L Q). Since the arc Q H encompasses the angle L I K, it remains to seek angle I, which we shall find in the same way we found angle G above, thus: Let a perpendicular line be drawn from point L onto the axis I; it terminates at point S and signifies the sine of arc I L. I say then: S L contains L V (the sine of arc L K); what does the total sine (namely line M Q) possess? The proportion yields line Q T. The arc of this line is Q H, representing the quantity of angle I. Hence, if you subtract arc Q H from 90, arc G Q remains, which was sought. <margin>Fifth Demonstration.</margin> But if G Q of the first triangle is set as known and the other as unknown, then arc L K as well as L Q will be investigated just as above, in this way: Let it be said that M Q produces Q T; what does S L produce? The arc K L will be shown in the result, which when subtracted from 90, leaves arc L G.

<image-desc>A detailed circular diagram at the bottom showing the intersection of the Solstitial Colure, Ecliptic, and Equinoctial at point G, with specific numerical values for the sines (86424, 100000, 34132) to assist in calculation.</image-desc>

<header>IMPERIAL ASTRONOMY</header>

<margin>Sixth demonstration.</margin>

With the sides GL and GQ of the previous triangle <term>trigonus<note>A triangle; Apianus uses this Greek-derived term interchangeably with 'triangulus'.</note></term> being known, you will find the less-known side LQ through the other two, if you use this proportion by saying: TQ gives QM (that is, the <term>whole sine<note>The 'sinus totus' or radius of the calculating circle, used as the base for trigonometric ratios.</note></term>), what does VL promise? For the arcs QH and KL are now clear (their complements having been revealed); in this search, you will see the magnitude of line LS, whose arc is IL, while the complement indeed offers the sought-after LQ in this manner. As is clear in the preceding figure.

<margin>Seventh demonstration.</margin>

There remains one thing of that first triangle not yet discussed, namely, how great the angle L is there in GLQ. This, however, may be seen in two ways. First, in this manner: Since LQ is now clear, its complement, which extends all the way to C, must be added to it, just as the complement of arc LG, which extends to B, must also be added. It must be stated thus: The sine of arc LG produces the sine of arc GQ; what will the whole sine cause? There, as soon as it shows how many times the arc BC occurs, it will reveal that which includes the proposed angle GLQ; likewise, the angle ILK is equal to angle GLQ, being vertically opposite. The second mode of demonstration is such that if it is said: the sine of arc LI produces the sine of arc IK (for both of those are provided), what does the whole sine produce? To one who is appropriately handling the rest, the arc YX will occur, representing the quantity of angle ILK. Thus, therefore, you will have demonstrated the same thing in two ways. You will understand the reason for this second demonstration if you imagine the triangle LIK to be constituted exactly like the triangle GLQ, and that spherical <term>trapezium<note>A four-sided figure; here referring to a section of the sphere's surface.</note></term> IYXK to be similar in all respects to the trapezium LKHQ. For this reason, the way of demonstrating YX or BC is the same as it was before in designating arc KH; which having been demonstrated, you have obtained the angles opposite to it, GLQ and ILK, which have now been found equal by a double path.

<image-desc>A circular diagram of a celestial sphere containing a triangle marked with points G, L, H. It includes labels 'COLVRVS SOLSTICIOR' (Solstitial Colure) and 'AEQVINOCTIALIS' (Equinoctial). Red and yellow accents are used for the arcs and the triangle.</image-desc>

It sometimes happens that a spherical triangle has no right angle, but has three known sides. To know the angles of that same triangle is not possible unless you distribute it into two, so that each contains a right angle; once this is done, it is altogether easy to measure the spaces of the individual angles according to the method of demonstration already brought forward. Furthermore, a non-right-angled triangle can be presented in three ways: it is proposed as having either three equal sides, two equal sides, or three unequal sides together. For a triangle of three equal sides, which is also called equilateral, cut one of its sides in half at point F, and imagine an arc proceeding from point H all the way to F; for that will divide the proposed triangle into two right-angled ones, after which you will learn the angles and that common side together by the way of demonstration already mentioned.

<image-desc>Two planar geometric diagrams of triangles labeled with vertices B, D, A. One triangle is highlighted in red (values 37-15, 31, 42) and the other in green (values 44, 42).</image-desc>

But if a triangle has two equal sides, such as the following figure shows, then similarly divide the third side (placed below the two equal ones) into two, and this at point F. Now if you extend an arc from H (that is, from the angle opposite to this side) all the way to F, you will notice the triangle proposed to you is divided by the same into two right-angled triangles; which triangles, you will grasp how great they are by the often-cited mode of demonstration. There follow now the figures of triangles in which the side HB is shown to be similar to side HD. The third side of the triangle being either greater or smaller than the other two.

<image-desc>Two spherical triangles depicted on circular bases, one green (marked 39, 44, 42) and one red (marked 44, 30), showing interior arcs and angles.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

But if it happens in practice that all the sides of the offered triangle are unlike each other, the first step is to divide the triangle into two right-angled ones, which you may accomplish very easily. I have additionally devised another use to be shown, which is of this sort. Draw the fourth part of a circle—that is, a quadrant—rightly expressed with its perpendicular semi-diameters upon some plane, whose center is A, and mark the ends of the semi-diameters with the letters B and C. Place the largest side of the triangle upon the edge of the quadrant and mark it with the letters BD. Locate the medium arc of the triangle by extending it from one end at D toward B, and mark the other end with G. Starting near B, send out the smallest side of the triangle toward D, and name it BE. Now, draw a straight line from D to the center A, and extend the arc GD (representing the medium side of the triangle) from D toward C, terminating at point P. Soon, connect the two points G and P with another straight line. That line will divide the semi-diameter AD perpendicularly through point I. GI is called the "right sine" of the proposed arc, namely GD. Afterward, from point E, drop a perpendicular onto the diameter AB, cutting it at point K, and call the line EK the sine of the smallest side of the proposed triangle. Then, cast an orthogonal line from point P onto the line AB, which, proceeding as far as N, shows the sine of arc BP. At this point, notice that I am speaking only of imaginary lines, and by a "line" I mean nothing other than to consider it the right sine of an arc. Next, double the arc GD, which when doubled produces GP. Look for the right sine of this GP, which is GO, and mark the same on line AB with the letters NM. The sine of arc BG is the line MG, and after you have drawn its equal NO upon the line NP, it is clear that lines MG and NO, as well as NM and GO, are equidistant. Since therefore KE and NP are parallel, and if a third line, namely GO, goes across them transversely, it follows altogether that angles GQE and GOP are both equal to each other and are right angles. Even if this should not happen, it is sufficient that they are equal for the present. Now, as we repeat the premises from Euclid, namely: *Of all two triangles whose angles are equal to the angles of the other, the sides facing the equal angles are also proportional.* The treatment will proceed in this way, so that the two equal and right angles also contain proportional sides, such as are the present triangles GOP and GQR; since these two angles are right, and angle QGR is common to both, it is clear that the third angle GRQ also exists as equal to GPO. Furthermore, we will investigate the side QR, still unknown, from the rule of proportions thus: Line GO shows the sine OP, what does GQ show? The quotient of the rule will show the sought-after sine QR, which if you add to arc BG—namely to the line KQ—the desired quantity of line KR will be made clear to you. Then, multiply the sine KR and the sine KN individually by themselves, and collect the product; the square root of the sum shows the quantity of line AR. Now if you subtract the arc of line AR from 90, the arc HF remains, which is carried from H to point D at spherical right angles; RF, however, is the sine of the same, which is called the <term>versed sine<note>The 'sinus versus' (1 - cosine); a common trigonometric function in older astronomy used to measure the height of an arc.</note></term>. If you wish to know this, subtract the sine AR from the whole; the remainder from the subtraction will be RF. Finally, we shall also seek the arc BF in this way. As we imagine the line LF (that is, the sine of arc BF) to be extended, and the line AR to be produced as far as F, two triangles ARK and AFL will arise. From which it will be said: AR gives RK, what does AF give? In the following rule, the quantity of line LF will be offered in the quotient, whose arc BF, when subtracted from arc BD, leaves the arc FD. These things having been performed, using the previous six ways of demonstration, you will fully achieve here nothing that is not necessary to know for your desire.

It then follows to seek [the remaining side]; this will be done with the help of the first demonstration. Since the arc LQ is found to be entirely equal [to the known values], and with BD already understood, the arc CD must also be tracked down in this manner. The fourth demonstration shows the side ABD; once this is held, you will subtract that which was previously found from the hypothesis, AC, from AD, and the remaining arc will be CD. There is yet another way to construct the same triangle, as if you place the maximum arc AC upon the base, as appears in the following figure. From here, the orthogonal arc BD falls within AC; where this occurs, examine the arc BD with the first demonstration, and the base AD with the fourth. Afterward, subtract AD from the arc AC, and DC will remain, also a known side. Now you again have triangle BDC, whose sides BD and DC are known; it remains for you to know the third, but the fifth demonstration teaches this through the arc GL. Although these [demonstrations] are few, do not doubt that they will be sufficient for understanding all the uses of the <term>Prime Mobile<note>The outermost sphere in the medieval geocentric model, which drives the daily motion of all other celestial bodies.</note></term>.

## NOW FOLLOW THE OBSERVATIONS OF FIVE COMETS.

In using examples of comets, I will act opportunely if I do not depart from those who came before. I am persuaded that it is not out of place for me to bring forward for the present instruction the five comets seen during the times of the Emperors CHARLES and FERDINAND, which appeared almost continuously. However, this exemplification of ours should be embraced by the studious observer not so much for the sake of fully executing the use of the instrument, but rather for the sake of perceiving the "cometic" essence of the star (if it is permitted to speak thus) and especially for observing the tail. Concerning this, it is established that neither philosophers, nor historians, nor astrologers have brought forth anything better-proven up to this day—to say nothing meanwhile of the method of contemplation, which we read has similarly been handed down or shown by no one before us. From this, it would be clear to us in what manner even the most ancient investigators established the celestial motions, which in the meantime (alas, what a deplorable negligence!) who does not see? But even if it were not difficult to know how the tail is generated by the rays of the Sun, it nevertheless seems advisable to indicate in what way I myself, with the help of the <term>meteoroscope<note>An instrument designed by Peter Apianus for measuring the positions and distances of celestial objects, particularly useful for phenomena like comets.</note></term>, might find this to be true, and for this reason:

<column-break/>

so that a record may exist for posterity, should the need arise later for some means by which they may observe comets of this kind (since until now, if I may speak with everyone's peace, there has been none, or it was very meager). Truly, I do not wish to include all types of comets under this name, of which some, emitting rays all around, are called "hairy" <note>original: "criniti"</note>; others drop tails all the way to the earth, such as the one that appeared in the year 1472, of which not a few old men are still found to be mindful, calling it the "Peacock's tail," because not unlike the light of an introduced lamp, it had fixed its tail to the earth. Others cast forth tails and rays in different ways, concerning which philosophers have already long ago disputed abundantly. However, we have undertaken to demonstrate in what manner the following five comets were positioned in relation to the Sun, and that sufficiently from the present meteoroscope; indeed, it is well known that we have taught this method of proof elsewhere through numbers as well. Furthermore, one using this instruction, although it shows or demonstrates the same thing not by one but by multiple methods, will nevertheless be content with a simple example of induction, by which he may know the rest through himself without difficulty, for it is not possible to comprehend everything within brevity.

### THE FIRST OF THE COMETS
shone in the year 1531, when the Diet of Augsburg was celebrated by the Emperors Charles and Ferdinand, from the 6th of August until the 23rd of the same month. I shall now open the observation of how I conducted it in 16 subsequent chapters.

#### Chapter One: Concerning the Observation first established and prepared.

Since the star had already been seen for several days, indeed as the thirteenth day of August was already taking hold, I began to think anxiously about its contemplation. Here, however, when I saw the fixed star of Boötes <note>referring here to the star Arcturus in the constellation Boötes</note> standing near the vertical circle, especially at that time when the Comet was shining most clearly after the setting of the Sun—namely, at 8 hours and 20 minutes after midday—I immediately turned my mind to another matter. But someone might perhaps object that I was anxious without reason, for it would have been very easy to observe the comet by the work of the <term>Torquetum<note>A complex astronomical instrument that allows for measurements in the horizon, equatorial, and ecliptic coordinate systems.</note></term>. Very well, I confess it, just as the subsequent declaration of the Torquetum will make clear. But for me acting in such a way, the logic of the tail could in no way have been investigated; therefore, it was necessary for me to proceed in the manner I now describe, through which, besides that, the uses of the Prime Mobile could also be shown, which I have observed no less diligently than any other thing. First, therefore, the longitude and latitude of the star Boötes were required; the first, Alfonso <note>referring to King Alfonso X and the Alfonsine Tables</note> testified to be 14 degrees and 8 minutes, the second 31 degrees and 30 minutes North. After this, from the tables of the same Alfonso, the motion of the <term>Auge<note>The apogee or highest point in an orbit; here referring to the movement of the fixed stars.</note></term> and the fixed stars had to be extracted, which can also be called the motion of the eighth sphere; such a motion from the time of Christ until the hour of the appearance seemed to have traversed 5 signs, 0 degrees, 11 minutes, 36 seconds, 2 thirds, and 39 fourths. Afterward, we collected the course of access and recess, which is also called the <term>Argument of the eighth sphere<note>A variable in the theory of trepidation, a medieval astronomical concept where the equinoxes were thought to oscillate.</note></term>, which was 5 signs, 2 degrees, 18 minutes, 9 seconds, 2 thirds, and 8 fourths. Having then sought this motion on the limb of the meteoroscope from letter C toward B, we found it to end at point E. Then, with a thread stretched over the line AB, and a <term>bead<note>original: "margarita"</note></term> fixed at 9 degrees of the same line, we expressed it with the letter H; for those 9 degrees represent the semi-diameter of the <term>trembling circle<note>The "circulus trepidans" used to calculate the precession/oscillation of the equinoxes.</note></term>. With the thread again extended through point E, I find the bead to touch point F in the area, where 8 degrees and 48 minutes are perceived. This, moreover, was the <term>equation of the eighth sphere<note>A correction factor added to the mean motion to find the true position.</note></term>, which, added to the mean motion of the same sphere, produces the common Auge, which is 5 signs, 0 degrees, 20 minutes, and 5 seconds; for so many degrees and minutes have the Auges of the wandering stars and the locations of the non-wandering stars varied from the time of Christ until the day of observation. By the same logic, seeking also the motion from Christ to Alfonso, I found the mean motion of the eighth sphere to be 5 signs, 0 degrees, 9 minutes, 11 seconds, 2 thirds, and 38 fourths. The Argument of the 8th sphere was 5 signs, 2 degrees, 3 minutes, 34 seconds, 2 thirds, and 4 fourths; its equation was 8 degrees and 4 minutes, which, added to the mean motion, creates a common Auge of 5 signs, 0 degrees, 17 minutes, and 14 seconds; for so much did the locations of the fixed stars and the Auges of the planets advance from Christ until the times of Alfonso. Finally, subtracting the smaller Auge from the larger, 2 degrees and 51 minutes remain; this residue indicates the progress of the Auges and fixed stars from Alfonso until the time of the observation. Therefore, that [residue] added to the longitude of Boötes represents the true place of the star itself at the time of the Comet, namely 16 degrees and 59 minutes.

### THE DECLINATION OF BOÖTES AND ITS
right ascension, as if they were already known. Chapter Two.

<margin>41.4</margin>
**F**IRST, therefore, the size of that angle must be investigated which is formed near the beginning of Libra <note>The autumnal equinox, where the ecliptic and celestial equator intersect.</note> by the <term>ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun through the stars; the central plane of the solar system.</term> and the great circle passing through the star Boötes <note>Also known as the Herdsman.</note>. This is represented in the following figure by the line A D. The process was as follows: the longitude of the star Boötes was taken in the <term>meteoroscopium<note>A complex sighting and calculating instrument designed by Peter Apian for spherical astronomy.</note></term> from A toward C, namely 16 degrees and 59 minutes, marked by point G. From point G toward B, the latitude was also counted as 31 degrees and 30 minutes, marked by point F. Then, a thread with a pearl bead stretched over F was seen to cut the rim at point E. The arc located between C and E shows the size of the proposed angle, which is 64 degrees and 34 minutes. With the thread and pearl now extended again over the line A B, the distance of Boötes from the beginning of Libra—which is 35 degrees—is presented. Now, by subtracting the maximum <term>declination<note>The angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator, approximately 23.5 degrees.</note></term> of the sun (23 degrees and 30 minutes) from the angle previously found, there remain 41 degrees and 4 minutes, which extend on the rim from C to I. Afterward, if the thread is drawn through I, the declination (which is located in the area) is indicated by the pearl near point L, which is 22 degrees and 22 minutes. The base A K contains 28 degrees and 8 minutes between the lines, encompassing the difference between the <term>ascensions<note>Right Ascension: the distance of a star measured eastward along the celestial equator.</note></term> of Libra and Boötes; when added to the ascension of Libra, these produce the right ascension of Boötes, namely 208 degrees and 8 minutes.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an arc and intersecting lines labeled A, B, C, D, and E. A vertical line from A is labeled "Latitudo Bootis" and annotated with "31.30". A curved line is labeled "Ecliptica". Points D and G are marked on the arc.</image-desc>

### THE ALTITUDE OF BOÖTES ABOVE THE HORIZON in the vertical circle. Likewise, the right ascension of the setting point and the midheaven at the time the Comet would reach the vertical circle, as though they were detected. Chapter Three.

**A**fter the declination was understood, the altitude of the pole at Ingolstadt, namely 48 degrees and 40 minutes, was counted on the rim of the meteoroscopium from C toward B and placed at the end of the letter E. The thread was soon passed through this and touched the declination of Boötes in the grid area, which occurred at point F with the pearl moved over it. Now, with the thread again placed over line A B, the pearl shows 30 degrees and 35 minutes, which is how high Boötes stands above the horizon when it touches the vertical circle, whether in the eastern or western part. The base between A and G gives the difference of the right ascensions—both of Boötes and of the setting equator—which is 21 degrees and 18 minutes. When this is subtracted from the right ascension of Boötes, it demonstrates the degree of the equator touching the horizon when Boötes touches the western vertical circle, which is 186 degrees and 50 minutes. Finally, by adding 90 degrees to this, the right ascension of the <term>midheaven<note>The point of the ecliptic that is at its highest on the local meridian.</note></term> is established as 276 degrees and 50 minutes.

### HOW THE DEGREE OF THE MIDHEAVEN in the Zodiac, and both its declination and its altitude above the Horizon, were detected. Chapter Four.

**W**henever that degree of the equator which is the right ascension of the midheaven (namely 276 degrees and 50 minutes) is found in the fourth quadrant of the equinoctial, it is necessary to subtract those same degrees and minutes from 360. The remainder, which is 83 degrees and 10 minutes, is then to be counted in the base of the meteoroscopium by going from A toward C and marked with the letter G. The thread should then be stretched through the maximum declination of the Sun found on the rim. Soon, from G upward to

<column-break/>

the intersection of the thread, 23 degrees and 21 minutes are encountered on the arc, which is the declination of the thread—specifically of the point of the ecliptic touching the middle. The pearl must be moved to this intersection of the thread and the arc G B, and the thread drawn over the line A B. When this is done, the pearl shows 83 degrees and 44 minutes. Taking these degrees and minutes against the order of the signs from the beginning of Aries, the 6th degree and 16th minute of Pisces (♓) is presented as the location of the midheaven in the Zodiac. Then, by subtracting the declination (that is, 23 degrees and 21 minutes) from the altitude of the equinoctial—which at Ingolstadt is 41 degrees and 20 minutes (for the sign of Capricorn is southern)—I recognize the remainder, which is 17 degrees and 59 minutes, to be the meridian altitude at 6 degrees and 16 minutes of Capricorn (♑).

<image-desc>A coordinate diagram showing intersecting lines labeled "Ecliptica", "æquinoctialis" (Equator), and "Meridiana" (Meridian). Values marked include "91.58", "44.58", and "23.28" for "maxima Solis decli" (maximum solar declination).</image-desc>

### HOW THE ANGLE MAY BE FOUND, which the meridian makes with the ecliptic, in the northern part of the east, with the comet occupying the vertical circle. Chapter Five.

**S**ince the distance of the degree of the midheaven of the equator and the ecliptic from the beginning of Aries was known from the previous steps, as well as the declination of the midheaven, it was easy to find the proposed angle as well. For it requires the declination, which is 23 degrees and 23 minutes, on the base of the meteoroscopium, marking it with the letter G. From there, imagining an arc upward toward B, and counting on that same arc the distance of the midheaven in the equator from the beginning of Aries (namely 83 degrees and 50 minutes) and marking it with the letter F, one then draws the thread over line A B and the pearl over 83 degrees and 44 minutes (which is the distance of the midheaven in the Zodiac from the beginning of Aries). Finally, by moving the thread from B toward C until the pearl holds point F, the thread demonstrates on the rim the size of the proposed angle—and this through the arc C E—which is 87 degrees and 17 minutes. There was no need to seek this angle specifically, but rather its opposite, the southern-western one; however, because a easier method of finding it was available, I preferred to demonstrate this one instead. Nevertheless, I will use its opposite in the other calculations, since the ratio of opposite angles is the same.

<image-desc>A small semicircular diagram on the right, showing an arc with labeled points A, D, and G. A sun-like symbol is positioned at point G.</image-desc>

### CONCERNING THE SETTING DEGREE OF THE ECLIPTIC and its difference from the true sunset, called the amplitude; furthermore, concerning the 90th degree from the ascendant, found by one and the same operation. Chapter Six.

**I**n this discovery, there was a need again, as in the previous ones, for the formation of a certain triangle to be called A B G. One side of this, A G, was the altitude of the degree of the midheaven above the horizon, containing 17 degrees and 59 minutes, as was clear from Chapter 4. The angle F A G was also established from the last chapter as 87 degrees and 17 minutes. Accordingly, counting the same number on the rim of the meteoroscopium, I marked it with point M. Then, holding the thread through that point unchanged, I computed 17 degrees and 59 minutes from A toward C and marked it with the sign G. Counting the degrees of the area upward toward B to the intersection of the thread near the letter F, I found 81 degrees and 15 minutes. Repeating these same steps from the contact of the meridian and the horizon in the southern part toward the west, I recognized the setting point of the ecliptic located on the horizon itself. From this, when subtracting that many degrees from 90, the space of the setting (or the <term>amplitude<note>The angular distance of a celestial body from the true East or West point at its rising or setting.</note></term>) appeared to remain as 8 degrees and 45 minutes; that is, the distance of the degrees and minutes of the ecliptic from the true sunset toward the south. Then, where the pearl of the thread would cut the segment of the arc G B, and the thread was again extended onto line A B, it was recognized from the bead that 81 degrees and 40 minutes were indicated. Taking this number and beginning from the midheaven in the order of the signs of the Zodiac...

Since it is established from the preceding sections how great that arc would be from the setting point of the ecliptic and the intersection of both the meridian and the horizon on the southern side, it should be immediately taken up again in the <term>meteoroscopium<note>A complex multi-layered sighting instrument designed by Apian for spherical trigonometry calculations.</note></term>. Having counted this from A toward B, I connect it with the letter L and a pearl; from this, I observe the altitude of the <term>equator<note>The celestial equator.</note></term> at <term>Ingolstadt<note>The German city where Apian was a professor; the text uses "In-folstadiani".</note></term>, which on the rim held 41 degrees and 20 minutes. ## ON THE OBSERVATION OF THE COMET
itself for the first time. Chapter Nine.

Now that sunset had occurred, when the comet appeared to be nearer to the vertical circle, taking the instrument called a <term>planimetrum<note>A flat sighting instrument used to measure angles on a plane.</note></term>, I first began to look at Boötes to see whether he was in the vertical circle or not. And since he appeared to hold the vertical exactly, directing the same sighting rule toward the Comet, I strove to find its <term>azimuth<note>The horizontal angle of a celestial object from a fixed cardinal point, in this case, the west.</note></term> from the setting point and its altitude above the horizon. This having been done, looking also at the tail with the same instrument, I imagined a certain point at its extremity, while simultaneously contemplating how much it differed from the setting point toward the north, and how great its elevation was above the horizon. This was the method of my entire observation, from which the following results presented themselves.

*   ¶ Altitude of the Comet above the horizon: 7 degrees, 56 minutes
*   ¶ Azimuth of the Comet from the setting point toward the North: 49 degrees, 26 minutes
*   ¶ Altitude of the Tip of the tail above the horizon: 20 degrees, 3 minutes
*   ¶ Azimuth of the tip of the tail, western and northern: 59 degrees

<column-break/>

I confess, however, that in the meantime I did not consider this comet before sunrise; and this was because on the 13th day of the month of August, when it was first observed by me, it was no longer seen as a morning star before the rising of the sun, as it appeared at the beginning. The cause of its disappearance will be learned very clearly in what follows; therefore, following my previous plan, I prefer to review the individual parts of the observations chapter by chapter.

## HOW THE DISTANCE OF THE COMET
from the western point of the ecliptic, and also the angle caused by this arc on the horizon, were first investigated. Chapter Ten.

The Sixth Chapter demonstrated that at the hour of observation, 14 degrees and 36 minutes of Libra <note>original: "♎"</note> occupied the west; in order to truly determine the distance of the Comet from that point, I add the Azimuth of the Comet (49 degrees 26 minutes) to the interval of the western degree which was 8 degrees 45 minutes. I note the sum of 58 degrees 11 minutes with a letter in the meteoroscopium, having sought it from A toward C. Proceeding from there toward B by 7 degrees 56 minutes (which was the altitude of the Comet), I mark it with the letter F. Dropping the thread through that letter, I observe its intersection on the rim near E, and I place the pearl at F. Finally, moving the thread on the line A B until point H is reached, I pronounce that point H represents the true distance of the Comet from the setting point. Likewise, taking the quantity of the angle which that arc of the distance just found creates with the horizon, and considering the arc of the rim G E, I see it to be 9 degrees and 19 minutes.

In the seventh chapter, the angle of the ecliptic and the horizon was also shown, namely 18 degrees 16 minutes. Connecting both of these now, the sum of 27 degrees 35 minutes arises. Repeating this sum on the rim of the meteoroscopium, starting from C and proceeding to E, I stretch the thread through the same E. Since the pearl already holds the distance of the comet on the line A B as 58 degrees 31 minutes, the same pearl at point F shows 23 degrees 15 minutes as the distance of the comet from the ecliptic, which may be called the northern latitude. Descending in the same circle as far as G, I show 53 degrees 51 minutes between A and G, which is the distance of the comet from 14 degrees 36 minutes of Libra <note>original: "♎"</note>. After counting these degrees and minutes in the Zodiac against the succession of the signs, falling upon 19 degrees and 15 minutes of Leo, I pronounce that to be the true place of the Comet in the ecliptic. This must be interpreted according to the line of our sight, for it is not presently the time to discuss how much diversity of aspect <note>parallax</note> might be caused in such a brief account.

How I achieved this more accurately, you shall hear in what follows.

## ON THE OBSERVED AZIMUTH AND ALTITUDE
## of the tail. Chapter 13.

<margin>c 36 E</margin>
With the conjecture now prevailing that the tail is generated by the Sun in the manner of a shadow, I could not neglect to examine this even more exactly; therefore, having set out with this purpose, I approached it thus. Choosing a point at the extreme end of the tail, I immediately collected its height above the horizon: it was, as before, 20 Scorpio <note>original: "♏"</note> 3; similarly its azimuth, which was 56 degrees North. To the space or amplitude of the setting, 14 degrees 36 minutes of Libra <note>original: "♎"</note>, I joined the connecting degrees, and 64 degrees 45 minutes were produced. That sum of degrees and minutes was then sought on the <term>meteoroscopium<note>A complex multi-layered sighting instrument designed by Apian for spherical trigonometry calculations.</note></term> from A toward C, and marked with point G. Now counting upward from G, I marked the altitude, 20 degrees 3 minutes, with E. Finally, the thread stretched through E cut the rim at 21 Scorpio <note>original: "♏"</note> 33 at point E; this is indeed the capacity of the angle caused by the horizon and the circle which is drawn from the extreme tail to the setting of 14 degrees and 36 minutes. After the pearl was set at the same F, and the thread moved over line A B, the union shows 69 degrees 10 minutes at point H, which I demonstrate by line A F; for the quantity of line A F must always be learned on line A B, as has been hammered home almost to the point of nausea until now.

## HOW IT WAS MOST CERTAINLY FOUND AT LAST THAT 
## the comet's tail is generated by the Sun. Chapter 15.

On the day the Comet was observed by me, namely August 13th, the Sun occupied 29 degrees of Leo <note>original: "♌"</note> and the twentieth minute, as the theory of the Sun then taught. Also, the true location of the Comet, known from Chapter 11, was 19 degrees of Leo <note>original: "♌"</note> and 15 minutes; so that the difference between the Sun and the Comet was exactly 10 degrees and 5 minutes. To this, the preceding chapter showed that the location of the extreme tail held 10 degrees and 57 minutes of Leo <note>Apian appears to be calculating the longitudinal distance here.</note>, from which it is also clear that the extremity of the tail was only 8 degrees and 18 minutes away from the true location of the Comet. With these things established, I imagined an arc that would pass from the Sun through the middle of the comet, and another arc drawn from the Sun through the extremity of the tail. Yet it was certain that both arcs drawn from the Sun—one going through the body of the Comet, the other through the extremity of the tail—are the same, since they make equal angles with the ecliptic relative to the Sun's degree. From this it follows again that a straight line which is drawn (or conceived to be drawn) from the Sun through the comet must pass longitudinally through the middle of the tail. If this is so, as it is, it is also concluded that the tail is caused by the light of the Sun, which matter we have discussed more deeply through this diligence. Counting from A of the meteoroscopium toward C 10 degrees 5 minutes (the distance of the Comet from the Sun), we marked the same with the letter G. Likewise, counting the comet's latitude (23 degrees 15 minutes) from G upward toward B, we noted it with letter I. Afterward, with the thread drawn through letter I, we saw point E shown from it. After looking at the arc from C toward E, we found 67 degrees 49 minutes offered as the quantity of the angle of the predicted arc—that is, the one imagined from the Sun through the comet and enclosed by the ecliptic. This done, from A we took the location of the outer tail distant from the Sun, which is 58 degrees 23 minutes, and having counted it, we placed the letter L. Then ascending from L toward B, we marked the latitude of the extremity (which is 36 degrees 44 minutes) with the letter F. From here, the thread sent through F was seen to cut the rim near point E, except for a few minutes which could undoubtedly be introduced by a fault of the instrument or by observations performed in unfavorable conditions. Therefore, since both those angles were equal to each other, it was absolutely necessary that the arcs drawn from the Sun—one through the Comet, the other through its tail—also agree and be the same. If this is so, the line going straight from the Sun through the body of the Comet must also be carried most straightly through the tail of the comet according to its length. Thus I am freed from all doubt; indeed, I am forced to believe, even against my will, that the tail must arise from the Sun. After this, connecting the union to point I, we moved the thread on line A B; having moved it, the pearl immediately at point H showed the difference of the Sun and the comet, namely 25 degrees 14 minutes. Finally, fixing the union over F, we learned at point M on line A B (at a distance from A of 40 degrees 20 minutes) the difference between the tail's extremity and the Sun. Subtracting the difference of the Sun and comet from 40 degrees and 29 minutes, the remaining 15 degrees 15 minutes were reached: the truest length of the whole tail.

<image-desc>A small triangular diagram showing "angle", "67.49", and "distance 3.14".</image-desc>

<image-desc>A larger triangular diagram depicting the relationship between the comet's distance from the sun and its tail. Labels include "distance of the comet from the Sun", "3.14", "angle", "67.49", "Ecliptic", "Latitude", "36.44", "11.15", and "15.15".</image-desc>

Furthermore, someone might perhaps wonder how it happened that, since the tail arose from the Sun, it nevertheless turned upward, rather than downward and resting upon the earth; regarding which matter, so that it may be clear even to the unlearned, it seemed fit to subjoin such an image, in which the matter is placed before the eyes without the need for speculation.

->ASTRONOMY OF THE CAESARS<-

### ON THE HIDING AND APPEARANCE
#### of the Comet. Chapter sixteen.

Although I first saw the Comet on the 13th of August, there is no lack of those who claim to have seen it on the sixth and seventh. In truth, it was seen by everyone in the west and by a few in the east. It is certainly impossible that it happened otherwise, even if it did not appear to everyone, for it did not cease to be seen in the morning many days after its first rising, for the reason that it hastened more and more toward its cosmic rising <note>A "cosmic rising" occurs when a celestial body rises at the same time as the Sun, making it difficult to see due to the Sun's glare.</note>. For on the 18th day, as can be seen in the following records, it began to rise with the Sun itself; therefore, on the 13th day, it was already too close to the Sun to be easily perceived while the Sun was preparing to rise. From this, it happened that many of the less experienced thought this was a different comet, as if there were two—one in the east and another in the west—not knowing that a comet, no differently than any other star, can appear at both rising and setting. This same error misled Matteo Palmieri of Florence in his *Chronicles*, where he asserted there were two comets in January in the year of Christ 729 <note>Matteo Palmieri (1406–1475) was a Florentine humanist; the reference to 729 AD likely refers to a historical entry in his chronological works.</note>, one preceding the Sun and the other following it, when in reality there were not two, but one and the same, shining now before and now after the Sun for the reason I have stated. 

But to the matter at hand: when the Sun occupied the 29th degree of Leo, it set at 6 hours and 54 minutes after noon; the Comet, however, set at 9 hours and 55 minutes, if its declination and right ascension are considered. From this, it is clear that the Sun was below the horizon for 10 hours and 12 minutes, and the Comet for 4 hours and 10 minutes, whose rising therefore ought to have been 2 hours and 10 minutes after midnight. When I speak of the rising and setting of the comet, however, I do not wish you to understand that I saw it through instruments at the exact moment it touched the horizon; for its declination and right ascension, once known, suggest that abundantly. Even if I had attempted to do so by instrument, it could by no means have been accomplished; for whenever it came closer to the horizon by an interval of 3 or 4 <margin>Pliny’s opinion on the setting of the Comet</margin> degrees, its flame seemed to be entirely extinguished, so much so that for some time I believed it was hidden by clouds, until Pliny reminded me in his *Natural History*, Book 2, Chapter 25: *Comets are never in the setting part of the sky*, that is, they never appear there. For that is the genuine understanding of Pliny, if I am not mistaken, which I also more willingly admit because I have found it to be so by my own eyes. I shall say no more about the use of the meteoroscopium <note>The meteoroscopium was a complex observational instrument designed by Apian to measure the positions of celestial bodies.</note> now, but after the comet has finished its course, I will teach how to find the daily motion through the meteoroscopium as well. Let it suffice to have handed down this one method of observation so extensively and, as it were, part by part; for in the following sections, I shall propose nothing but pure observations obtained through the meteoroscopium. Furthermore, the following figures show only the altitudes of the Comets existing above the horizon at the time the Sun sets, and similarly how deep the Sun was below the horizon <note>original: "finitore," a classical term for the horizon.</note> while the comet was climbing above it.

### ON THE FOURTEENTH DAY OF AUGUST
#### the second observation of the Comet was performed.

¶ Altitude of the Comet above the horizon: 8 degrees, 29 minutes
¶ Azimuth of the Comet from the northwest: 45 degrees, 22 minutes
¶ Altitude of the tip of the tail: 23 degrees, 18 minutes
¶ Azimuth of the tip of the tail from the North: 57 degrees, 38 minutes

->The following results arise from the observation:<-

->THE CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY<-

<image-desc>A diagram at the top of the column showing the path of the sun and a comet across the horizon. The sun is depicted in several positions with rays. Labels include "Arctic Pole," "NORTH," "HORIZON," "REVOLUTION OF THE SUN," "RISING," and "SETTING."</image-desc>

->The rising and setting performed by the Sun and the Comet on the 23rd day of August.<-

->On the twenty-fourth of August, the Comet was still visible to me in some part, though not observed with the same diligence as before—namely, how the tail followed the Sun, which was the reason I undertook this method of observation.<-

<margin>
How the daily movement of the Comet is to be investigated.
</margin>
TWO things still remain to be sought through the <term>meteoro-scope: an astronomical instrument designed by Apianus for solving problems of spherical astronomy and tracking celestial bodies</term> for the use of the Comet: namely, its daily motion (that is, how much it advanced each day) and the path it described in its transit (that is, in which part it crossed the <term>ecliptic: the Sun's apparent path across the sky</term>). These two points, should anyone wish to call them the <note>original: "caput & caudam draconis" — the Head and Tail of the Dragon. These terms usually refer to the points where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic, but here Apianus applies the concept of "nodes" to the comet's path.</note> "head and tail of the dragon," would not be in error. Finally, in knowing the motion, we shall take as an example the position which the Comet held in the ecliptic during the time of observation on the thirteenth day of August, as well as its latitude, and similarly the positions it occupied on the 14th day. On the 13th day, therefore, the true position of the Comet was 19 degrees 35 minutes of <term>Leo: the constellation of the Lion</term>. Its latitude was 23 degrees 15 minutes North. On the 14th day, however, the true position of the Comet was 23 degrees 39 minutes of Leo. Its latitude was 23 degrees 2 minutes. The difference in longitude is now 4 degrees 14 minutes; seeking this difference on the rim of the meteoro-scope from C toward B, let him mark it with the letter D. After this, counting the complement of the smaller latitude, namely 66 degrees 58 minutes, from A toward B, let him inscribe it with the letter G and attach a thread with a bead to it. With the thread again over D, let him mark the free D; the bead shows the number at point H of the area, and the number H F is to be placed for the <term>cathetus: a geometric term for a perpendicular line</term>. This being placed, let the degrees from F be counted toward A, and the complement of the latitude subtracted from them will leave the quantity E F. Afterward, computing the quantity E F from A toward C, let him inscribe it with the letter F, as appears in the second quadrant; from there, ascending toward B and calling the quantity of the number H F, let him mark it with the letter I. Fixing the bead upon I, let him move the thread onto the line A B; for once moved, he will see 4 degrees 3 minutes cut at point K by the union—namely, the daily motion of the Comet from the first to the second observation. By the same reasoning, for those investigating the motions of individual days, they present themselves as follows:

<image-desc>Two small geometric diagrams in the left margin. The top one is a green quadrant labeled with letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G. The bottom one is a line diagram with intersecting arcs and lines labeled with letters A, E, F, I, M.</image-desc>

<margin>a</margin> ¶ From the 13th to the 14th day: 4 degrees 3 minutes.
¶ From the 14th to the 15th: 4 degrees 0 minutes.
¶ From the 15th to the 16th: 0 degrees 0 minutes. <note>This likely indicates a day where no progress was measured or observation was impossible.</note>
¶ From the 16th to the 17th: 5 degrees 24 minutes.
¶ From the 17th to the 18th: 5 degrees 0 minutes.
<margin>c</margin> ¶ From the 22nd to the 23rd: 3 degrees 40 minutes.

NOW for investigating the head and tail of the dragon, let the thread be drawn through I; from A toward C, let the greater latitude be expressed with the letter M. Then, ascending from M toward B, 84 degrees 45 minutes being found at point N, let them be added to the finished position of the Comet, which is 19 degrees 35 minutes of Leo. These being added indicate the "head of the dragon," namely the 14th degree of <term>Leo</term>, and the tail the 14th degree of <term>Aquarius</term>, and the "belly" the 14th of Leo. In the same way, the head and tail are found through any daily motion; although in this business a tiny bit of difference may sometimes occur, it is to be considered as nothing at all. Mention of this kind of operation will present itself more fully in our *Cosmographia*, where the treatment of finding the distances of places and degrees of longitude and latitude will be completed. Anyone even moderately skilled may easily perceive the position of the Sun below the horizon and how the tail was created by the Sun. For from the beginning it was seen inclining toward the North, and afterward it was bent toward the South, doubtless because of the velocity of motion by which the Comet surpassed the Sun, which was especially noticed on days 17, 18, 22, and 23, just as the subordinate figure shows most clearly.

<column-break/>

->the thirteenth. Then the fourteenth, fifteenth,<-
->sixteenth, etc., until it began to disappear,<-
->and almost the movement it performed daily,<-
->and how the tail, initially bent toward<-
->the North, was finally produced by<-
->the Sun toward the South.<-

<image-desc>A large circular astronomical diagram. In the center is the Sun (Sol). Surrounding it is a path of a comet showing various dated positions (13 through 23). For each position, the comet's tail points away from the central sun. The outer edge of the diagram is labeled with "Boetes" (the constellation Bootes), "WEST," "HORIZON," "NORTH," "Ecliptic," "Equinoctial," and "SOUTH." A vertical line is labeled "NORTH" and "SOUTH." A horizontal line is labeled "HORIZON."</image-desc>

But perhaps someone here will say that the daily motion of the Comet, its circle of revolution, and its head and tail are assigned wrongly, as if for something that does not possess a regulated path. This is because it was long ago perceived by philosophers and astrologers, and handed down, that comets are nothing other than earthly <note>original: "halitus" — vapors or exhalations</note> vapors or hot and dry exhalations, fatty and sticky, raised by the power of the stars all the way to the highest region of the air and there set ablaze; and that comets certainly do not have orbits, and therefore also lack regular motion. Indeed, I would not dare to deny that, yet since our Comets have been observed to complete a motion very similar to a regular one, and have not been snatched hither and thither in the manner of a bird flying in the ether, nothing should surely stand in the way of binding its motion to some rule. There are those, however, who say the comet is a subtle exhalation, not set on fire, but shining from the light of the Sun; we also agree with this opinion, since it is most certain that our comets are such a thing. This being supposed, it is not difficult to imagine the tail. However, I do not wish all Comets to be understood here, for there is no doubt that some are ignited by themselves, as we also mentioned in earlier sections. But as to what generates such motion in a comet besides the more violent snatching of the upper spheres, and especially the one closer to the Moon, I have nothing to say.

### OF THE FIRST POSITION OF THE SECOND COMET.

THE SECOND Comet shone in the eastern region in the Year 1532; it began to be seen on the 25th of September, and lasted until the 20th day of November, observed by me seven times and most studiously. FIRST of all, on the second day of October in the town of <note>Dreseno Missiae: Dresden, in the March of Meissen</note> (the altitude of which place is 51 degrees), at the fifth hour preceding the rising of the Sun. In which contemplation the Azimuth and altitude were found as follows:

¶ Altitude of the Comet above the horizon: 13 degrees 10 minutes.
¶ <term>Azimuth</term> of the same from the east toward the south: 24 degrees 30 minutes.
¶ Altitude of the <note>original: "cordis Leonini" — the Heart of the Lion, the star Regulus</note>: 34 degrees.
¶ Azimuth of the same: 19 degrees 22 minutes.

From these things, therefore, it was now possible to see truly whether the tail followed the Sun like a shadow; it was entirely established to be so, by this reasoning. The distance of the Comet, which was 38 degrees 2 minutes from the Sun, was plotted on the <term>meteoroscope: Peter Apianus's complex multi-disked instrument for calculating celestial coordinates</term>, namely from A toward C, ending at point E; from E upward, the latitude of the Comet was similarly measured as 10 degrees 12 minutes, and where measured,

<column-break/>

the letter I was placed. A single thread with a pearl fixed over I showed 17 degrees 20 minutes on the rim near point D; this was the size of the angle contained between the ecliptic and the arc drawn from the Sun through the body of the Comet. Here again, with the thread pulled to line A B, the pearl at point K indicated the distance of the Comet from the Sun, namely 39 degrees 10 minutes. After this, again from A toward C on the meteoroscope, the letter F was placed for one seeking the distance of the tip of the tail from the Sun, namely 53 degrees 3 minutes. Rising from that point to H, the latitude of the tip was measured as 13 degrees 8 minutes. In H, therefore, the thread placed with the bead indicated the same 17 degrees 20 minutes at point D on the rim as before; it was so clear that, since the angles were equal, it was necessary that the tail also be produced by the Sun. Finally, for one drawing the thread over A B, the same distance of the Sun and the tip of the tail was seen to be indicated at point L as 54 degrees 8 minutes, from which it was also easy to conjecture that the tail had reached 14 degrees 58 minutes in length, a more manifest understanding of which will be gathered from the next figure.
