## SIXTH OBSERVATION.

In our sixth examination of the Comet on the 1st of November, at the same location as before, we found the following:

¶ The altitude of Boötes: 26 degrees.
¶ The altitude of the Comet: 12 degrees 40 minutes.
¶ Its azimuth: 8 degrees 50 minutes South.

->The following details are drawn from the observation:<-

Right Ascension of the Comet: 207 degrees 33 minutes.
Its latitude: 14 degrees 42 minutes North.
True position of the Comet in the ecliptic: 23 degrees 57 minutes of Libra ♎.
Its distance from the Sun: 28 degrees 34 minutes.

That Comet first directed its tail toward the south; after this, it raised the tail more and more each day until today, when it was raised almost perpendicularly toward the Zenith <term>Zenith: the point in the sky directly overhead</term>. Without a doubt, it appeared after the setting of the Sun as well, though only slightly, as can be seen from the attached figure.

->Setting of the Comet. Rising of the Comet.<-

<image-desc>Two circular diagrams showing the comet's orientation and position relative to the horizon and sun at sunset and sunrise.</image-desc>

## SEVENTH OBSERVATION.

The seventh and most recent observation of the Comet was celebrated on the 8th day of November, at the place mentioned above, at 5 hours 12 minutes after midnight. Although the Comet persisted until the 20th day of November, it was not visible at all due to the turbulence of the air. This study collected the following:

¶ The altitude of Boötes: 25 degrees 40 minutes.
¶ The altitude of the Comet: 7 degrees 20 minutes.
¶ Its azimuth: 0 degrees 30 minutes from West to North.
¶ True position of the Comet in the Ecliptic: 3 degrees 35 minutes of Scorpio ♏.
¶ Its latitude: 19 degrees 36 minutes North.

In these days, the tail was moved quite clearly toward the north, and could be seen after the setting of the Sun, just as this figure represents.

<image-desc>A small illustration of the sun and a comet with its tail pointing away.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram at the top right showing the "Setting of the Comet" (Occasus) and "Rising of the Comet" (Ortus). It maps the path of the comet relative to the horizon and the sun's position.</image-desc>

If that MOTION is considered deeply, it shows how that Comet proceeded with a downward tilt and in a direct path, and how it cut the ecliptic at the beginning of Libra. I might rightly call this intersection the "head," just as the beginning of Aries is the "tail," and the start of Cancer is the "belly of the Dragon" <note>Apianus is using the metaphor of a celestial dragon to describe the nodes and arc of the comet's path, similar to how the moon's nodes were traditionally described</note>. Furthermore, the Comet is found to have declined from the ecliptic by 9 degrees 24 minutes. Moreover, it is also known how the tail of the Comet in the first days crossed the meridian transversely, forming right angles with it. In the following days, however, it gradually leaned more and more toward the meridian, until on the last day of its appearance, it lay exactly upon the line of the meridian, and that was while the Sun was making its noon. 

I am not surprised that many are amazed at this, because the Comet appearing in the year 1531 <note>This refers to Halley's Comet, which Apianus also observed</note> took a path diametrically opposite to this one; it initially lay upon the meridian, but finally caused right angles and transverse angles with it. The following figure clearly displays the daily progress of the present Comet and the emission of its tail from the Sun—now stretching toward the north, now toward the south—and the daily measurement through the signs of the zodiac.

<image-desc>A detailed astronomical map showing the path of the 1532 comet through the constellations Boötes and Corona Borealis. The curved horizon is marked, and specific dated positions are plotted along the path.</image-desc>

## OBSERVATION OF THE THIRD COMET

**T**he THIRD of the Comets appeared in the year 1533 in the month of June. Although it shone for many days, it was seen by me for no more than four; for I recognized very quickly that its tail was also generated by the Sun <note>This is one of Apianus's major scientific contributions: the discovery that comet tails always point away from the Sun</note>, so much so that it seemed I would be spending my efforts in vain as a more diligent observer. 

First, I prepared myself for the first observation on the 18th day of June, and there I immediately saw the Comet inhabiting 3 degrees 40 minutes of Gemini ♊, deviating 32 degrees north from the ecliptic, and sitting not far from the star called Algenib <note>original: Alchenib; likely Alpha Persei (Mirfak) or Gamma Pegasi</note>. Its tail was directed toward that same fixed star. SECONDLY, on the 21st day of the same month, having watched the Comet, I found it at the 29th degree 20th minute of Taurus ♉, at a distance of 36 degrees 20 minutes from the ecliptic, with its tail equaling 15 degrees in length. THIRDLY, inspecting the Comet on June 23rd, I found it at 21 degrees 30 minutes of Taurus ♉, with a latitude of 40 degrees 30 minutes from the ecliptic. FOURTHLY, on the 25th day of the month, the Comet was found to occupy the 15th degree of Taurus ♉, moved 43 degrees from the ecliptic. 

Indeed, that Comet was never able to set because of its proximity to the North Pole <note>original: poli arctici</note>; for it was so close to the Pole that it could not touch the horizon. In the first observation, it was 38 degrees from the pole; in the second, 35 degrees; in the third, 33 degrees 59 minutes; in the fourth, 33 degrees 20 minutes. It was visible around midnight and diligently followed until the rising Sun, perpetually inhabiting the same region of the sky, situated between the North and the East <note>original: intra Boream & subsolanum</note>. When the Sun was just about to rise, the comet held a position almost elevated to the meridian. The path of the Comet was furthest from the ecliptic
about <meta>Catchword: circa (around/about)</meta>

->ASTRONOMICAL CAESAR<-
->O III<-

<margin>A new motion of the Comet, and against the order of the signs.</margin>
It was moving near the beginning of Aries; for in that place it was a full 60 degrees away from the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the Sun's apparent annual path across the sky</term>. This location was the "Belly of the Dragon" <note>original: *venter Draconis*; a region in the constellation Draco</note>, whereas the beginning of Cancer ought to have been the Head and the beginning of Capricorn the Tail of the Dragon. But I know that this Comet will cause no small amount of disagreement among astrologers and philosophers because its motion is "against the order of the signs" <term>against the order of the signs: moving backward through the zodiac (retrograde), such as from Gemini toward Taurus, rather than the standard sequence</term>. For it receded out of Gemini, as is clear from the following figure. Nor do I know well enough how we shall extricate ourselves from this difficulty in this place, we who with one voice have affirmed until now that the sphere of the Moon revolves—and with it the sphere of fire and the highest region of the air—according to the order of the signs (which is from West to East). Yet it appears that the present Comet moved in no such way, even though it would have been more fitting for this one to move so than any other, seeing as it was further from the Earth than others, for it was at a very great distance from the Sun. For if it had been near the Earth and further from the Sun, it could not have happened otherwise than that it would have fallen into the Earth's shadow, and thus remained hidden. Furthermore, this question will also arise: whether Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> correctly defined, in the hundredth aphorism of his *Centiloquium* <note>original: *centiloquii*; a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy</note>, that Comets are distant from the Sun by eleven signs <note>eleven signs equals 330 degrees, placing the comet almost behind the Sun from the observer's perspective</note>. For the present Comet, detected by the first method of observation, was 66 degrees from the Sun; by the second, 73 degrees; by the third, 83 degrees; and by the fourth, 88 degrees. This distance was indeed most direct; even if someone should demand that it ought to be numbered from the true place of the Comet in the ecliptic, they still would not have saved Ptolemy's rule. For the true place of the Comet in the ecliptic was found to be 61 degrees 26 minutes from the Sun in the first observation; 68 degrees 30 minutes in the second; 78 degrees 23 minutes in the third; and 86 degrees 48 minutes in the fourth. The Sun, meanwhile, was found at 5 degrees 6 minutes of Cancer ♋ in the first; 8 degrees of Leo ♌ in the second; 9 degrees 53 minutes of Leo ♌ in the third; and 11 degrees 48 minutes of Leo ♌ in the fourth. From such motion, it will certainly not be difficult to judge 
<margin>The fiery and highest sphere of air is not carried by the Moon.</margin>
that the fiery and highest sphere of air is by no means carried along by the force of the Lunar sphere; otherwise, it would be natural for the Comet to be carried from West to East. Moreover, because its motion was almost regular, I cease to wonder that some have existed who thought a Comet to be a star of the kind that now approaches the Sun and now departs from it, and being near the Sun is not seen, just like Mercury. Although this opinion is invalid and contrary to all Comets, it is especially so for these five: for the more distant they were from the Sun, the less they were seen; and so they vanished entirely at a much smaller elongation—indeed, when removed sometimes by 30, 60, or 80 degrees from the Sun, or sometimes a bit more, as is evident everywhere in the figures.

The bottom of the chart is labeled "EASTERN HORIZON".</image-desc>

### OBSERVATION
### OF THE FOURTH COMET.

The FOURTH Comet in the series was seen in the year 1538 in the month of January, from the 17th until the 21st of the same month after sunset, raising its tail directly toward the Zenith <term>Zenith: the point in the sky directly above the observer</term>. Its true place in the ecliptic was 5 degrees of Pisces ♓, with a Northern latitude of 17 degrees, calculated in the neck of Pegasus. The tail encompassed nearly 30 degrees in length, though with a narrower width. In the morning, it was seen by no one before the rising Sun, from which it was distant by 32 degrees 30 minutes, a fact which the present image depicts.

### OBSERVATION
### OF THE FIFTH COMET.

The LAST of the Comets and the Fifth in number shone in the year 1539 from the sixth day of the month of May until the 17th of the same month, when it was also seen by me at the tenth hour of the night, standing 19 degrees above the horizon near the vertical circle, except that it was five or six degrees further South, situated at 17 degrees of Leo ♌, 3 degrees from the ecliptic toward the South, with the Sun being in 5 degrees of Gemini ♊. The distance between the Sun and the Comet appears to be 72 degrees, which is also quite inconsistent with Ptolemy's assertion. That Comet was very thin and somewhat faint, displaying a shorter and narrower tail, as will be clear in some way from the figure placed below.

->ASTRONOMICAL CAESAR<-

# CONCLUSION OF THE SECOND PART AND OF THE ENTIRE ASTRONOMICAL WORK.

Thus far, we have sufficiently explained the motions of both the wandering stars <note>original: *errantium*; the planets</note> and the fixed stars <note>original: *inerrantium*</note> as far as was possible. But if anyone should still hesitate, saying that they indeed understand everything as it has been stated and grasp all the calculations of all the motions according to the rules, yet still doubts whether or not things are truly so in reality—or rather, wishes to be allowed to perceive the same with their own eyes—therefore, my good friend, we have added this instrument. In it, everything is established by the evidence of the eyes. I speak of the instrument named the TORQUETUM <term>Torquetum: a complex medieval astronomical instrument used to measure celestial coordinates in three systems: horizon, equatorial, and ecliptic</term>, the structure of which is described first, followed by its use. For through this, anyone can, by themselves and without the help of a teacher, recognize any stars, whether planets or fixed stars. Indeed, it offers the most ready and absolute use of all instruments and is comparable to the very best. 

Now, what further benefit the First Mover <term>First Mover: the outermost sphere in the geocentric model that moves all other celestial spheres</term> first encompasses, or what further demonstration can be made beyond these things brought forth through the Comets and the Torquetum, will be spoken of more fully in our *Cosmographia* <note>original: *Cosmographia*; Apianus's famous work on geography and mapping the universe</note> soon to be published. In that work, I intend to describe the surface of the Earth at length (for it corresponds to the First Mover by a certain similarity). In that book, unless I am mistaken, every question that occurs in Cosmography will be elucidated and made clear with examples and figures. But for now, it has pleased me to place this instrument of the TORQUETUM as the conclusion of the work, for the reason that it encompasses nearly the entire technical ingenuity of this volume.

## THE CONSTRUCTION OF THE TORQUETUM DESCRIBED AS BRIEFLY AS POSSIBLE.

### FIRST PROPOSITION

->Preparing the Base of the Torquetum.<-

If you wish to build the TORQUETUM well—which is the most delightful of all instruments and the easiest to understand and use—first set before yourself a flat, square metal plate. It should not be too thin, however, so that it maintains a proper thickness (for it is hardly possible to make a well-durable Torquetum from wood that will not warp). The wider this plate is, the better it will be and more suitable for every use. Let it be exactly square, with no side exceeding the others. Mark the four corners with these four letters: A, B, C, D. We shall call this entire plate the Base of the Torquetum. Then, adapt a similar plate which likewise does not bend easily; mark its corners with the letters E, F, G, H. We shall call that the Table of the Equator, since it must also be raised to its proper height. This plate will be attached by its side B G to the side of the Base B D with firm hinges, so that the equator table can be tilted and inclined toward the base, and in turn raised from it. Its center shall be called K.

<image-desc>A schematic diagram showing the 'Basis Torqueti' (base) and 'Tabula æqunoctii' (equinoctial table) as two connected rectangular plates with a central pivot point marked K. The corners are labeled A, B, C, D for the base and E, F, G, H for the upper plate.</image-desc>

With both these tables thus prepared, construct a quadrant for yourself, of whatever kind you wish, provided it is not too small. For here, as elsewhere, the larger such instruments are, the better and more certain they will be. Divide it in the usual manner into 90 degrees. We shall call the whole quadrant A B, its center E. From B itself, count upward 23 degrees and 30 minutes, which is the maximum declination of the sun <note>original: *maxima solis declinatio*; the tilt of the Earth's axis, known today as approximately 23.4°</note>; mark it there as F. Then from B again, count toward A the height of the equator, which is the complement 

<column-break/>

of the polar elevation <note>original: *eleuationis polaris*; the latitude of the observer</note>, and write C there. Afterward, erect a perpendicular line from B itself; it will be equidistant or parallel to the radius E A. Extend it to whatever height you wish. And when you then place a ruler with one part over the center E and the other over C, and draw a line from the center, it will surely touch that perpendicular line at point D. You will now have the triangle B E D; the base will be E B, and it shall be called the Triangle of the Equator. Similarly, draw a line from point E through F, and it will touch the perpendicular at point G, creating the triangle E B G; it shall henceforth be called the Triangle of the Sun's Maximum Declination. This single figure places before your eyes all that we have described so far.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a right-angled triangle labeled 'BASIS TORQUETI' (Base of Torquetum) and 'AEQUATOR', with a hypotenuse indicating 'MAXI: DECLI: SOLIS' (Maximum Declination of the Sun). Labels include G, B, E, and F.</image-desc>

### SECOND PROPOSITION

->To construct and elevate the other table, called the Equator.<-

Furthermore, set before yourself again the table of the equator, and mark it also on the other side with four letters, so that above F and L, you place M over E, N over G, and write O over H. Let its center be K, as before. Divide this top part of the table through the center with two diameters into four equal parts, and describe the largest circle you can from the center. Then, having moved the compasses slightly inward, draw another slightly narrower circumference from the same center, so that you can write the number of hours in the interval between these two circles. Move the compasses slightly narrower still and make a third circle, in the space between which and the next larger one you may paint the quarter-hours, or degrees, each of which represents 4 minutes of time. Place the noon hour <note>original: *meridianā quidem horam*</note> in the middle between L and O, the hour of 12 midnight between M and N, 6 in the morning between N and O, and diametrically opposite to it, the hour of 6 in the evening. Having made this division of the equator into 24 parts, or hours, you will immediately raise that table with the two triangles made for the elevation of the equinoctial <note>original: *æquinoctialis*; the celestial equator</note>, just as we found at the end of the first proposition. Thus you will see the Torquetum elevated, as the following figure shows you.

<image-desc>A technical illustration of the torquetum base with the circular equinoctial plate tilted at an angle. The plate is inscribed with degree scales and labeled 'Æquinoctialis'. The base is labeled 'Basis Torqueti'.</image-desc>

### THIRD PROPOSITION

->Adapting the Zodiac according to both elevation and division.<-

The composition of this manner is as follows: first of all, establish two orbs of the same size and suitable thickness; their width should be such that they are neither wider nor larger than that interior or smallest circle of the equinoctial which contains the degrees or quarter-hours. You must divide the lower orb or zodiac on its side or surface. In this way: divide the entire circumference into 4 parts; divide each of these again into 3, and each of these again into 3. Then divide each of those into 2, and finally these also into 5. Thus you will have 360 parts or degrees. But do all this work secretly <note>meaning: draw light guide lines</note> so that they are not seen. Now finally, set before yourself the subject table and contemplate where you are to place the beginnings of each sign, and in what way you are to divide all the signs by five degrees. For instance, when you wish to mark 5 degrees of Aries in the Zodiac, take 4 degrees and 35 minutes.

<image-desc>A circular diagram with concentric rings and axes labeled A, B, D, E. Below it is written 'æquinoctialis'.</image-desc>

Next, if you wish to mark 10 degrees of Aries, take 9 degrees and 11 minutes of the equator, etc., according to the requirements of the table of right ascensions <note>Right ascension is the distance measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</note> which follows. The upper zodiac disc, however, should have only the Zodiac divided equally on its upper part or surface; it will hereafter be called the "upper Zodiac." Its division is the simplest and easiest of all, by which we first divide the circumference into 12 equal parts (which we call signs), and then divide each of those again into 30 equal parts or degrees. Once these are thus established, assemble both Zodiacs, placing the upper over the lower in this manner: Make two triangles for yourself, encompassing the capacity of the Sun's maximum declination <note>The maximum declination of the Sun is approximately 23.5 degrees, representing the tilt of the Earth's axis.</note>, according to the third proposition. Place them with the base—that is, line A B—upon the lower Zodiac, having first observed this one thing: that you draw a diameter from the beginning of Aries ♈ through the center to the beginning of Libra ♎. Then draw two other lines parallel to that diameter on either side, which will touch the inner circle of the zodiac wherever they may; there draw two oblique lines, and you will have a rectangle longer on one side, marked with the four letters A B C D. Then you will be able to properly erect those two triangles. Finally, place the upper Zodiac upon those triangles so that the upper Aries ♈ stands directly above the Aries ♈ of the lower disc; and you shall understand the same for Libra ♎, provided that Aries here occupies the highest altitude of the triangles, as is clear enough from the figures. Furthermore, because the Zodiac is composed of only two discs, it must be attached to the equinoctial plate by a certain pin <term>original: *clauo*; here referring to a central pivot pin</term>, which the Arabs call the *Alchitot* <term>Alchitot: an Arabic-derived term for the central axis or axle of an astronomical instrument</term>, in such a way, however, that this rounded pin passes through the very center of the equinoctial and the center of the lower zodiac, and the zodiac can be conveniently rotated upon it.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two overlapping circles labeled "Upper Zodiac" and "Lower Zodiac", with a central rectangular frame marked with points A, B, C, D.</image-desc>

# ## FOURTH PROPOSITION
### To prepare the Alidade together with the Crest.

When you are about to prepare the rule or Alidade <term>Alidade: a straight-edged rule with sighting vanes used for measuring directions or angles</term>, make a straight line upon the wood or plate and call it A B. Place C in its middle, and from center C shape a small circle according to the width you wish the rule to have. Furthermore, divide it with an oblique diameter E C D, which should nevertheless be intersected at right angles with the line A C B. Then draw a line parallel to A C from point E, as long as you want the rule to be, and similarly from D. We are accustomed to calling that line A C B the *fiducial line* <note>The fiducial line is the baseline or reference edge of an instrument used for alignment.</note>. Then make the rule of such a length that it exceeds the zodiac on both sides. Also place a vane <note>original: *tabulam*; here a sighting plate</note> with a small hole on both ends, so that they align correctly with the fiducial line. Next, make 4 holes in the small circle described from center C, so that the "crest" can stand there, which are marked with the letters F G H I.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>An illustration of an alidade or rule with a central circular hub and markings A through I. Text above it reads: "Alidade or Rotation of the Torquetum."</image-desc>

Furthermore, you shall fashion the Crest <note>The "Crest" is the vertical superstructure of the Torquetum that supports the latitude scale.</note> thus: first of all, make a small column with four supports, which are to be placed perpendicularly into the holes F G H I of the aforementioned rule. Moreover, above the column itself, upon the supports, make a small disc and divide it into four equal parts, that is, into four quadrants, in such a way that the diameter F H, dropped down to the rule, would fall directly into the center C of the small circle, and the other diameter E G, passing through the center of the crest, would be parallel to the fiducial line A B. For you should understand this as if they ought to be parallel on one surface, but so that E G passes through the middle of the crest; know also that this very E G is the Ecliptic <note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere.</note>. Therefore, the numbers of the degrees on the crest ought to be inscribed from the line E G upwards and downwards, as far as 90. Whatever is above the line E G is called "Northern Latitude"; however, below it, it is the "Southern Latitude" of a star or the planets.

<image-desc>A complex diagram labeled "FORM OF THE CREST" showing a circular scale divided into "Northern Latitude" and "Southern Latitude", connected to a 3D-perspective drawing of a structural support with labels "Support", "Column", and "Fiducial Line".</image-desc>

Finally, make another rule, a little more delicate and not as sturdy as the former one, but fashioned in every way according to the manner used in an Astrolabe. However, I would judge it advisable here that you do not make two perforated vanes <note>original: *pinnulas*</note> in this place, but only one with a single hole, the size of a single lentil grain; on the other side, however, erect a thin stylus, and at its summit make a bead <note>original: *nodum*; literally a knot or ball</note> slightly larger than the lentil grain. For I have found this to be good, not by chance but through frequent experience: that observations of stars are made quite correctly through small beads of this kind. The sighting vane with the small hole must always be turned toward the eye, but never the bead.

<image-desc>An illustration of a rule with a semicircular scale attached to its side, labeled "FIDUCIAL LINE".</image-desc>

Lastly, a semicircle must now be attached to the rule of the crest, and it should hang from two small supports or rods at a sufficiently large distance. You will experience the reason for this matter below, when you move the zodiac of the Torquetum here and there. Furthermore, make the semicircle hang so that the diameter L M N also hangs parallel to the fiducial line of the rule itself; whether it be a little higher or lower matters little, provided the circumference of the semicircle is divided into its 180 degrees. Let the numbers be inscribed from the letter P on both sides toward the diameter L M N as far as 90, and from the center M let a thread hang with a small mass of lead, as is evident here from the figure below.

# THE USE OF THE TORQUETUM

## THE FIRST PROPOSITION.
### How to find the sign and degree of the Sun for each day.

If you desire to find the SIGN AND DEGREE OF THE SUN, first make sure you consider whether the days are decreasing or increasing in length. Once you know this, place the <term>Torquetum</term> <note>A complex astronomical instrument used to measure celestial coordinates in the horizon, equatorial, and ecliptic systems.</note> upon a flat surface that is level with the horizon and not tilted in any direction. Next, place the compass upon the base so that the side of the compass is parallel to the line C B or A B, for both of those are meridian lines. Then move the Torquetum along with that traveler’s sundial <note>original: "horologio illo viatorio"</note> back and forth until you see the magnetic needle come to rest correctly and the side of the base A C is oriented toward the south; thus you will know the Torquetum is well-positioned and most fit for every use. 

Then, if the days happen to be increasing, turn that side of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The plate on the instrument representing the path of the Sun</note> which contains Aries ♈, Taurus ♉, and Gemini ♊ toward the Sun. If the days are decreasing, turn the other part which has Libra ♎, Scorpio ♏, and the remaining descending signs. After this, with one hand turn the lower ruler (the swivel) this way and that, and with the other hand move the whole zodiac until you have received the rays of the sun through the holes of the two <term>pinnules</term> <note>Small sighting plates or vanes with holes used for alignment</note> on the lower ruler. Next, look to see upon which degree of which sign the <term>fiducial line</term> <note>A precise reference or "trustworthy" line used for taking readings</note> of the <term>Alidade</term> <note>The pivoting sighting arm of the instrument</note> itself has fallen; that will be the degree in which the sun is on that day. Immediately look for that same degree in the lower zodiac as well, and observe at what hour and minute you find it; this will also give you the exact time in hours and minutes.

## THE SECOND PROPOSITION.
### Having now learned the degree of the Sun, to know the hour of the day from the solar rays.

<margin>on the circle of the equator,</margin>
If you also desire to know the hour during the day after the sun's degree has been observed, come now and place the fiducial line upon that degree of the sun, and turn the whole zodiac together with the ruler back and forth until the solar ray penetrates the holes of the pinnules; thus the degree of the Sun on the lower zodiac will show you the hour and minutes.

## THE THIRD PROPOSITION.
### At any hour of the day, to investigate the sign and degree of the moon.

First, make sure you find the hour by the first or second propositions, and thus (the hour being found) hold the zodiac unmoved. Turn the lower ruler together with the <term>crest</term> <note>The vertical structure of the Torquetum</note> toward the center of the body of the Moon ☽. If the Moon is too small for you to correctly discern its center, imagine it at least; and when you see the fiducial line <note>original: "ficulnam," likely a typo for "fiduciam"</note> next to the surface of the crest, take up the upper ruler. Turn its perforated sighting vane toward your eye, diligently observing how you may catch the moon through the pinnule and that small bead <note>original: "nodulum"</note>. Once you have done this correctly, the fiducial line of the lower ruler will now show you the degree of the Moon ☽ in the zodiac, and the fiducial line of the upper ruler will show the distance from the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The Sun's apparent path; the Moon's distance from it is its latitude</note>, either toward the south or toward the north.

## THE FOURTH PROPOSITION.
### To detect the hour, both of day and night, from the lunar rays.

Place the fiducial line of the lower ruler upon the degree of the Moon in the Ecliptic, and when you have thus directed your sight through the upper sighting vanes—or directly along the crest—until it reaches the Moon, then the degree of the Sun in the lower zodiac will show you the sought-after hour on the equator.

## THE FIFTH PROPOSITION.
### From some known star, to find the certain hour of the night.

Provided you have already learned and understood from the first chapter of the "First Comet" how you may gather the degree of longitude and latitude of any star that you already know, then place the lower ruler in the upper zodiac upon the degree of the star's longitude, and at the same time place the upper ruler in the crest upon the degree of latitude—observing, however, whether the star is in northern or southern latitude. Then 

<column-break/>

revolve the whole zodiac (with the rulers remaining unmoved) this way and that, until you can see that star through the upper ruler, or cover it with the bead of the pointer itself. Thus, immediately, the degree of the sun on the lower zodiac will show you the sought-after hour of the night on the equator.

## THE SIXTH PROPOSITION.
### Having first known a fixed star, to detect the true locations, according to longitude and latitude, of all the others, both wandering and fixed.

From the previous proposition, find the hour by some fixed star. Once that is found, you now have the zodiac set for that moment; keep it unmoved in this way, and turn the crest back and forth, and also raise and lower its ruler until you have brought the star whose degree you wish to know into the sighting vanes. Thus, the fiducial line of the lower ruler will show you the degree of the star's longitude, and the upper one the degree of latitude. At the same time, you will learn here whether it is southern or northern.

## THE SEVENTH PROPOSITION.
### To accomplish the same without previously known stars.

If you also desire to know the certain degrees of longitude or latitude of stars currently unknown to you, let it be that you have previously learned the true minutes of the hours, and that by a most accurate clock. At that hour and minute, move the degree in which the Sun is on that day (or even at that very hour), and you will have the zodiac correctly ordered. Then turn the upper ruler to whatever star you wish, and both fiducial lines will show you the degrees, both above and below, of both longitude and latitude.

## THE EIGHTH PROPOSITION.
### To arrive at the knowledge of any star, whether fixed or wandering, without the help of a teacher, by the aid of the present Astronomical [instrument] alone.

If by chance you know only one fixed star, and you set both rulers to its degrees of longitude and latitude, and then rectify the Zodiac, and así you wish to recognize a star or planet without any master: come, see that you seek out its degrees of both longitude and latitude from this "Caesarean Astronomy" of ours, or from the <term>Alphonsine Tables</term> <note>A famous set of astronomical tables providing data for computing the positions of the Sun, Moon, and planets</note>, or from elsewhere. Then, with the zodiac correctly established, move the lowest ruler over the degree of longitude of the planet or fixed star; place the upper one in the crest over the degree of latitude, and soon through the sighting vane of the upper ruler look at the bead which touches the star for you: the one previously desired in the heavens is now also truly found.

## THE NINTH PROPOSITION.
### To most swiftly detect the ascending degree of the Zodiac due at any moment by the present instrument.

With the Zodiac now properly located together with the crest, as the previous propositions have taught, direct the point N marked on the ruler of the crest toward the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferum," the "sign-bearer"</note> (specifically that part of the Zodiac which is seen to be elevated highest above the horizon). Move the crest together with the ruler back and forth until the plumb line occupies the highest degree of its semicircle. Now, observe the degree of the Zodiac which the fiducial line expresses on both sides from the 90th degree of the Horizon. If you add another 90 degrees to it, the rising or <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> degree results; if, however, you subtract 90—counting backwards against the order of the signs in the Zodiac—the setting or descendant degree is produced.

## THE TENTH PROPOSITION.
### To find the longitude of a region with prompt ease.

It is DECOROUS, Reader, that we approach teaching here and investigate by this proposition. For if by chance you have not seen the sky for some years: you might even be ignorant (which happens not rarely) where in the world, in what lands or places you might be, nor could you inquire of it; yet still relying on your art and industry—which, as the proverb says, "Every land nourishes"—you may desire to find this out from yourself. Here is the way by which you may find it most easily with a Torquetum of this kind. In the beginning,

# CAESAREAN ASTRONOMY

First, you must be well-practiced in calculating the lunar motion for any given hour. Whenever you wish to find the longitude of a region—whether by day or by night, provided you can see the Moon—propose a specific certain hour for yourself. Align the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The circular plate on the instrument representing the ecliptic</note> by the Sun during the day, or by a planet or fixed star at night. Once the instrument is properly set, turn the upper ruler along with the <term>sight</term> <note>original: "crista"</note> toward the Moon; you will find the true degree along the <term>fiducial line</term> <note>The straight edge used for taking readings</note> of the lower ruler. However, in considering the degree of longitude, the <term>parallax</term> <note>original: "aspectuum diuersitas," the difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight</note> can introduce some error, which may cause a mistake in the longitude of the place. Therefore, to avoid this error, the <term>nonagesimal</term> <note>original: "90 mus ab ascendente gradus," the 90th degree from the rising point, where lunar parallax does not affect longitude</note> must be sought above all else according to the preceding rule. Once this is known, the ruler should be directed toward the moon; if the degree of the moon is the same as the 90th degree from the ascendant, you are certain that the moon lacks any parallax regarding its longitude. In this way, you can also know the longitude of your place or town through the degree of the moon: first find the hour, as you know, then take the corresponding degree of that hour from the <term>lunar theory</term> <note>The mathematical models/tables of the moon's motion</note> matching the <term>meridian</term> of Ingolstadt. You should take the motion of one hour from the daily motion of the Moon. For as soon as you have the difference between the location found from the theory and the location taken from the Torquetum, divide it by the hourly motion. This product gives the difference between the meridian of Ingolstadt and the other proposed place. If the Moon's position found via the Torquetum is greater, it indicates the proposed place is further west than Ingolstadt, and therefore the difference must be subtracted from Ingolstadt's value. If the Torquetum degree is less than what the theory shows, it suggests the proposed place is further east than Ingolstadt, and so that difference in longitude must be added to produce the true longitude of the offered place.

### ELEVENTH PROPOSITION

->To find the rising and setting of the Sun, as well as the length of day and night.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a scholar in academic dress holding an astronomical instrument, possibly a quadrant, while observing a celestial sphere or globe.</image-desc>Wishing to recognize the rising of the Sun, place the lower fiducial ruler upon the degree of the Sun in the highest zodiac, and the upper ruler of the sight upon line E G. Then rotate the zodiac together with the degree of the Sun toward the east (ensuring the Torquetum is always aligned by the compass and correctly set before you use it) and turn it back and forth until it hangs with the lead weight in the semicircle over point P (which is the zero degree). Then see what hour the Sun's degree on the lower zodiac points to on the equator; that will be the hour of sunrise and the <term>half-night duration</term>. Subtracting this from 12 leaves the time of sunset and the <term>half-day duration</term>. Double the half-day duration and you will have the length of the whole day; similarly, the doubled half-night duration gives you the length of the night.

### TWELFTH AND FINAL PROPOSITION

->To find the hour of a star's setting or rising, and its diurnal and nocturnal arc.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'R' depicting an astronomer seated at a desk, surrounded by books and astronomical tools, gesturing toward a large instrument.</image-desc>Place the ruler with its fiducial line on the zodiac over the degree of longitude of the star or planet (though you have little need for the star's latitude here) and turn that degree toward the east until the thread with the lead falls over the middle line of the semicircle. Wherever the degree of the sun then stands, it shows you the hour and its minute at which that star rises. Proceed with the half-night duration just as you were taught in the previous proposition.

->THE END.<-

### A DIALOGUE POEM BY MASTER CHRISTOPHER STATMION ON THE COAT OF ARMS OF PETRUS APIANUS

Why does Peter Apianus now have new symbols, gifts not previously seen in his house? He stood out as the first glory of his kind, and thus received such gifts for an eternal name. Tell me, I pray, why is an Eagle shown? Because, just as the eagle does, he also strives to go close to Jupiter <note>Jupiter refers both to the god and the planet, as well as the Emperor Charles V</note> forever. Why does it fly high among the clouds? Because he scrutinizes the highest stars of the heavenly pole. Why are there only seven clouds? (For I see no more than that.) You may consider them to be twice seven. It is well; they are seven, for it could not be otherwise for an Apelles <note>A reference to the famous Greek painter, signifying great artistry</note>; he depicts the clouds in this way. These represent as many wandering stars of the vast heaven, to be watched by a man of vigilant mind. Why do the top of the head and the bottom of each foot shine with gold, while the rest of the bird's body is black? Because he possesses a genius more precious than any gold, and a mind to fashion learned things with his hands. If anyone wishes to learn these two things, this present book is enough and more than enough. What, I ask, does the golden crown added above the shield mean for itself? It is said to be the "Royal Star" <note>likely Regulus</note> of honor. For just as this glory stands in the adorned sky, so it wishes the honor to belong to the learned man of heaven. Truly, the highest insignia suit the highest studies; these gifts are not from a light spirit. Who is the author of this honor? It is God. Who is that God, I ask? Charles the Fifth, powerful in the Roman world. My mind correctly predicts one thing: but tell me, why do you allow a man of the earth to be a god? What forbids us to call them similar or even the same, since nothing separates these two except their location. This one rules the stars powerfully, that one governs all things of the earth; the scepters sing of the former, the scepters speak of the latter. Do you not see how both carry the arms of the Eagle bird, famous in both heaven and the world? Hence they are truly called similar to each other: one is the Jupiter of the pole, the other the Jupiter of the soil.

### A ten-line poem by Master Simon Minervius on the Eagle of P. Apianus, granted to him by the Divine Emperor Charles V as a family crest.

Why is the bird of Jupiter the image of the Apian family? Because Apianus holds many things in common with the Eagle from Jupiter. That bird hides its course beneath the clouds like a lightning bolt; he, swift, penetrates the clouds, the stars, and the poles. The eagle views the Sun with opposing rays, but he keeps his eyes fixed on the Sun and the heaven. The minister of the Thunderer <note>Jupiter</note> carries the chief of birds above the stars; Peter, you were second to none of the star-dwellers. How well the symbols given by the Emperor suit the reality; deny if you can that a divine power dwells in the Emperor's genius.

### ON THE COAT OF ARMS OF P. APIANUS, MATHEMATICIAN of Ingolstadt, by Marcus Tatius.

Jupiter was born, and taken away to Mount Ida in Crete, he had fled from his father's devouring ear; and while the Gaul <note>The Corybantes/Curetes</note> strikes shields and sounding brass, the Boy may cry in safety with an unheard voice. Behold, the Bee <note>original: "Apis," a pun on Apianus's name</note>, excited by the melodious sound of Benewitz <note>Apianus's original German name was Bienewitz, meaning "Bee-wit"</note>, flies near and ministers honey to Jupiter. After the victorious King Jupiter had driven his father from the ancestral kingdom, he spoke these words: "Having been made powerful in heaven by the gift of Amalthea’s milk and Benewitz’s honey, I shall give a reward to both. One shall be a constellation; the other, a watcher of the stars, let him rejoice to have placed the stars beneath his mind. He who was Benewitz shall hereafter be Apianus among the Latin people, his name being changed. And just as my bird, flying sublime in the clouds, looks back at the solar beam with facing countenance, so shall Apianus watch the ether with such a gaze, and open the heavenly riches by his own power. Hence let him bear his divine insignia from his art: the outstretched Eagle and the folds that wander through the clouds; let the seven volumes of the cloud denote the seven wanderers <note>The seven planets</note>, and let the Eagle herself denote me, Jupiter, the author." And after many centuries had slipped away, the Roman Emperor Charles the Fifth ordered these things to be ratified.

# A POEM BY MARCUS TATIUS, IMPERIAL POET

<columns>2</columns>

### ON THE EARLIER ARMS.

> Jupiter was fed in his first cradle with the honey of Apian <note>A pun on the name Apianus, from the Latin "apis" for bee</note>,
> And Jupiter avenged the Titans with the help of the Eagle:
> He makes the Eagle a star, and by a learned condition, 
> He makes Apian at the same time the craftsman of the star-bearing heavens.
> And so that the grace of such great things may flourish for a long time,
> He hallows that very Bird upon the helmet of Apian.
> Pouring himself and six companion Planets <note>original: "Planetas," referring to the seven celestial bodies of antiquity</note> in a winding cloud,
> He protects his head with an enclosed sphere.

### ON THE LATER ARMS.

> He had fed Jupiter before: now he teaches you, best Caesar:
> Both are worthy of being honored: Both are ready to give:
> The former [Jupiter] bestowed the Eagle, the Cloud, the Wanderers <note>original: "Errones," meaning the planets</note>, and the venerable Shield,
> And he contributed his own Arms to his nourisher.
> But through you, thrice-greatest Charles, with added gifts,
> The Honor of Nobility is added to what was offered.
> And with the gift of the insignia of the double-headed Eagle,
> You give the Imperial <term>Cæsariana</term> <note>pertaining to the Emperor</note> Arms to your Teacher.

# Charles the Fifth, by Divine Favoring Clemency, Emperor of the Romans,

Augustus, and King of Germany, Spain, of both Sicilies, Jerusalem, Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia etc., Archduke of Austria. Duke of Burgundy, Brabant etc. Count of Habsburg, Flanders, Tyrol etc. To our faithful and beloved Peter Apian, also known as Benewitz <note>Benewitz was the original German family name of Apianus</note>, Mathematician or Astronomer & our <term>Familiar</term> <note>original: "Familiari," a member of the imperial household or inner circle</note>, a continuous member of our household, our Imperial Grace and all good. 

IMPERIAL Majesty gains the splendor of true praise for itself when it bestows benefits upon worthy men, especially those endowed with virtue and devoted to perpetual study, and adorns them so that virtue, approved by such a great author, adds stronger impulses daily, and minds inclined toward it are more sharply incited by the proposed rewards of merit. Therefore, attending to the distinguished and famous gifts of your mind—Virtue, Talent, Learning, Dexterity, and knowledge and experience of many things—and considering that in presenting these, there is no less success than ease; also weighing those things which you have achieved above the common skill of men, especially in the art of Mathematics and Astronomy. To these, your singular loyalty and observance toward us and the Holy Roman Empire, and the grateful services which you can and ought to provide to us and the same Holy Roman Empire in the time to come, lead us, not unworthily, to decorate you with Imperial ornaments. 

WE THEREFORE, because of this your erudition, and so that you may henceforth be more and more useful to the State, and serve us all the more eagerly, have elected, received, and assumed you, the aforementioned Peter Apian, as our Mathematician or Astronomer & Familiar, a continuous member of our household, and by these presents do elect, receive, and assume you. 

This is so that you may and ought to use, enjoy, and delight in each and every pre-eminence, grace, prerogative, exemption, liberty, emolument, privilege, and immunity which other Mathematicians or Astronomers and our familiars, continuous members of the household, are accustomed to and are able to use, enjoy, and delight in by right or custom, all contradiction and impediment ceasing. Wherefore we command all and singular, Princes Ecclesiastical and Secular, Archbishops, Bishops, Dukes, Marquises, Counts, Barons, Governors, Captains, Regents, Guardians of fortresses, cities, and any places, Judges, Burgomasters, Consuls, Citizens, and any other officials and subjects and faithful beloved of us and the Holy Roman Empire, by whatever name they are reckoned, and of whatever state, grade, and condition they may be, that they have, honor, and hold you, the remembered Peter Apian, as our Mathematician or Astronomer & Familiar, and cause you to be had, honored, and held by others. 

And that they permit you to freely and without any impediment use, enjoy, and delight in all and singular the aforesaid pre-eminences, graces, prerogatives, exemptions, emoluments, privileges, liberties, and immunities, and cause you to be permitted by others. Also, as often as you come to our or their Dominions and Jurisdictions, together with servants, horses, valises [traveling bags], and all things, as often as necessary, and when requested by you or in your name, they should strive to provide safe and secure conduct, exacting no payment of toll, customs tax, or any other exaction from you, unless they wish to incur our gravest indignation, as well as a penalty of ten marks of pure gold, to be irremissibly exacted. 

In witness of these letters, signed by our hand and fortified by the hanging of our Seal. Given in our Imperial City of Ratisbon <note>Modern day Regensburg</note>, the twenty-fourth day of the month of July, in the Year of our Lord one thousand five hundred forty-one, the twenty-first of our Empire, and the twenty-sixth of our Kingdoms.

Seen by the Palatine <note>An official of the imperial court</note>

Seen by Naves.

### CONCERNING THE SAME APIAN BEING MADE THE EMPEROR'S MATHEMATICIAN. BY THE SAME TATIUS.

> Emperor Charles captures learned men with this art:
> He ennobles, enriches, hires, and adopts them into his court.

<summary>This page presents the formal Imperial diploma issued by Charles V in 1541, appointing Peter Apian as Court Mathematician and granting him noble status. The text is accompanied by heraldic poetry by Marcus Tatius explaining the symbolism of Apian's old and new coats of arms.</summary>
<keywords>Petrus Apianus, Charles V, heraldry, nobility, Imperial diploma, Regensburg, Marcus Tatius, astronomy, patronage</keywords>
